##### [Federated learning-enabled privacy-preserving framework for seizure forecasting and affective state analysis using multi-modal EEG-ECG data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-50003-5)

```
## Abstract 
Seizure forecasting and affective state analysis using EEG-ECG data play a pivotal role in advancing neurological and mental health monitoring. However, existing methods such as Fed-Transformer, Res-1D CNN, and Fed-ESD suffer from privacy risks, inefficient feature extraction, and high computational overhead, limiting their effectiveness in real- world applications. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes NeuroFedSense, a novel Federated Learning- enabled Privacy-Preserving Framework that integrates a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with an Attention Mechanism for accurate seizure forecasting and affective state analysis using EEG-ECG data, ensuring enhanced feature selection, interpretability and efficient decentralized training. The model leverages adaptive attention-based optimization and weighted feature selection to improve classification performance while ensuring data privacy.
Implemented using TensorFlow, NeuroFedSense achieves 99.54% accuracy, 99.62% precision, 99.34% recall, and a 99.46% F1-score, outperforming Fed-Transformer (97.10% accuracy), Res-1D CNN (81.62% accuracy), and FML (99.10% accuracy). The ROC-AUC score of 0.99 further establishes its superiority over competing models.
Additionally, the federated approach reduces energy consumption per node by 30% and optimizes communication efficiency by minimizing data transmission by 15% over 100 rounds. By ensuring high accuracy, improved privacy, reduced computational overhead, and enhanced energy efficiency, NeuroFedSense sets a new benchmark for decentralized, real-time seizure prediction and affective state monitoring. These findings underscore its potential for deployment in intelligent, privacy-preserving healthcare applications, addressing critical challenges in remote neurological monitoring.

## Introduction

Epileptic seizures are unpredictable neurological events that have a direct impact on the quality of life of the individuals. Predicting epileptic seizures with physiological data, which includes EEG and ECG, is performed early to carry out the necessary interventions and to enhance the level of patient safety. Also, recent clinical and cohort- based studies portray a considerable correlation between emotional stress and anxiety with seizure susceptibility, in which neurophysiological modifications of stress, e.g. autonomic imbalance and cortical excitability, make a contribution to the onset and intensity of seizures (Muralidharan et al., 2025; Perez-Sanchez et al., 2024; Thakare and Ranawat, 2024; Islam et al., 2024; Kamakshi and Rengararaj Massive observational studies also suggest that new emotional dysregulation is the preictal in a large percentage of patients, which supports the practicality of considering affective biomarkers in seizure prediction systems. Federated Learning (FL) presents a hopeful approach by supporting collaborative model training from multiple institutions or devices without raw data sharing, maintaining privacy and enhancing prediction accuracy. Most current seizure prediction models are built using centralized Deep Learning (DL) architectures and demand large labeled data from diverse sources (Ayus & Jena, 2025; Gahlan & Sethia, 2024; Grubov et al., 2024). Yet, centralization methods create vital privacy threats and it is impractical because of data-sharing limitations within healthcare environments.
Moreover, most of the existing methods fail to considerate affective state analysis, which can give valuable insights to the emotional triggers related to seizures. Standard DL architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), tend to find it difficult to learn long-range dependencies in time- series physiological data, which in turn results in poor performance. To address these issues, this study proposed NeuroFedSense, FL-Enabled Privacy-Preserving Framework for Seizure Prediction and Affective State Analysis with multi-modal EEG-ECG data. NeuroFedSense can protect data privacy through the use of federated learning and make precise and reliable predictions. Further, the study also suggests the correlation that has been previously found among seizure activities and emotional distress and recommends counseling as a possible intervention measure. Unlike recurrent models, TCN-based architectures are more scalable and more efficient in time modeling, which makes them more appropriate to continuous analysis of EEG-ECG signals.
1.1 Research Motivation The issue of seizure prediction is one of the most important in neurological studies because the process of epileptic activity is unpredictable in nature. Previously existing methods (mainly before 2022), like traditional machine learning models (e.g. Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests (RF), and early deep learning architectures (e.g. CNNs and RNNs), were mostly single-modal EEG-based methods. These approaches gave little attention to multimodal physiological integration and they did not take into consideration the dynamics of affective state like stress and anxiety. Even though the recent research has delved into multimodal EEG-ECG fusion, transformer-based architectures, the combination of both physiological and affective signals is still disjointed and lacking in integrated modeling formats. Therefore, a significant gap in the creation of integrated models to analyze both neurological and emotional biomarkers to predict seizures better exists.
1.2 Significance of the Study This paper reveals a statistically significant correlation between the emotional conditions and the events of seizures, which indicates the possible importance of the affective biomarkers in enhancing the prediction of the seizures.With TCN coupled with Attention Mechanism, the model is able to adequately grasp temporal relationships in EEG-ECG data. In contrast to traditional methods, this study identifies a causal relationship between seizure events and emotional states, indicating counseling's potential as a pre-emptive intervention. The results carry far-reaching implications in terms of personalized epilepsy care, early seizure prevention, and privacy-centered AI application in medicine. The hypothesis of the study is that the ability to predict the onset of a seizure with the help of affective state indicators (e.g., stress and anxiety based on EEG-ECG measurements) in comparison to the models that involve the use of neurological signals exclusively can greatly enhance the quality of prediction.
1.3 Problem Statement Although machine learning and deep learning have made progress in seizure detection, most of the current methods are based on a centralized training paradigm which by default exposes sensitive medical information and thus limits their use to a clinical setting. Although privacy-preserving solutions like differential privacy and homomorphic encryption have been proposed, they still demand computationally expensive implementation into large-scale multimodal medical systems and are sufficiently computationally limited to make a practical implementation feasible.
Specifically, in Federated Learning (FL) setups, there exist difficulties in entrusting privacy assurances, effectiveness of communication, and model effectiveness of processing heterogeneous EEG-ECG data. Thus, the research weakness, the focus of this paper, in particular, relates to the absence of an effective, scalable, and privacy-sensitive framework, which will incorporate multimodal physiological and affective responses into a federated environment. In this paper, two predictive tasks are defined: seizure prediction and affective state prediction: one independent and the other dependent. Although both tasks share common multimodal EEG-ECG input, they are differentiated by their goal of prediction: a seizure forecast predicts neural preictal patterns, whereas an affective state predicts neural emotional and autonomic changes, e.g. stress and anxiety. To prevent the situation of ambiguity, proposed framework models these tasks as the part of the ordered multi-task learning paradigm, which allows the shared representation learning and the task-specific prediction.
1.4 Recent Innovation and Challenges Some of the recent developments in AI for healthcare include the use of self-supervised learning for EEG feature extraction, Transformer models for time-series forecasting, and FL for privacy-preserving medical AI applications.
However, challenges still remain, such as data heterogeneity between institutions, computational expense of deep models, and the demand for interpretable AI in medical decision support. Additionally, existing FL frameworks are not equipped to deal with unbalanced medical information and dynamic patient conditions, so new architectures must be designed that improve model adaptability, stability, and clinical applicability.
1.5 Key Contributions of the Study  FL-Based Seizure Forecasting and Affective State Analysis: NeuroFedSense introduces a privacy-preserving FL framework for seizure prediction and affective state analysis from multi-modal EEG-ECG data.
 TCN with Attention Mechanism for Enhanced Temporal Feature Extraction: The method employs TCN with attention to achieve improved seizure prediction and stress analysis.
 Privacy-Preserving and Decentralized Learning: NeuroFedSense ensures patient data confidentiality by decentralizing model training on various edge devices, thus removing data security risks.
Hypothesis-Based Modelling of Seizure-Emotion Interaction: The researchers develop and support a hypothesis of the relationship between alterations in affective state and the onset of a seizure, which allows interpretable clinical findings and proactive intervention measures.
Unlike the current methods that mainly emphasize on integrating the common deep learning architectures, the proposed method, NeuroFedSense, has a number of methodological advances. First, it uses an attention-guided multimodal fusion mechanism, which adapts EEG and ECG weights in real time on the basis of time relevance, eliminating constraints of early and late fusion strategies. Second, it incorporates affective state modeling as part of the seizure prediction pipeline in a federated learning setting, which allows jointly learning neurological and emotional biomarkers. Third, a hybrid approach to feature selection is offered, integrating domain knowledge, statistical filtering, and attention-based weighting to make it more interpretable and efficient. In addition, the framework proposes a federated optimization architecture, which is privacy-efficient and minimizes communication overhead and energy consumption, at the same time maintaining data confidentiality. Lastly, the Bayesian probabilistic formulation is added to form predictions of the effect of affective states on the risk of seizure, to give clinically interpretable information as opposed to the traditional black-box forecasts.

## Discussion

The proposed NeuroFedSense framework exhibits the potential of privacy-focused DL in medicine by facilitating FL- Enabled Privacy-Preserving Seizure Forecasting and Affective State Analysis. By incorporating TCN and an attention mechanism, NeuroFedSense can efficiently learn meaningful temporal patterns from EEG-ECG signals, resulting in precise seizure prediction and affective state analysis. The FL paradigm facilitates decentralized training on various edge devices while maintaining patient privacy and model performance. This decentralized methodology overcomes the conventional data-sharing issues, making the proposed model a suitable option for clinical and telemedicine applications in real-world settings. Additionally, the framework provides enhanced patient monitoring by associating seizure onset predictions with affective states, facilitating proactive intervention measures that enhance the quality of care.

In addition, the study underscores the pivotal interaction between affective states and physiological signals, justifying multi-modal data fusion in clinical AI applications. Experimental results provide strong evidence of critical performance improvements over centralized learning methods, demonstrating robustness in seizure prediction and affective state estimation. However, despite its merits, the provided model does not directly address personalized model adaptation to patient-specific variance. Furthermore, the framework's dependence on stable network connectivity for FL synchronization poses practical issues in remote healthcare settings. Future development should aim at adaptive FL methods and personalized federated optimization to overcome these shortcomings while enhancing real-time inference efficiency.

## Conclusion and Future Work

Low-latency real-time performance is also attained by the framework; hence it can be applied to clinical condition where quick seizure detection and intervention are needed. The study successfully meets its objectives using real-time seizure prediction and affective state monitoring without invading data privacy. Integration of TCN with an attention mechanism significantly enhances feature extraction to enable improved temporal pattern detection. This advancement provides better prediction results than traditional approaches. Experimental results illustrate significant performance, validating the efficacy of NeuroFedSense for seizure prediction and affective state estimation. The results further show an easily identifiable correlation between seizure-prone patients and mood states caused by stress, presenting the possibility of integrative treatment approaches for patients with physical and also psychological facets. The current study is performed in controlled experimental conditions and with a limited diversity of datasets, which makes the study high in accuracy and high in AUC values. These can help to give optimistic performance estimates. Subsequent studies will place more focus on cross dataset validation, incorporation of more diverse patient groups and intensive real world testing to further confirm the scalability and generalizability of the NeuroFedSense framework.
Irrespective of its innovations, this research has some limitations which should be solved to apply it in practice clinics.
The federated learning synchronization that depends on a stable network connection can be a problem in remote or resource-limited healthcare settings. To alleviate this, future efforts will consider asynchronous federated learning and edge based model updating techniques, whereby local models may run on their own and synchronize with each other at regular intervals and not rely on a persistent connection. Besides, other communication-efficient methods like model compression and update sparsification can also reduce network load.The other limitation is a failure to adapt individually to the variability of patients, the existing framework uses models that have been aggregated on a global basis. To solve this, the future research will be directed to personalized federated learning methods, such as client- specific fine-tuning, clustered federated learning, and meta-learning-based adaptation. They have potential to allow the model to better represent patient-specific physiological patterns, and allow more accurate prediction of diverse clinical profiles with rare epilepsy subtypes. Although the dataset applied in the current study considers multimodal EEG-ECG measurements with variability in subjects, complete large-scale validation in diverse populations is one of the key directions in the future. The next steps to increase the strength and applicability of the proposed NeuroFedSense framework will be to increase the dataset size and number of subjects, extend the recording time, and multi-centers clinical data.
```
##### [External validation of ECG artificial intelligence for emergency and cardiac assessment across a large-scale U.S. healthcare system](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02682-7)

```
## Abstract

An ECG-based artificial intelligence (AI) model was previously developed to generate ten digital biomarkers for emergency and cardiac assessment and is currently deployed in clinical practice in Korea (ECG Buddy, ARPI Inc.). Its external validity within U.S. healthcare settings has not been established. This study evaluated model performance using a large-scale, multi-center U.S. dataset via the Mayo Clinic Platform (MCP) Discover. Two validation cohorts were assessed: an emergency-diagnosis cohort (mortality, AMI, STEMI and equivalents, hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema) using initial ED ECGs, and a cardiac-function cohort (left and right ventricular systolic dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, hemodynamically significant pericardial effusion) anchored to echocardiography or right-heart catheterization. The primary objective was non-inferiority of the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) relative to prespecified benchmarks. Across ten target conditions, AUCs ranged from 0.883 to 0.949; all met non-inferiority criteria. Performance was consistent across sex and age strata. In a paired subset (_N_ = 1368), ECG-AI outperformed initial troponin T for AMI (AUC 0.920 vs. 0.878) and STEMI equivalents (AUC 0.932 vs. 0.736; all _P_ < 0.001). These findings support the model’s potential for ECG-based screening and triage, and provide a foundation for prospective evaluation of calibration, clinical integration, and impact across diverse populations.

## Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) applications in electrocardiography (ECG) have expanded rapidly across diverse clinical domains and are increasingly being evaluated for real-world deployment. Prior studies have reported that ECG-based AI can identify a range of acute and chronic conditions, including acute myocardial infarction (AMI), cardiac dysfunction/heart failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), and hyperkalemia, with promising diagnostic discrimination [1–5].
ECG Buddy® (EB) is an ECG-AI system that analyzes standard 12-lead ECG to classify cardiac rhythms and generate ten digital biomarker scores intended to estimate the likelihood of time-sensitive emergency conditions and cardiac functional abnormalities [6–15]. EB has been deployed in multiple regional emergency medical centers in Korea, and prior studies have reported its performance for several clinically relevant targets, including myocardial infarction, cardiac dysfunction, and hyperkalemia [6–15].
Nevertheless, the underlying model has an inherent limitation: it was originally developed and trained using data from a single hospital in Korea. Although the model has been evaluated in additional domestic and international datasets, systematic external validation across independent health systems remains essential, particularly when clinical workflows, ECG acquisition and formatting, and patient case mix differ from the development setting.
We therefore hypothesized that EB’s digital biomarkers would maintain discrimination comparable to that observed in Korean population when applied to a multi-center U.S.
dataset. To test this hypothesis, we conducted an external validation study using the Mayo Clinic Platform (MCP) Discover, which provides linked multimodal clinical data and ECGs from Mayo Clinic tertiary hospitals and affiliated Mayo Clinic Health System (MCHS) sites. In this study, we evaluated ten digital biomarkers spanning emergency and cardiac-function endpoints to assess performance in a U.S. practice environment.

## Results

### Emergency Diagnosis Datasets

We identified a total eligible source pool of 253,069 adult ED encounters involving 151,748 unique patients across Mayo Clinic and MCHS sites (2020–2022, Supplemental Table 2).
Within this pool, 44.1% of visits occurred at tertiary referral centers and 55.9% at community hospitals. The median age at presentation was 65 years (Interquartile range [IQR], 48–77), 48.3% of encounters involved male patients, and 90.8% involved White patients. From this source pool, specific validation datasets were sampled for each endpoint as detailed in Table 2. In these specific datasets, patients with positive outcomes were generally older and predominantly male compared to controls. However, age was similar between groups for STEMI and equivalents (P=0.832), and sex distribution did not differ for pulmonary edema (P=0.649).
Cardiac Function Datasets The evaluation datasets for cardiac function were sampled from MCP-wide data spanning 2003 to 2022 (Table 3). Datasets for LV systolic dysfunction, RV systolic dysfunction, and pulmonary hypertension were balanced, whereas the pericardial effusion dataset included fewer positive samples due to the limited number of cases. Regarding demographics, positive cases were generally older than negative cases, with the exception of the pericardial effusion group, where positive cases were slightly younger (median 64 vs. 67 years, P<0.001).
Biomarker Performance Across the ten biomarkers, AUCs ranged from 0.883 to 0.949, and for all endpoints the lower bound of the 95% CI exceeded the prespecified non-inferiority threshold (Figure 1, Table 4). The highest discrimination was observed for STEMI and equivalents with AUC of 0.949 (95% CI, 0.931-0.967) and ACS with AUC of 0.931 (95% CI, 0.917-0.945), and the lowest for pulmonary hypertension with AUC of 0.883 (95% CI, 0.876-0.890). Results from an additional analysis restricted to non-pacemaker rhythms, aligned with intended use recommendations, are provided in Supplementary Table 3.
In the AMI evaluation dataset, an initial troponin T result was available in 1,368 (66.1%). In this subset, EB biomarkers demonstrated higher discrimination than initial troponin T for AMI and for STEMI and equivalents (Table 5). For AMI, troponin T yielded an AUC of 0.878 (95% CI, 0.859–0.896), compared with AUCs of 0.920 (95% CI, 0.904–0.936) for the ACS biomarker and 0.918 (95% CI, 0.901–0.934) for the Myocardial Injury biomarker (all P < 0.001). For STEMI and equivalents, troponin T yielded an AUC of 0.736 (95% CI, 0.699–0.774), compared with an AUC of 0.932 (95% CI, 0.911–0.953) for the STEMI biomarker (P < 0.001).
Subgroup Analysis Subgroup analyses by sex and by age (≥ 65 vs < 65 years) showed broadly consistent performance (Supplementary Table 4). Notably, the lower bound of the 95% CI for the odds ratio was ≥ 10.0 in all subgroups examined.
Estimation of Predictive Values To further contextualize clinical utility, we estimated positive and negative predictive values under a range of assumed disease prevalences (1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, and 50%) using Bayes’ theorem applied to the observed sensitivity and specificity at the operating threshold.
Across all ten biomarkers, the negative predictive value remained ≥97% at assumed prevalences up to 10%, declining at higher prevalences; the positive predictive value increased substantially with rising prevalence (Supplemental Table 5).

## Methods 

### Study Design and Data Source 

We conducted a retrospective external validation study using MCP Discover. This secure, cloud-based research environment aggregates multimodal clinical data including electronic health records (EHRs), physiologic waveforms, and imaging from Mayo Clinic’s integrated healthcare system, spanning 3 tertiary referral centers, 16 community hospitals, and 53 affiliated clinics across the United States. The primary objective was to evaluate the discrimination of EB’s ten digital biomarkers against prespecified reference outcomes. We hypothesized non-inferiority relative to benchmark Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) values established in prior validation studies.
Digital Biomarkers and Clinical Endpoints EB generates ten digital biomarkers intended to estimate the likelihood of time-sensitive emergency conditions and cardiac functional abnormalities (Table 1). Each biomarker yields a continuous score, where higher values indicate greater likelihood of the corresponding condition.
Biomarker performance was evaluated against prespecified reference outcomes chosen to reflect each biomarker’s intended clinical application. For retrospective validation, predefined refinements were applied to the reference outcomes for three biomarkers to ensure reliable labeling: Specifically, although the Critical Condition biomarker is designed to detect impending shock as well as cardiac arrest, we evaluated it using 24-hour in-hospital mortality as a clinically meaningful surrogate. In addition, the ACS and Myocardial Injury biomarkers were evaluated against chart-adjudicated myocardial infarction (ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction [STEMI] or NSTEMI) to minimize ambiguity in retrospective labeling.

## Discussion

In this external validation using MCP Discover, the QCG model underlying EB demonstrated consistently high discrimination across ten digital biomarkers spanning emergency and cardiac-function endpoints. AUCs ranged from 0.883 to 0.949, and for every endpoint the lower bound of the 95% CI exceeded the prespecified non-inferiority threshold. Discrimination was also broadly consistent across prespecified sex and age strata.

In addition, EB biomarkers demonstrated higher discrimination than the initial troponin T result for AMI and for STEMI and equivalents. These findings provide initial evidence that the ECG-AI model maintains discrimination when applied to clinically meaningful outcomes in a U.S. practice environment, though calibration and clinical effectiveness remain to be established.

Rapid screening and triage at ED arrival is constrained by incomplete clinical context and delayed availability of some laboratory tests. Our results suggest that EB has a potential to provide complementary, immediately available information at the time of the first ECG, particularly for conditions in which early recognition can change downstream testing intensity and monitoring (e.g., AMI, hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, and short-term deterioration). However, it should be noted that the present study was designed as an external discrimination validation, not a clinical implementation study. Clinical impact data including clinician adoption rates, alert override rates, effects on door-to-balloon time, and downstream diagnostic changes are being collected in ongoing prospective implementation studies and will be reported separately.

In the AMI evaluation dataset, EB biomarkers demonstrated higher discrimination than the initial troponin T result for both AMI and STEMI and equivalents. This finding should be interpreted in the context of clinical practice: initial troponin is not intended as a standalone diagnostic tool for AMI, and its diagnostic value lies in serial measurements and kinetic patterns. The comparison therefore addresses the specific clinical question of how much discriminative information is available at the time of the first ECG, when the initial troponin may still be below decision thresholds. ECG-AI and troponin serve complementary roles: ECG-based assessment provides immediate risk signals that can guide early monitoring intensity and testing urgency, while serial troponin remains essential for definitive diagnostic confirmation. Future prospective studies should evaluate whether integrating ECG-AI scores with initial troponin improves early triage decisions and time- sensitive clinical actions such as door-to-balloon time.
Beyond acute ED outcomes, EB maintained strong discrimination for cardiac-function phenotypes anchored to echocardiography and/or right-heart catheterization, including left and right ventricular systolic dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and hemodynamically significant pericardial effusion. This breadth is clinically relevant because ED and inpatient workflows often require both immediate triage decisions and downstream selection of confirmatory testing. In practice, a single ECG-based system that can flag both acute emergencies and cardiac structural/hemodynamic phenotypes could support more coordinated diagnostic pathways, particularly in settings where advanced imaging or specialist interpretation is not immediately available.

It is notable that the model maintained strong performance in a population distinct from the development cohort derived from a single Korean center. The reasons for this cross-population robustness remain unclear, although prior ECG-AI studies have reported similar transportability across geographically and ethnically distinct cohorts [19-23].

However, the validation cohort is predominantly White (approximately 90%), which limits the ability to draw conclusions about performance across racial and ethnic groups. Validation across independent health systems with greater demographic diversity is essential to establish broader generalizability. Further work is needed to clarify the drivers of transportability across populations, clinical environments, and ECG acquisition practices.

In clinical AI deployments, continuous performance monitoring and model updating are essential to maintain accuracy as patient populations, clinical practices, and data characteristics evolve over time. Regulatory frameworks such as the FDA's predetermined change control plans are evolving to accommodate iterative model improvement while maintaining safety standards. Future work should incorporate prospective post-deployment surveillance to detect performance degradation and guide timely model recalibration.

This study has several limitations. First, the validation population represents a single U.S. health system with a predominantly White population; generalizability to diverse demographics requires confirmation. Second, evaluation of certain biomarkers relied on surrogate endpoints narrower than their full intended clinical scope: Critical Condition was validated against 24-hour mortality rather than the composite of cardiac arrest, shock, and respiratory failure; ACS and Myocardial Injury were validated against confirmed MI only, excluding unstable angina and non-MI injury, respectively. Third, some operational endpoints were standardized for retrospective ascertainment: AMI labeling relied on peak troponin levels rather than kinetic criteria, and patients with prior CABG were excluded.
Fourth, the case-enriched sampling design precludes direct estimation of prevalence- dependent metrics, including PPV and NPV. Fifth, the study was not designed to assess calibration. Sixth, as a retrospective study conducted within an integrated health system, only patients with digitally available 12-lead ECGs were eligible, which may introduce selection bias relative to all-comers in the ED. Seventh, for endpoints requiring specific confirmatory testing (e.g., AMI requiring angiography, cardiac function requiring echocardiography), verification bias may be present if the decision to test was influenced by ECG findings. Eighth, detailed information on specific ECG device manufacturers was not available in the research dataset, precluding device-stratified analysis. Ninth, for pulmonary hypertension, the mixed reference standard combining right-heart catheterization and echocardiography may introduce misclassification bias, as echocardiographic estimates have lower specificity than invasive measurements. Finally, inherent retrospective biases including selection bias, information bias from reliance on documented clinical data, and verification bias from clinically driven test ordering underscore the need for prospective evaluation.

In this large-scale external validation using Mayo Clinic Platform Discover, the ECG- AI model demonstrated robust discrimination across ten emergency and cardiac-function endpoints, successfully meeting all prespecified non-inferiority criteria. Building upon this, future research will transition toward prospective clinical evaluations. Subsequent steps will focus on assessing calibration, decision curve analysis, and integration into triage workflows across independent, demographically diverse populations. Furthermore, leveraging federated research frameworks will facilitate these broader multi-site validations while securely preserving data governance.

##### [A self-supervised electrocardiogram foundation model for empowering cardiovascular disease prediction and genetic factor discovery](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72436-2)

```
## Abstract

Electrocardiogram (ECG) has been widely used in the diagnosis of cardiovascular disease (CVD).
Current deep learning methods for CVD prediction using ECG often lack generalizability and interpretability, resulting in limited performance. Here, we have developed a self-supervised Electrocardiogram Large-scale Foundation Model (ECG-LFM) through pre-training over ten million 12-lead ECGs from multiple ECG datasets. To enhance ECG representation, ECG-LFM integrates contrastive learning with masked language modeling in a self-supervised manner, enabling the model to capture both global contextual information and fine-grained patterns within ECG signals. It was fine-tuned to predict eight types of CVDs and achieved an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.930 from multiple datasets, which demonstrates improved performance compared to existing methods. The important ECG-LFM derived features (EDFs) are able to represent known CVD biomarkers, indicating the high interpretability of ECG-LFM. Applications of the EDFs in genome-wide association study identified 24 significant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (P-value<5×10-8, LD r2<0.01) associated with ECG, including 8 novel findings. The genetic causal effects of EDFs on the CVDs were evaluated by Mendelian randomization, indicating 2 CVDs and 4 EDFs having causal relationships. Overall, ECG-LFM provides accurate prediction for CVDs and novel genetic insights for ECG.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death worldwide, necessitating early and accurate diagnosis [1]. The most frequently used tool for CVD assessment is the electrocardiogram (ECG), a non-invasive and cost-effective technique that has been widely employed in clinical practice[2]. However, traditional methods for ECG analysis, such as the Glasgow algorithm [3], often lack the flexibility to capture complex spatiotemporal relationships in ECG signals, resulting in limited CVD risk prediction.
Recently, deep learning techniques have been used in ECG analysis, and have achieved superior performance. For example, A. Sau et al. employed a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict mortality and cardiovascular risk through ECG [4]. T. Tohyama et al. infer 5-year incidence of atrial fibrillation (AF) using 12-lead ECGs through a deep learning technique [5].
However, training these models requires manually labeled high-quality data, which poses significant challenges in terms of scalability, as obtaining such data is time-consuming. More importantly, these models lack generalizability for various diagnostic tasks and fail to fully leverage the rich information embedded in large ECG datasets, highlighting the need for novel computational strategies.
Foundation models have recently shown remarkable generalization abilities in various medical tasks by leveraging large-scale pre-training and transfer learning paradigms. For example, the Clinical Histopathology Imaging Evaluation Foundation (CHIEF) model provides a generalizable foundation to efficiently evaluate digital pathology for cancer patients [6]. In retinal disease diagnosis, the RETFound model has achieved excellent performance across various clinical diagnostic tasks through pre-training on a large number of retinal images [7]. In the field of ECG analysis, foundation models are also beginning to demonstrate their potential. For example, HeartBEiT [8] leverages a vision-based transformer to capture both the temporal and spatial features of ECG signals. Besides, KED utilizes GPT-4 to incorporate domain-specific knowledge of ECG signals by training on approximately 800 thousand ECGs [9]. However, these ECG foundation models still face common limitations. Firstly, while some recent foundation models like HeartBEiT have been trained on substantial datasets (over 8 million ECGs), the potential of models pre-trained on more than 10 million ECGs remains to be fully explored. Secondly, the predictions of these models lack interpretability, resulting in a fundamental barrier to adoption by cardiologists who demand interpretable decision support for cardiac diagnoses. Besides, they fail to capture the relationships between genotype and ECG representations from the pre-training, limiting their ability to identify genetic variations associated with ECG and CVD. Therefore, it is critical to develop an interpretable ECG foundation model that leverages larger datasets, provides accurate predictions, and uncovers genetic insights for various CVDs.
In this study, we have proposed the Electrocardiogram Large-scale Foundation Model (ECG- LFM), a general-purpose self-supervised framework that provides the foundation for various CVD diagnosis and prediction tasks. We performed self-supervised pre-training for ECG-LFM using over ten million 12-lead ECGs from two large-scale ECG datasets, the Harvard-Emory ECG Database (HEEDB) and MIMIC-IV-ECG database. ECG-LFM extracts the latent representations (tokens) from raw 12-lead ECG inputs by a feature encoder, discretizes the tokens to obtain the target context vectors and discretized IDs by a quantization module, and extracts contextual representations for each latent representation by an embedding module. Finally, ECG-LFM employs a multi-task learning strategy, combining contextual contrastive loss, masked language modeling (MLM) loss, and multi-segment contrastive loss to enhance representation learning. Our results demonstrate that ECG-LFM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predicting various CVDs in multiple datasets (PTB-XL, Chapman, CODE-15, CPSC-2018, and UK Biobank), and has achieved an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.930. The performance of ECG-LFM has not been influenced even if it is fine-tuned by a set of samples with a much smaller size. To enhance model interpretability, we further evaluated the contributions of ECG-LFM derived features (EDFs) in CVD prediction and detected the biological connections of EDFs with ECG morphologies through the perturbation-based EDF interpretation (PEI) method. The phenotypic relationships of the EDFs showing importance in predicting CVDs with 215 cardiac function-related factors were examined by the Phenotype-wide association study (PheWAS), indicating that these EDFs are significantly associated with 167 factors, especially the physical measures and the features of cardiac MRI. The genetic characteristics of the important EDFs were evaluated by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) that have identified 12 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (P-value<5×10-8, LD r2<0.01) at 11 loci. The genetic causal relationships of these EDFs with the CVDs were evaluated by Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses, indicating that 4 EDFs and 2 CVDs had causal relationships. GWAS for all 1,024 EDFs identified 8 new significant SNPs associated with ECG.
Thus, ECG-LFM is a highly generalizable self-supervised learning foundation model for ECG analysis, which has shown significant improvement in predicting cardiovascular diseases. Features derived by ECG-LFM have improved our understanding of phenotypic and genetic characteristics of ECG in cardiac abnormalities

## Results

### Overview of this study

Figure 1 depicts the overall workflow of this study. We collected ECGs from the Harvard- Emory ECG Database (HEEDB)[10] and MIMIC-IV-ECG dataset[11], leading to a total of 11,571,587 12-lead ECG records of 1,979,599 individuals (Supplementary Data 1 and Supplementary Figure S1) for model pre-training. By using this large ECG dataset, we constructed ECG-LFM, an ECG foundation model that captures intricate patterns of signals, providing the foundation for various cardiovascular disease (CVD) prediction tasks. ECG-LFM converts 12-lead ECG data into a series of latent representations (tokens) through a feature encoder. These tokens are discretized into context vectors and indexes (IDs) by the quantization module for efficient encoding. ECG-LFM then masks the tokens from the feature encoder and extracts contextual information from ECGs through multiple conformer blocks. The context vectors and the discretized IDs of the masked tokens were predicted by ECG-LFM using the contextual information from the surrounding tokens through solving a contextual contrastive task and a masked language modeling (MLM) task. To further improve ECG-LFM, two segments of ECG were taken as input and the multi-segment contrastive loss was used to learn consistent representations of consecutive information in each ECG (Figure 1A).
Once pre-trained, ECG-LFM was then fine-tuned for CVD risk and heart functional phenotype predictions (Figure 1B). The genetic and phenotypic interpretations of the ECG-LFM derived features (EDFs) showing important contributions in predicting risks of CVDs were investigated by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and Phenotype-wide association studies (PheWAS).
The ability of EDFs in empowering the identification of genetic variants associated with ECG was examined by GWAS for the top 10 components of all EDFs.
Pre-training of ECG-LFM provides individual-specific and disease-relevant ECG representations To investigate whether the pre-training of ECG-LFM provides ECG representations that capture individual-specific biometric patterns, we evaluated the performance of the pre-trained model on individual identification through linear probing. Briefly, from the feature encoder of the pre-trained ECG-LFM, 1,024-dimensional embeddings were extracted, which were used to characterize the individuals through training a single-layer perceptron. The extracted embeddings have achieved an average Top-3 accuracy (Top-3 ACC) of 0.65 in recognizing the individuals in Chapman and CPSC-2018 datasets (Figure 2A). ECG-LFM is compared to HeartBEiT [8] that is the only publicly available model generating the embeddings. The embeddings generated by HeartBEiT have achieved Top-3 ACC = 0.43 that is a significant (one-sided t-test P-value =3.81×10-22) decrease comparing to ECG-LFM. To visualize the individual identification performed by ECG-LFM and HeartBEiT, we randomly selected 100 individuals aged from 40 to 60 from CPSC-2018 dataset and characterized them by embeddings through t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) (Figure 2B). The embeddings generated by ECG-LFM are more well-separated with adjusted rand index (ARI)=0.73 than HeartBEiT (ARI=0.41). This result demonstrates that pre-training of ECG-LFM captures more individual-specific information from ECG than HeartBEiT.
To further evaluate the embeddings extracted from pre-trained ECG-LFM and HeartBEiT in disease relevance, we performed the cardiac arrhythmia prediction for individuals in the Chapman and CPSC-2018 datasets. The embeddings of ECG-LFM achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.885 and 0.891 in two independent test sets derived from Chapman and CPSC-2018, respectively (Figure 2C). In comparison, HeartBEiT achieved AUROC of 0.847 and 0.849 in these two independent test sets (Figure 2C). The superior performance of ECG-LFM was further substantiated by visualizing embeddings of cases and controls using t-SNE (ARI=0.33, Figure 2D). In comparison, HeartBEiT exhibited an overlap in the embedding space that could undermine cardiac arrhythmia prediction accuracy (ARI=0.12). In summary, these results highlight the superior capability of ECG-LFM in capturing both individual- specific biometric patterns and disease-relevant ECG representations.
Finetuning ECG-LFM for predicting cardiovascular diseases and heart functions To evaluate the performance of ECG-LFM in predicting risks of CVDs, we fine-tuned the model for predicting eight types of CVDs that are conduction disturbance (CD), hypertrophy (HYP), myocardial infarction (MI), ST/T change (STTC), ventricular ectopics (VE), sinus bradycardia (SB), atrial fibrillation (AFIB) and general supraventricular tachycardia (GSVT) for individuals from the PTB-XL and Chapman datasets. Additionally, to evaluate its generalizability across multiple datasets, ECG-LFM was fine-tuned by the ECG data from the PTB-XL and Chapman datasets was independently tested by the ECG data from the CODE-15, CPSC-2018, and UK Biobank (UKB) datasets. The number of samples in each data set is shown in Supplementary Data 1.
On the PTB-XL dataset, ECG-LFM achieved average AUROC of 0.951 in the independent test (ranging from 0.916 to 0.986) for predicting conduction disturbance (CD) (AUROC = 0.986), hypertrophy (HYP) (AUROC = 0.916), myocardial infarction (MI) (AUROC = 0.958), ST/T change (STTC) (AUROC = 0.951) and ventricular ectopics (VE) (AUROC = 0.942) when it was fine-tuned by the ECGs of 14,495 individuals (80%) and was tested by the ECGs of 3,623 (20%) individuals (Figure 3A and Supplementary Figure S2). This performance significantly (two-sided t-test P-value <4.55×10-24) surpasses other state-of-the-art methods, HeartBEiT [8] (average AUROC 0.908), ECG-ResNet [12] (average AUROC 0.893) and DCNN-LSTM [13] (average AUROC 0.890) with an increase of 4.6%, 6.5% and 6.8%, respectively.
When ECG-LFM was fine-tuned by ECGs of 51,297 individuals (80%) and was tested by 12,824 individuals (20%) from Chapman dataset, it achieved an average AUROC of 0.993 in the independent test set (ranging from 0.990 to 0.996) for predicting sinus bradycardia (SB) (AUROC = 0.996), atrial fibrillation (AFIB) (AUROC = 0.993) and general supraventricular tachycardia (GSVT) (AUROC = 0.990). The performance is significantly better than other methods (two-sided t-test P-value <8.88×10-6) (Figure 3A and Supplementary Figure S2).
The ECG-LFM was further fine-tuned by using PTB-XL and Chapman datasets as the training set, and independently tested by the external test sets, CODE-15, CPSC-2018, and UKB, respectively. ECG-LFM achieved an average AUROC of 0.925 for predicting four types of CVDs in CODE-15, an average AUROC of 0.971 for predicting four types of CVDs in CPSC-2018, and an average AUROC of 0.807 for predicting six types of CVDs in UKB (Figure 3B). The performance is significantly better than the existing methods, HeartBEiT (average AUROCCODE-15 = 0.896, average AUROCCPSC-2018 = 0.945, and average AUROCUKB = 0.778), ECG- ResNet(average AUROCCODE-15 = 0.889, average AUROCCPSC-2018 = 0.939, and average AUROCUKB = 0.772), and DCNN-LSTM (average AUROCCODE-15 = 0.878, average AUROCCPSC- 2018 = 0.939, and average AUROCUKB = 0.768) (Figure 3B). Table 1 shows the AUROC of all these models in predicting each type of CVD, indicating that ECG-LFM shows better performance in predicting all these CVDs than others.
Finally, ECG-LFM was further fine-tuned to predict eight heart functional phenotypes, including left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction, LV stroke volume, left atrial (LA) ejection fraction, LA stroke volume, right ventricular (RV) ejection fraction, RV stroke volume, LV circumferential strain global and LV mean myocardial wall thickness global by using 32,988 individuals as training set (80%) from UKB. It was independently tested by using 8,247 individuals (20%) from the UKB dataset. ECG-LFM achieved an average Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.649 that is significantly (P-value <7.74×10-4) better than HeartBEiT (average PCC = 0.607), ECG-ResNet (average PCC = 0.594), and DCNN-LSTM (PCC = 0.592) (Figure 3C, Supplementary Figure S4).
Influence of fine-tuning dataset on ECG-LFM performance To investigate the influence of fine-tuning dataset on ECG-LFM, the ECG-LFM was evaluated in predicting eight types of CVDs after it was fine-tuned by the training data with varied sizes. The sizes of the training data are ranged from 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, to 100% of the PTB-XL training set, respectively. When ECG-LFM was fine-tuned by 1% of the training set and evaluated by the CVDs of 3,623 individuals from the PTB-XL test set, the model achieved an average AUROC of 0.872, outperforming HeartBEiT (average AUROC of 0.778) by 12.1%, ECG-ResNet (average AUROC of 0.711) by 22.6% and DCNN-LSTM (average AUROC of 0.708) by 23.2% (Figure 3D). With the increase of sample size in the training set, the performance of ECG-LFM is increased and is always better than others (Figure 3D). All these models are further independently tested by the external set CODE-15. ECG-LFM fine-tuned by different sizes of the training set continued to exhibit the best performance with AUROC ranging from 0.833 to 0.915 than other methods (Figure 3D).
ECG-LFM derived features interpret the associations between ECG morphology and CVDs In predicting CVDs, ECG-LFM was pre-trained through self-supervised learning to capture features of ECGs by converting ECGs to 1,024-dimensional embeddings (ECG-LFM derived features, EDFs). For each individual, the importance score of each EDF was calculated according to the performance of the EDF in predicting CVDs for individuals from the PTB-XL and Chapman test sets by integrated gradient (IG) [14]. IG discovered 16 important EDFs (average important score > 5.4×10-3 across 2,000 samples in the PTB-XL and Chapman test sets) in predicting eight types of CVDs (Supplementary Figure S7).
To map these important EDFs to ECG morphology, we designed a perturbation-based EDF interpretation (PEI) method. Using this method, the EDF of interest was perturbed and used to reconstruct ECG signals. The differences between the reconstructed ECG signals and the original ECGs were evaluated by paired t-tests. Regions with higher absolute t-values were identified as most likely to be represented by the EDFs, and the smoothed t-value maps highlighted these regions (see Methods).
Figure 4 shows the ECG regions represented by the top three most important EDFs in predicting each type of CVD. The ECGs of cases and controls in Figure 4 were randomly selected from PTB-XL and Chapman datasets. Out of these EDFs, EDF#102 is most likely to represent the ST-segment of ECG on V4 lead and is the key feature for predicting risks of myocardial infarction (MI) (importance score = 5.4×10-3) and ST/T change (STTC) (importance score = 6.3×10-3).
Consistently, patients with MI or STTC exhibit abnormalities in the ST-segment, including ST- segment elevation or depression that reflects underlying ischemic or infarction processes [15] (Figure 4). The EDF#19 is most likely to represent P-wave duration and P-wave amplitude on V2 lead, and is an important feature for predicting atrial fibrillation (AFIB). Indeed, P-wave duration and P-wave amplitude are reported as associated with AF by previous studies [16, 17].
Of the important EDFs, EDF#945 is most likely to represent the features of QRS morphology, particularly increased R wave amplitude on V5 lead (Figure 4), and other features, EDF#238 and EDF#381 are most likely to represent S wave depth on V3 lead (Figure 4). These three EDFs are the key features for predicting hypertrophy (HYP). A previous study has demonstrated that these QRS morphological changes reflect the increased ventricular mass and altered electrical conduction patterns due to hypertrophy [18].
Phenotypic associations between the important ECG-LFM derived features and risk factors of cardiovascular disease To identify the associations between 16 important EDFs and 215 CVD-related phenotypes (Supplementary Data 5), a phenome-wide association (PheWAS) study was performed by using information on 41,235 individuals from the UKB dataset. A total of 1,387 significant associations were identified (Supplementary Data 6, P-value<0.05/(16×215) ≈1.5×10-5) between these EDFs and 167 CVD-related phenotypes that are 32 physical measures, 5 blood assays, 112 cardia magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) traits, 11 ECG traits, and 7 disorder outcomes (Supplementary Data 6). The associations of EDFs with the CMRI traits and ECG traits are more significant than with other phenotypes (Figure 5A). Specifically, the EDFs are more likely to be associated with the ECG traits, including ventricular rate (beta = -0.321, P-value < 1.0×10-250), QT interval (beta = 0.241, P-value < 1.0×10-250), RR interval (beta = 0.321, P-value < 1.0×10-250), PP interval (beta = 0.337, P-value < 1.0×10-250) and QRS num (beta = -0.488, P-value < 1.0×10-250), indicating the electrophysiological linkages between EDFs and fundamental cardiac conduction properties. Moreover, the EDFs are significantly associated with CMRI traits, including left atrium max volume - 2 channel (beta = -0.131, P-value < 1.0×10-250), heart rate during PWA (beta = - 0.205, P-value < 1.0×10-250), number of beats in waveform average for PWA (beta = 0.152, P- value = 1.0×10-176) and LV circumferential strain AHA 9 (beta = -0.139, P-value = 6.7×10-153).
This result indicates that EDFs can reflect underlying cardiac structure and function as measured by imaging techniques.
Interestingly, the EDFs are found significantly associated with the phenotypes of blood assays that are Cholesterol (beta = 0.049, P-value = 2.7×10-20), Sodium in urine (beta = -0.035, P-value = 1.4×10-11), Alanine aminotransferase (beta = -0.031, P-value = 5.3×10-10), and Alkaline phosphatase (beta = -0.030, P-value = 9.6×10-9). Many physical measures are also identified as significantly associated with the EDFs, which include leg fat mass (right) (beta = -0.095, P-value = 4.3×10-114), leg fat mass (left) (beta = -0.094, P-value = 1.2×10-113), whole body fat mass (beta = -0.117, P-value = 2.0×10-112), and trunk fat mass (beta = -0.117, P-value = 1.3×10-107). These findings have demonstrated that the EDFs have the potential to monitor the risk factors associated with cardiovascular diseases.
Genetic associations between ECG-LFM derived features and CVDs To further detect biological meanings of EDF, we performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for 16 important EDFs on 41,235 individuals from the UKB dataset. The Manhattan plots and QQ plots for all 16 EDFs were shown in Supplementary Figure S8 and Supplementary Figure S9, respectively. Totally, 12 significant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (P-value < 5×10- 8, r2<0.01 within a 250kb window) were identified (Supplementary Figure S8, Supplementary Data 7). These SNPs are adjacent to 7 genes, PLEKHA3, HAND1, FAM53A, SCN5A, NFIA, MIR297, and TBX3. Notably, several of the identified genes (HAND1, SCN5A, NFIA, and TBX3) have been reported to be associated with PR interval [19], RR interval [2], and QT interval [20], consistent with the PheWAS analysis showing significant associations (P-value < 1.0×10-250) between EDF and ECG intervals. The lead SNP rs1896347 near TBX3 is significantly associated with EDF#19 (beta = -0.026, P-value = 9.3×10-10) that was a key feature for predicting AF. The individuals carrying rs1896347 are known to have significantly increased risk for AF (beta = 0.0402, P-value = 2.3×10-7) [21]. Two SNPs, rs13185595 (beta = -0.014, P-value = 1.7×10-9) and rs6587924 (beta = 0.013, P-value = 2.6×10-9) are identified as significantly associated with EDF#900 that is critical for predicting SB and VE. The SNP rs6587924 has been known to be associated with QRS duration [22] and QT interval [23], which is located near NFIA. This aligns with the well-known role of NFIA in ventricular cardiomyocyte development that regulates SB and VE [24].
To investigate the causal relationships between these EDFs and CVDs, we performed Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses by leveraging GWAS summary statistics for EDFs and CVDs. The GWAS summary statistics for CVDs (MI, AF, CD, GSVT, and HYP) were downloaded from the FinnGen database, which are generated based on more than 175 thousand samples. For SB, VE and STTC, there are no GWAS based on large sample size, and they were not used in MR analysis. The instrumental variants (IVs) for MR analysis are those with P-value < 5×10-8 and r2 < 0.01 for CVD and P-value < 1×10-5 and r2 < 0.01 for EDF. If the number of IVs for the exposure, EDF or CVDs is less than five, the MR analysis was not conducted. After the quality control, 16 EDFs and 5 CVDs participated in the MR analysis. A significant causal relationship was determined if the P-value surpassed the Bonferroni-corrected significance level (i.e., P-value < 0.05/(5×16×2) ≈3.1×10−4, considering two causal directions). The bidirectional MR analysis revealed significant causal relationships between EDFs and the CVDs (Figure 5B). When using CVD as exposure and EDF as outcome, the analysis indicated AF as a putative causal effect on the decreased EDF#700 (PIVW = 6.9×10-16, OR = 0.968, 95% CI of 0.961 to 0.976), EDF#19 (PIVW = 3.7×10-9, OR = 0.983, 95% CI of 0.978 to 0.989) and EDF#238 (PIVW = 1.4×10-4, OR = 0.982, 95% CI of 0.973 to 0.992) (Figure 5B, Supplementary Data 9). No horizontal pleiotropy was found by using the global test of MR-PRESSO. EDF#700, EDF#19, and EDF#238 are most likely to represent the ECG traits, R-wave and T-wave on I lead, P-wave on V2 lead and S-wave on V3 lead, respectively (Figure 4). When using EDF as exposure and CVD as outcome, the MR analysis indicated that EDF#945 has putative causal effects on HYP (PIVW = 1.8×10-4, OR = 0.033, 95% CI of 0.005 to 0.213) and AF (PIVW = 2.4×10-4, OR = 0.285, 95% CI of 0.140 to 0.580). EDF#945 is most likely to present the features of QRS amplitude. This supports the notion that abnormality of QRS amplitude is a core feature of the ventricular depolarization associated with AF and HYP, consistent with previous pathological studies [25, 26].
Empowering genetic discovery for ECG by using ECG-LFM derived phenotypes Most of the GWAS for ECG are performed only for the known risk factors associated with CVDs because of the difficulty to reduce the data dimension and keep the biological meaning of ECG signal. To expand genetic insights into ECG, we extracted the first 10 principal components (PCs) from 1,024 EDFs, and performed GWAS for each PC on 41,235 individuals of UKB dataset.
These 10 PCs accounted for 85.2% of the total variance in 1,024 EDFs, suggesting they capture the majority of electrocardiographic variability of the individuals. For 10 PCs of the EDFs, multi- trait genome-wide meta-analysis was performed using METAL [27]. We identified 24 significant SNPs (P-value < 5×10-8, r2 < 0.01 within a 250kb window) at 19 loci from the meta-GWAS (Figure 6A, Supplementary Data 10). Of the 24 significant SNPs, 16 were located <100 kb away from the lead SNPs reported by the most recently published GWAS based on more than 77,898 samples for the ECG traits including spatial QRS-T angle, PR interval, QT interval, P wave duration and QRS duration (Supplementary Figure S10 and Supplementary Data 11) [28-30]. The remaining 8 significant SNPs (rs77188861, rs2562829, rs13081065, rs6843082, rs9400981, rs11756440, rs67467637 and rs2066626) are novel findings of this study. Among these 8 novel SNPs, 5 are intronic variants located within CEP85L, PRDM16, ADCY5, DLEU1 and VTI1A, two are intergenic variants close to genes, VGLL2 and MIR297, and one is an exonic variant located within TTN (Supplementary Figure S10). Indeed, 6 of the 8 novel SNPs are reported to be significantly associated with CVDs [21, 31, 32] (Figure 6B, Supplementary Data 12-13). Especially, the variant rs6843082 (P-value=1.2×10-15), located near MIR297 is reported to be significantly associated with atrial fibrillation (beta = -0.371, P-value = 3.4×10-155) [21], generalized supraventricular tachycardia (beta = -0.100, P-value = 1.3×10-8) [32], and heart failure (beta = -0.075, P-value = 2.6×10-15) [31], indicating its pleiotropic effects on cardiac conduction and ventricular function (Figure 6B).
To identify genes associated with the EDFs, multi-marker analysis of GenoMic annotation (MAGMA) [33] and FUMA [34] on the meta-GWAS result were performed. In total, 63 unique genes were identified by at least one of the three FUMA gene mapping strategies or considered as significant by MAGMA. Briefly, MAGMA analysis revealed 9 genes (NFIA, TTN, SAP30L, HAND1, CDKN1A, CEP85L, PLN, KLHL38 and SIPA1L1) as significantly (P-value<0.05/18762 ≈2.7×10-6) associated with the EDFs (Figure 6C, Supplementary Data 14), FUMA identified a total of 62 candidate genes (Supplementary Data 15). Out of these 63 genes, 39 are reported as associated with ECG traits, such as QRS duration [35], QT interval [36], and PR interval [28].
Moreover, 28 of them were found by previous studies to be associated with CVDs in the GWAS Catalog [37], such as myocardial infarction [38], heart failure [31] and atrial fibrillation [21]. The MAGMA analysis indicated SAP30L as the most significantly associated with the EDFs (P-value = 2.8×10-13). SAP30L is known to play roles in the regulation of cardiac development and heart function [39]. These findings suggest that the genes identified in our analysis may be involved in the genetic architecture of ECG features and cardiovascular diseases.

## Discussion

In this study, we introduced an ECG foundation model, ECG-LFM, and evaluated its generalizability in adapting to diverse downstream tasks. ECG-LFM significantly outperformed other methods for predicting various CVDs across multiple datasets, including PTB-XL, Chapman, CODE-15, CPSC-2018, and UK Biobank, with an average AUROC of 0.930 (ranging from 0.807 to 0.993). These results highlight the ability of ECG-LFM to be applied across diverse populations and clinical scenarios. The better performance of ECG-LFM is attributed to its self-supervised pre- training on over ten million ECGs, which enabled it to capture intricate spatiotemporal patterns in ECG signals. Unlike traditional rule-based systems or task-specific deep learning models, ECG- LFM leverages a multi-task learning strategy that combines contextual contrastive loss, masked language modeling (MLM) loss, and multi-segment contrastive loss, enabling the model to align local ECG features with their contextual representations, reconstruct masked segments to learn long-range relationships, and enforce patient-level consistency across ECG segments, respectively.
The generalizability of ECG-LFM was evaluated across multiple dimensions. First, we tested the model on independent datasets with diverse demographic characteristics: PTB-XL (N=18,118, European ancestry), Chapman (N=10,646, Chinese ancestry), CPSC-2018 (N=6,877, Chinese ancestry), and UK Biobank (N=41,235, mainly European ancestry). These datasets represent populations from different geographic regions and healthcare systems. Second, the datasets include individuals with varying clinical presentations, ranging from healthy controls to patients with acute myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, and conduction disorders. Third, the model was evaluated on ECGs acquired using different recording devices and protocols, demonstrating robustness to technical variations. Detailed information for these datasets was shown in Supplementary Data 1 and Supplementary Figure S1. The consistent performance of ECG-LFM across these diverse settings (average AUROC of 0.930, ranging from 0.807 to 0.993) supports its generalizability to different populations and clinical scenarios. The advantage of ECG-LFM was also particularly evident in scenarios with limited labeled data. For instance, when fine-tuned on just 1% of the PTB-XL dataset, ECG-LFM outperformed other models by up to 23.2% in AUROC. This finding is clinically significant, as it addresses one of the major challenges in medical AI, the scarcity of high-quality labeled data. By minimizing the need for extensive annotated datasets, ECG-LFM enables quick implementation even in resource-constrained environments.
One of the critical barriers to the adoption of AI in clinical practice is the "black-box" nature of many deep learning models. ECG-LFM addresses this challenge through saliency maps generated using Grad-CAM. These maps provide visual explanations of the predictions, highlighting regions of the ECG that contribute most significantly to the diagnosis. For example, in cases of myocardial infarction (MI) and conduction disturbances (CD), the saliency maps of ECG-LFM aligned closely with expert annotations (Supplementary Figure S6), while also revealing subtle patterns that might be overlooked during manual analysis. This transparency not only enhances clinician trust but also facilitates the integration of AI into routine diagnostic workflows. Furthermore, the perturbation-based EDF interpretation (PEI) method allowed us to link specific ECG-LFM derived features to clinically relevant ECG waveforms. For instance, EDF#102 was associated with ST-segment abnormalities in lead V4, a well-known marker of MI [40]. For prediction of hypertrophy (HYP), EDF#945 and EDF#238 are considered as the most significant morphological features. These two features are most likely to represent QRS morphology according to the perturbation-based EDF interpretation (PEI) method. Indeed, QRS morphological changes have been discovered to reflect the increased ventricular mass and altered electrical conduction patterns due to hypertrophy [18]. Such interpretability is crucial for validating the predictions and ensuring their alignment with established cardiological knowledge.
A key contribution of this study is on using EDFs to uncover genetic associations underlying ECG morphology. Traditional GWAS rely on handcrafted ECG features (e.g., QT interval), which are limited in their ability to capture complex waveform interactions. In contrast to traditional models that necessitate high-quality labelled datasets for downstream analysis, ECG-LFM leverages self-supervised pre-training to extract comprehensive, label-independent representations, referred to as ECG-LFM derived features (EDFs). While previous studies have linked deep learning-derived features to genetic variants [41], our approach uniquely combines deep representations from an ECG foundation model with comprehensive genetic and phenotypic analyses to provide novel insights into the genetic architecture of cardiac electrophysiology. ECG- LFM enables the discovery of novel genotype-phenotype relationships, paving the way for personalized risk assessment and targeted interventions. Through genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for EDFs, we identified 24 independent SNPs at 19 loci where genetic associations reached the genome-wide significance threshold (P-value < 5×10-8, r2<0.01 within a 250kb window), including 8 new SNPs located within CEP85L, PRDM16, ADCY5, DLEU1, VTI1A, VGLL2, MIR297 and TTN. These findings provide new insights into the genetic architecture of cardiac electrophysiology and its relationship with CVDs. Among these novel SNPs, the lead SNP rs2562829 is near to TTN that is a gene known to be associated with QT interval [42] and PR interval [43]. While TTN is an established gene for arrhythmia [44], the specific variant rs2562829 represents a novel association with cardiac conduction. Another intergenic variant rs6843082 is significantly associated with EDF, and is known to be significantly associated (P-value<5×10-8) with AF [21], generalized supraventricular tachycardia (GSVT) [32], and heart failure (HF) [31].
The ability of ECG-LFM to derive phenotypes that correlate with genetic variants represents a paradigm shift in electrogenomic research.
This study has several limitations. First, the limited availability of accessible datasets containing both ECG and CVD information restricts our comprehensive evaluation of ECG-LFM.
Expanding available datasets is crucial to propel research forward in this challenging domain.
Second, the computational resources required for pre-training and fine-tuning ECG-LFM are substantial. Although the efficiency of ECG-LFM improves with transfer learning, real-time deployment in clinical settings may still pose challenges. Third, while the interpretability of ECG- LFM is a step forward, further validation is needed to ensure that the explanations align with clinical reasoning across a broader range of conditions. Collaborative efforts with cardiologists to refine the saliency maps and EDF interpretations will be essential.
In conclusion, ECG-LFM represents a transformative approach to ECG analysis, combining state-of-the-art performance, interpretability, and genetic discovery. By leveraging self-supervised learning on large-scale datasets, the model overcomes many of the limitations of traditional methods, offering a robust and generalizable framework for CVD diagnosis and prediction. ECG- LFM further provides new insights into the genetic architecture of cardiac electrophysiology and its relationship with CVDs. With continued refinement and validation, ECG-LFM has the potential to revolutionize the way we diagnose, monitor, and treat cardiovascular diseases.

## Methods

### Ethics

The UK Biobank has approval from the North West Multi-Centre Research Ethics Committee as a Research Tissue Bank (application ID: 51732).

### Data sources

In this study, we collected a total of 11,571,587 12-lead ECG records of 1,979,599 individuals in Harvard-Emory ECG Database (HEEDB) [10] and MIMIC-IV-ECG dataset [11] for model pre- training. HEEDB dataset is currently the largest open-access ECG dataset, containing 10,608,417 ECG records of 1,818,247 individuals. MIMIC-IV-ECG dataset is part of the MIMIC series, containing 800,035 ECG records of 161,352 individuals treated in the intensive care unit (ICU).
Most of the 12-lead ECG records in HEEDB and MIMIC-IV-ECG are 10 seconds long with a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
Our task-specific data comprised five ECG datasets, PTB-XL [45], Chapman [46], CODE-15 [47], CPSC-2018 [48] and UK Biobank [49]. The PTB-XL dataset contains 21,837 12-lead ECG records of 18,885 individuals, where each ECG signal is 10 seconds long with a sampling rate of 500 Hz. It also contains records of various cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) grouped into five super- diagnostic classes: conduction disturbance (CD), hypertrophy (HYP), myocardial infarction (MI), ST/T change (STTC) and ventricular ectopics (VE). A detailed summary of the size of the individual classes is presented in Supplementary Figure S1 and Supplementary Data 1.
Chapman dataset consists of 10,646 12-lead ECG records of 10,646 individuals. Each ECG signal is 10 seconds long and sampled at a frequency of 500 Hz. Chapman dataset contains six types of CVDs that are atrial flutter (AF), atrial fibrillation (AFIB), sinus irregularity (SI), sinus bradycardia (SB), sinus tachycardia (ST), and supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). These six types of CVDs were grouped into three classes following a previous study [46], which are sinus bradycardia (SB), atrial fibrillation (AFIB) and general supraventricular tachycardia (GSVT) (Supplementary Figure S1, Supplementary Data 1).
CODE-15 is a ECG database that includes 345,779 ECG records collected from 233,770 patients. The ECG records in this database were pre-processed as in a previous study[50]. CODE- 15 contains patient diagnosis information for five types of CVDs that are atrial fibrillation (AFIB), sinus bradycardia (SB), sinus tachycardia (ST), left bundle branch block (LBBB) and right bundle branch block (RBBB). We grouped these CVDs into their upper-level types, resulting in four super- diagnostic classes that are sinus bradycardia (SB), atrial fibrillation (AFIB), general supraventricular tachycardia (GSVT) and conduction disturbance (CD) (Supplementary Figure S1, Supplementary Data 1).
The CPSC-2018 dataset consists of 9,569 12-lead ECG records of 6,877 individuals. The ECG is sampled at a rate of 500 Hz. It contains patient diagnosis information for seven types of CVDs (Supplementary Figure S1, Supplementary Data 1), which are atrial fibrillation (AFIB), first- degree atrioventricular block (I-AVB), left bundle branch block (LBBB), right bundle branch block (RBBB), ST-segment depression (STD), ST-segment elevated (STE) and ventricular ectopics (VE).
Following a previous study [51], we grouped the CVDs into four upper-level types, resulting in conduction disturbance (CD), ST/T change (STTC), atrial fibrillation (AFIB) and ventricular ectopics (VE), where CD consists of I-AVB, LBBB and RBBB and STTC consists of STD and STE.
The UK Biobank (UKB) is a longitudinal study of more than 500,000 participants aged from 40 to 69. At baseline assessment, participants provided genotype data, information on health and lifestyle via questionnaire, physical measurement, and donated samples of blood urine. A subgroup of participants was invited back for subsequent visits for additional investigations, including collecting ECG. Totally, 41,235 participants in UKB have both ECG data and genotype data. The ECG signal of each individual in UK Biobank was a 12-lead and 10-second-long signal with a sampling rate of 500 Hz. ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes were used to define the presence or absence of CVDs for each individual. There are patients diagnosed as conduction disturbance (CD), hypertrophy (HYP), myocardial infarction (MI), ST/T change (STTC), ventricular ectopics (VE) sinus bradycardia (SB), atrial fibrillation (AFIB) and general supraventricular tachycardia (GSVT) (Supplementary Figure S1, Supplementary Data 1). The UKB has approval from the North West Multi-Centre Research Ethics Committee as a Research Tissue Bank (Application ID: 51732).

### ECG data pre-processing

To standardize ECG data from multiple sources, we applied linear interpolation to sample the data to force the sampling frequency to be 500Hz. To address signal artifacts, we implemented a series of filtering steps. First, a high-pass filter (1 Hz cutoff) was applied to remove baseline drift, followed by a second-order Butterworth lowpass filter (30 Hz cutoff) to attenuate high-frequency noise, and finally a notch filter (50/60 Hz) was employed to suppress powerline interference. If the duration of ECG was less than 10 seconds (5,000 data points), zero padding was used to extend the ECG signal into 10 seconds for each lead. All signals were normalized using z-score standardization and segmented into non-overlapping 5s segments before inputting them into the model. The ECG data pre-processing pipeline was shown in Supplementary Figure S12.

### Constructing the electrocardiogram evaluation foundation model

The electrocardiogram foundation model, ECG-LFM is composed of a feature encoder that extracts latent representations (tokens) from raw 12-lead ECG inputs. The feature encoder consists of several blocks containing a 1D-convolution layer followed by layer normalization and a GELU activation function [52]. It takes raw 12-lead ECG as input and outputs latent representations 𝑧1, 𝑧2, … , 𝑧𝑇for T time-steps.
A quantization module is included in ECG-LFM for discretizing the latent representations to target context vector and discretized ID. The quantization module is used to discretize the latent representations 𝑧𝑡 of the feature encoder to a finite set of representations. This module selects discrete codebook entries from multiple codebooks [53] and concatenates them, which has resulted in efficient and compact representation of encoded features. To enable differentiable selection of discrete codebook entries, the Gumbel softmax is employed, which allows the quantization process to be integrated into the end-to-end training pipeline. Specifically, the quantization module utilizes G codebooks, each of which contains V entries e ∈ 𝑅𝑉×𝑑/𝐺, where d is the dimensionality of the feature encoder output 𝑧𝑡. The feature encoder output 𝑧𝑡 is mapped to logits 𝑙 ∈ 𝑅𝑉×𝐺 , which represent the scores for each entry in the codebooks. For each codebook, one entry 𝑒𝑡 is selected according to the probability 𝑝𝑔,𝑣, which is computed as 𝑝𝑔,𝑣 = exp((𝑙𝑔,𝑣 + 𝑛𝑣)/𝜏) ∑ exp((𝑙𝑔,𝑘 + 𝑛𝑘)/𝜏)𝑉 𝑘=1 (1) , where 𝜏 is a non-negative temperature parameter controlling the sharpness of the distribution, 𝑛 = −log(−log(𝑢)) and u are uniform samples from uniform distribution 𝒰(0,1). Finally, the resulting vectors 𝑒1,𝑒2, … , 𝑒𝐺 are concatenate to form the discretized ID for each token, and the linear transformation is applied to obtain target context vectors 𝑞𝑡 ∈ 𝑅𝑓 for each latent representation 𝑧𝑡.
ECG-LFM used an embedding module for extracting contextual representations for each token, as well as three tasks that are a contextual contrastive task to identify the quantized representation from quantization module, a masked language modeling task for predicting the discretized ID of each token and a multi-segment contrastive task to capture functionally relevant information (Figure 1A). The embedding model of ECG-LFM is inspired by BERT [54]. ECG- LFM masks the token 𝑧𝑡 from the feature encoder and reconstructs the masked tokens by leveraging contextual information from the surrounding tokens. Each token has a 6.5% probability of being a starting index, where if selected, we mask the subsequent 10 tokens. This results in approximately 49% of sample tokens being masked. The masked tokens were then fed into the linear projection layer followed by the stack of conformer blocks [55] to produce high-level contextual vectors 𝑐𝑡. Conformer is a hybrid neural network architecture that integrates depth- wise convolution (enabling multi-scale feature extraction) with multi-headed self-attention mechanisms (capturing long-range dependencies) to enhance the modeling of both local acoustic patterns and global contextual relationships in ECG signals.

##### [Risk stratification of patients with syncope in the emergency department using ECG based artificial intelligence models](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-49475-2)
