```
## Abstract

Syncope is a common presentation in the emergency department, yet risk stratification for adverse events remains a substantial clinical challenge. In this study, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) models for identification of patients at high risk of 1-year cardiovascular death was investigated. The study included 39,735 patients aged 18 years or older who presented to a Danish emergency department with a discharge diagnosis of syncope and had an electrocardiogram recorded on the same day. Using multiple electrocardiogram parameters four different models were developed - artificial neural network, logistic regression, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting. Additionally, the models’ ability to stratify patients into low- and high-risk groups of 1-year cardiovascular death was assessed. The mean area under the receiver operating curves was 0.85 (0.01), while the mean area under the precision-recall curve was 0.11 (0.01).
Stratification into low- and high-risk groups showed hazard ratios ranging from 10.80 (95% CI, 8.55-13.63) to 17.97 (95% CI, 12.32-26.20) in univariate Cox Proportional Hazards regression analysis across the four models. These findings demonstrate that AI-based models can successfully distinguish high-risk from low- risk patients with syncope, allowing for targeted evaluation and efficient clinical decision making.

## Introduction

Risk stratification of patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with syncope is an on-going challenge [1]. Patients with low risk of cardiac syncope and cardiovascular events may be unnecessarily admitted to the hospital wasting useful resources, while on the other hand high-risk patients could inappropriately be discharged and experience serious adverse events [1, 2]. Therefore, determining the risk of adverse events in the initial evaluation is essential [1, 3, 4].
The electrocardiogram (ECG) can provide essential information in the early risk stratification of syncope patients [1, 5], and is also utilized in current syncope risk stratification scores for both short- term serious events such as arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and death, and long-term mortality. [6-10]. Unfortunately, the current risk stratification scores do not perform better than clinical judgment [11]. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has been utilized to improve risk estimation of cardiac syncope with AI models performing better than current risk stratification scores [12].
AI models have the potential to improve risk stratification by identifying high-risk patients and determining the appropriate ED disposition and determining whether acute treatment is needed [13-15]. In addition, AI models could potentially support clinicians in clinical decision making, ensuring correct diagnostics and treatment strategies [15, 16]. Nonetheless, further research is needed before AI models might be integrated in risk stratification of syncope patients and more robust AI models must be developed before being a part of the clinical practice [16]. Thus, the aim of this study was to investigate the use of AI models for risk stratification of patients presenting to the ED with syncope using the ECG.

## Results

### Population Characteristics

A total of 39,735 patients presenting to the ED with syncope between October 21st, 2002, and December 31st, 2021, were included in this study. The derivation of the study population is shown in Figure 1. 1,819 (4.6%) patients experienced cardiovascular mortality during the follow-up period, while 554 (1.3%) had cardiovascular mortality within 1-year after the index date. Baseline characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1.

### Model Evaluation

Results on the validation set for each model are presented in Table 2, while the ROC and PR curves for each model are displayed in Figure 2 and Figure 3. The logistic regression model and the ANN had the highest AUC-ROC of 0.86, which was only slightly higher than the random forest and XG Boost models of 0.85.
Overall, there was only a small difference between the models’ performance with a mean AUC-ROC of 0.85 (0.01). Regarding AUC-PR, the XG Boost model outperformed the other models with an AUC-PR of 0.13, however only slightly higher than the logistic regression of 0.12. The F1 score was highest for the XG boost model with 0.23, but only slightly differed across the other models with a mean of 0.21 (0.02). Sensitivity was highest in the random forest model with 0.96 and lowest in the ANN with 0.78. Specificity was highest in the ANN with 0.80, and lowest in the random forest model with 0.59. The mean sensitivity and specificity of the models were 0.88 (0.07) and 0.67 (0.08), respectively. For all four models, age had the highest mean absolute SHAP value, as shown in Figure 4. Notably, the SHAP analysis showed that heart rate, atrial fibrillation or flutter, QTc interval, and QRS duration contributed to the predictions for all four models.
The results of the threshold-based analysis are shown in Table 3 and Table 4. At the safety-oriented rule-out threshold (high sensitivity), the models achieved moderate specificity, resulting in low PPVs and high NPVs. At the efficiency- oriented rule-in threshold (high specificity), but sensitivity and PPVs were low. 

### Risk Stratification and Survival Analysis

Kaplan-Meier curves for the predicted risk groups are shown in Figure 5. Log- rank test showed significant differences in survival between the low-risk group and the high-risk group for all models (p < 0.001). For all models the Cox regression showed a significant higher hazard ratio of cardiovascular death for the high-risk group compared to the low-risk group with hazard ratios ranging from 10.80 to 17.97. When adjusting the Cox regression for age and sex the hazard ratios ranged from 1.97 to 2.75. Hazard ratios from the univariate- and multivariate Cox regressions are shown in Table 5.

### Results on holdout test set

Overall, model performance on the holdout test set showed similar results to those in the validation cohort with a mean AUC-ROC of 0.89 (0.00) and mean AUC-PR of 0.12 (0.02). Results from the holdout test set are presented in Table 6.

### Sensitivity Analyses

Sensitivity analysis, shortening the event cut-off from 1-year to 100 days, showed similar results (Supplementary Table 2) with the logistic regression achieving the highest AUC-ROC with 0.89 and a mean AUC-ROC and AUC-PR across the four ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPTARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS models of 0.87 (0.01) and 0.13 (0.03), respectively. Secondly, only including patients >55 years old (Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Table 4), showed a slightly lower mean AUC-ROC and mean AUC-PR for both 1-year (0.82 and 0.13) and 100-day (0.81 and 0.09) cardiovascular death. The baseline model including only age and sex achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.82 and an AUC-PR of 0.09.
The ECG-only model achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.82 and an AUC-PR of 0.07. Both models showed lower discrimination than the full model presented in the main results (AUC-ROC 0.86, AUC-PR 0.12), which included age, sex, and ECG variables. Comparison of correlated AUC-ROC curves using the paired DeLong test demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in discrimination for the full model (p < 0.001) compared to the baseline model and no significant differences in discrimination compared to the ECG-only model (p = 0.055).
Cumulative incidence curves of 1-year cardiovascular disease demonstrated a significantly higher incidence of subsequent cardiovascular diagnoses in the high- risk group compared with the low-risk group, as shown in Figure 6.

## Discussion

In this study, four different AI models for estimating the risk of 1-year cardiovascular death in patients presenting to the ED with syncope was developed and tested. All models were able to identify high-risk patients requiring further evaluation as well as low-risk patients who can be discharged. Notably, no considerable differences between the models’ performance were observed and no AI model outperformed the traditional logistic regression model which scored the highest AUC-ROC.
Risk stratification of patients with syncope presenting to the ED remains a challenge, since syncope can be a symptom of both benign and life-threatening conditions [1, 2] Multiple risk scores have been developed to assess the risk ofboth short- and long-term adverse cardiac events and mortality [6-10], nonetheless, none of these were superior to clinical judgment [11]. To improve risk estimation of cardiovascular events in patients with syncope, AI models have been proposed as a potential solution [13-15]. Constantino et al. 2017 [30] developed a neural network to predict the risk of short-term adverse events in patients presenting to the ED with syncope, with an AUC-ROC of 0.78, and sensitivity and specificity of 1.0 and 0.79, respectively. In validation of currently available risk scores, du Fay de Lavallaz et al. 2018 [11] reported that, for predicting death and major adverse cardiovascular events the best performing scores achieved AUC-ROCs of 0.71. Also, Zimmerman et al. 2021 [31] developed a risk stratification tool for cardiac cause of syncope in patients with syncope.
Utilizing a logistic regression model they demonstrated an AUC-ROC of 0.80, while in the same study acknowledged syncope risk scores such as the ECGSYS score [8] and San Francisco Syncope Rule (SFSR) [10] only achieved AUC-ROCs of 0.73 and 0.67. Furthermore, the study by Zimmerman et al. 2021 [31] also demonstrated that clinical judgement (AUC-ROC of 0.87) was superior to both the logistic regression model and the traditional risk scores. However, combining clinical judgement with the logistic regression model improved classification with an AUC-ROC of 0.90 demonstrating that these models may support clinical decision-making rather than replace clinical judgement.
Although the discriminative performance of the evaluated models was modest, it should be interpreted in the clinical context of syncope, where 1-year cardiovascular mortality is a rare outcome. Across all models, the AUC-PR ranged from 0.09 to 0.13, reflecting a relatively high number of false positives. Part of this may be attributable to the 1-year event cut-off, as patients experiencing events shortly after this period, despite remaining at elevated risk, are classified as false positives. This pattern is also reflected in the Kaplan-Meier curves, where the high-risk group continues to show declining probability of cardiovascular survival beyond 1 year. Therefore, assessing model performance may benefit from approaches beyond standard metrics, as these rely on manually defined thresholds that can influence observed results. Furthermore, the cumulative incidence of cardiovascular disease suggests that the model does indeed identify patients with an increased likelihood of underlying or emerging cardiovascular disease, which indicates that the model captures clinically meaningful cardiac risk rather than nonspecific vulnerability alone. In line with the observations of this study, Constantino et al. 2017 [30] similarly reported a substantial number of false positives, however still with better performance than the current study. This could be because they focused on 7-10 days serious adverse events rather than longer term cardiovascular death, as short term events are more directly linked to ECG abnormalities, whereas longer term mortality is influenced by a wider range of clinical and demographic factors which may explain the higher false positive rate observed in this study. In the present study, the primary endpoint was defined as 1-year cardiovascular mortality to capture underlying or emerging cardiovascular disease that may be amenable to intervention. While shorter-term outcomes could be more directly linked to acute ED management, the low number of events within such horizons limited the feasibility of building reliable models in this study. Our findings should thus be interpreted as identifying patients with elevated risk over a clinically meaningful timeframe, rather than guiding immediate discharge or admission decisions. Further, the study included all patients 18 years and older, which might have impacted the results as the younger population rarely experiences cardiac related syncope. Supporting this, excluding the younger population in a sensitivity analysis improved the specificity of the models, indicating that the models might have been confused by young adults suffering cardiovascular death within 1 year. Importantly, the observed performance is comparable to that reported for existing syncope risk scores and reflects the prognostic information available in routinely collected clinical and ECG data Stratification of patients into a high-risk group and a low-risk group showed promising clinical utility. With hazard ratios ranging from 10.80 to 17.97 of cardiovascular death for the high-risk group compared to the low-risk group, these patients should undergo further evaluation and cannot safely be discharged upon initial evaluation. However, the models evaluated in this study are not intended to replace clinical judgement and should be viewed as a potential supplement to clinical evaluation, offering a standardized and objective risk assessment that may contribute to identifying patients who could benefit from closer monitoring or further evaluation. However, to ensure patient safety, the models should be used as a tool alongside clinicians’ own assessments, rather than as a replacement for clinical judgment. Conversely, the high number of false positives, as indicated by the low AUC-PR, highlights the need for further refinement of the models to improve precision and facilitate effective translation into clinical practice. Also, some models demonstrated moderate specificity, reflecting the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity in a setting with a very low event rate. In this context, prioritizing sensitivity may be appropriate to reduce the risk of missing high-risk patients, particularly when the model is intended to support clinical triage. Further, evaluation of the models at clinically oriented thresholds highlights important limitations. While a safety-oriented rule- out threshold with high sensitivity, the specificity was only moderate, and PPV was low. Conversely, an efficiency-oriented rule-in threshold with high specificity, the sensitivity remained limited. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the models do not support use as standalone tools for binary decision-making at the point of care. Importantly, discriminative performance and threshold-based metrics are not the sole determinants of a prognostic model’s potential value. The primary aim of this study was not to directly guide immediate emergency department disposition, but to identify patients with syncope who are at higher overall cardiovascular risk and who may benefit from closer evaluation, monitoring, or structured follow-up.
The SHAP analysis identified age as the primary contributor to 1-year cardiovascular death predictions across all four models. This finding was consistent with the multivariate Cox regression analysis adjusted for age and sex, where hazard ratios were substantially attenuated compared to the univariate analysis. The strong predictive value of age in cardiovascular death is expected as the elder population carry a higher burden of cardiovascular disease [32].
Sensitivity analysis comparing models including only age and sex or only ECG features demonstrate that while age is the strongest individual predictor, as shown from the SHAP analysis, ECG variables contribute additional predictive information. While the incremental gain in AUC-ROC was modest in absolute terms (0.82 to 0.86), statistical comparison between the baseline and the full model confirmed that the addition of ECG variables significantly improved discrimination beyond age and sex alone. The comparable performance of the ECG-only model and the full model, which was non-significant, further underscores the contribution of ECG-derived information in risk stratification.
These findings support the inclusion of ECG data in risk stratification models, while also emphasizing that much of the model’s performance is driven by patient age.

```
##### [Low-latency HRV analysis from ultra-short ECG windows using a modular deep-learning framework](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-48463-w)

```
## Abstract

We present a universal modular deep-learning framework and demonstrate its application to low-latency, streaming-compatible heart rate variability (HRV) analysis using RMSSD as an exemplar metric. A convolutional autoencoder is first pretrained and then reused as a frozen encoder that maps raw ECG windows to a compact latent sequence. Task-specific heads, each comprising a BiLSTM adapter, a shallow Conv1D refinement, and temporal attention pooling operate on this shared representation. A discriminator head screens low-quality windows, while a regression head estimates RMSSD; a gated inference block routes outputs so RMSSD is produced only when the discriminator exceeds a threshold, replicating a robust “mask-then-estimate” pipeline in a single deployable graph.
Using LUDB and PTB-XL with segmentation-assisted peak extraction for PTB-XL, plus an out-of-distribution Apple Watch subset, we enforce rigorous quality assurance to derive validity labels and RMSSD targets. Compared to two strong classical baselines (HeartPy and NeuroKit2), our discriminator improves combined-set accuracy to 92.12% (vs. 80.54% / 85.58%) with F1 of 95.43% (vs. 88.82% / 91.99%). On RMSSD estimation, the proposed model reduces combined MAE to 10.56 ms (from 45.12 ms / 27.93 ms) and sharply curtails tail errors (P95: 47.00 ms vs. 313.35 ms / 167.84 ms), indicating substantially improved robustness under pathological and noisy ECG. On a small out-of-distribution Apple Watch subset used as a sanity-check for acquisition shift, where the model attains the lowest MAE (7.57 ms vs. 13.96 ms / 9.61 ms) under a selective gating regime.
The end-to-end model is compact (2.62 M parameters; 10.07 MB on disk) and real-time capable, achieving 15.0 ms mean latency at batch size 1 (66.5 windows/s) and scaling to ∼4.49k windows/s at batch size 1024 on a single consumer-grade GPU.

## Introduction and Motivation

Heart rate variability (HRV) summarizes autonomic nervous system dynamics from the timing of successive heartbeats. Among standard indices, the Root Mean Square of Successive Differences (RMSSD) captures short-latency vagal modulation and is widely used in clinical cardiology and applied physiology1. Delivering reliable RMSSD estimates with low latency in streaming settings is essential for bedside monitoring, telemedicine, and wearable feedback systems, yet remains challenging where motion artefacts, arrhythmias, and device heterogeneity undermine standard signal-processing heuristics.
Despite its clinical importance, the real-time computation of HRV metrics such as RMSSD is difficult in multi-patient settings. Hospital environments often involve simultaneous monitoring across multiple leads (e.g., 12-lead ECG), producing high-throughput streams under nonstationary and noisy conditions. Traditional algorithmic approaches typically rely on hand-engineered heuristics that can be computationally expensive, brittle under noise, and hard to generalize across sampling rates, lead configurations, and hardware platforms.
Well-established algorithmic toolkits (e.g., HeartPy2, 3) combine adaptive peak detection with rule-based quality checks to compute HRV from ECG or PPG. These methods are transparent and reproducible, but their performance can deteriorate under distribution shifts (sampling frequency changes, multi-/single-lead differences, consumer sensors) and they often require task-specific tuning to remain stable across use cases.
Complementing HeartPy, NeuroKit24 is a widely adopted, general-purpose Python toolkit for neurophysiological and cardiovascular signal processing that provides a unified pipeline for ECG preprocessing, R-peak detection, and downstream HRV computation. In contrast to single-purpose HRV libraries, NeuroKit2 emphasizes breadth and modularity: it exposes multiple detector options and standardized post-processing utilities, which makes it a natural reference implementation when evaluating portability across datasets and acquisition settings. Nevertheless, like other rule-based pipelines, its performance ultimately depends on peak-detection stability and heuristic post-processing, and can therefore degrade under severe noise, morphology variability, or rhythm irregularities encountered in heterogeneous real-world ECG.
n parallel, deep learning–based methods have shown promise by learning noise-tolerant representations directly from raw signals. However, many end-to-end solutions entangle representation learning with target-specific losses, which limits reusability and complicates clinical maintenance, validation, and updates when adding new metrics or adapting to new devices.
We introduce a modular deep-learning framework for real-time ECG analysis that separates universal feature extraction from task-specific decision making. A convolutional autoencoder is first pretrained; its encoder is then frozen to provide a stable latent sequence shared by lightweight heads. In our exemplary use case, two heads illustrate the pattern: (i) a discriminator that learns processability (i.e., whether a window is safe for HRV computation) and (ii) an RMSSD regressor operating on the same latent. A gated inference layer composes them so that RMSSD is produced only when the discriminator affirms sufficient quality, mirroring the clinical intuition of “screen first, then measure.” Importantly, the contribution of this paper is the scientific framework and its empirical validation - a modular architecture designed to be integrated into real-time monitoring stacks rather than an end-to-end clinical system implementation.
To operationalize these ideas in a deployment-ready manner, we structure the sample framework application around four pillars that map directly to clinical and systems requirements - generality, reliability, and throughput: • General and Flexible Framework: A robust architecture that uses RMSSD as a proof of concept while remaining easily extensible to additional HRV indices (time, frequency, nonlinear) and other ECG-derived metrics.
• Frozen, Reusable Encoder: A pretrained Conv1D encoder maps raw ECG windows to a compact latent sequence shared across tasks, decoupling universal feature learning from metric-specific heads and simplifying future updates.
• Gated Inference for Reliability: A discriminator head filters low-quality segments and conditionally routes only processable windows to the RMSSD regressor, preventing spurious estimates on corrupted data.
• Operational Efficiency and Scalability: The shared latent enables batched, multi-lead, multi-patient inference with low latency; practical system elements (e.g., windowed streaming with a circular buffer) support real-time throughput in noisy environments.
This design yields three practical benefits for the real-time care: robustness - learned features and explicit gating curb misleading HRV on corrupted segments; extensibility - new indices can be added as independent heads without retraining the encoder; and operational efficiency - the shared latent supports ICU-like high-throughput monitoring scenarios involving multi-lead processing under low-latency constraints. In effect, our method serves as a principled, learned alternative to standard algorithmic pipelines, preserving their emphasis on quality control while providing the adaptability required by modern, heterogeneous ECG ecosystems.
This paper proceeds as follows. Section “Related Works” surveys prior HRV estimation approaches with an emphasis on neural network–based methods and their real-time advantages over traditional pipelines. In “Proposed Solution,” we introduce our modular framework and detail its components: the convolutional autoencoder (with the encoder reused as a frozen feature extractor), head design (BiLSTM adapter, Conv1D refinement, and temporal attention pooling), the discriminator and RMSSD heads, and the end-to-end gated inference block, along with the training protocol and architectural advantages. “Data Acquisition and Preprocessing” describes the construction of our corpora from LUDB and PTB-XL, the out-of-distribution Apple Watch subset, windowing and normalization, segmentation-assisted peak extraction for PTB-XL, and the quality- assurance gate yielding validity labels and RMSSD targets. In “Results,” we report discriminator metrics and RMSSD errors—both aggregate and per-dataset—highlighting tail robustness and real-time suitability. “Discussion” interprets these findings, outlines limitations, and presents directions for future work. Finally, “Conclusions” summarize the main contributions.

## Results

As strong classical baselines, we compare against HeartPy and NeuroKit2, two widely used and widely cited open-source frameworks for heart rate and HRV analysis. HeartPy has been validated on both PPG and ECG datasets and is designed for real-time and offline use, with adaptive peak detection, outlier handling, and configurable preprocessing (e.g., FIR filtering). Its robustness to motion artifacts and signal clipping, together with accessible and well-documented Python tooling, has made it a de facto reference in many applied studies. In our evaluation, HeartPy serves as an algorithmic baseline for RMSSD estimation: peaks are detected using its adaptive-threshold pipeline, inter-beat intervals are derived, and RMSSD is computed from the resulting interval series.
NeuroKit2 is a general-purpose neurophysiology and biosignal processing toolkit that also provides ECG peak detection and HRV computation in a unified, extensively used Python API. Relative to HeartPy, NeuroKit2 typically offers a broader set of ECG processing utilities and detector variants, making it a natural second comparator when evaluating robustness across heterogeneous signal conditions. In our evaluation, NeuroKit2 is used as an additional rule-based baseline for RMSSD: R-peaks are detected using its ECG processing pipeline, inter-beat intervals are extracted, and RMSSD is computed from the resulting intervals.
These choices provide (i) transparent, reproducible comparators and (ii) a stringent stress test of our learned model against respected rule-based approaches optimized for challenging, noisy data.

The proposed discriminator achieves higher accuracy and F1 than both classical baselines (Table 1), indicating more reliable gating of RMSSD estimation to processable windows while maintaining very high precision. NeuroKit2 improves over HeartPy on this combined benchmark, but still falls short of the proposed discriminator, particularly in overall accuracy and F1.
Across the clinical ECG datasets (LUDB, PTB-XL, and their combination), the proposed solution yields lower RMSSD error than both classical baselines (Table 2). HeartPy exhibits large absolute errors and heavy tails (e.g., P99 near 450 ms on LUDB and PTB-XL), consistent with peak-detection failures in challenging rhythm and morphology regimes. NeuroKit2 substantially improves upon HeartPy, reducing both MAE and tail percentiles across all ECG datasets, but it still shows larger errors than the learned model, especially in the upper tail (e.g., Combined P99 of 374.58 ms for NeuroKit2 versus 151.49 ms for the proposed method).

To contextualize the practical magnitude of these errors, we compare them against commonly reported resting RMSSD ranges for healthy adults (e.g., on the order of 27-72 ms, noting that normative values vary with age, posture, and acquisi- tion/processing choices)1. Using this illustrative span of 45 ms, the proposed model’s MAE corresponds to approximately 23% of the span on the combined set (10.56/45), 17% on LUDB (7.69/45), and 24% on PTB-XL (10.70/45). In contrast, the baselines’ MAE values represent substantially larger fractions of the same span (HeartPy: ∼100%; NeuroKit2: ∼62% on the combined set), consistent with their heavier error tails.
From an applicability standpoint, these results indicate that the proposed approach is suitable for low-latency, streaming use where RMSSD is consumed as a continuously refreshed indicator (e.g., for monitoring trends, detecting abrupt changes, or enabling feedback that is robust to occasional corrupted windows via gating). In this setting, an MAE on the order of 8-11 ms on valid windows supports practical tracking of relative changes in vagal modulation without the catastrophic outliers observed in rule-based pipelines. However, because estimates are produced on ≈3 s windows, they should not be interpreted as a direct substitute for guideline-oriented short-term HRV assessment on multi-minute recordings; instead, they are best used either as rapid updates with explicit quality control or as inputs to longer-horizon aggregation (e.g., smoothing over consecutive gated windows) when clinically comparable stability is required.
To complement the tabulated absolute-error statistics, Figure 5 visualizes agreement with the reference RMSSD on the combined test set using Bland-Altman plots. The proposed model exhibits near-zero bias and substantially tighter limits of agreement than both baselines, consistent with the reduced tail errors reported in Table 2.

On LUDB, PTB-XL, and their combined set, both parametric (paired t-test) and non-parametric (Wilcoxon signed-rank) analyses reject the null hypothesis with high confidence for both baselines (Table 3), indicating that the model’s absolute error is consistently lower than HeartPy’s and NeuroKit2’s whenever the corresponding tool produces an estimate.
The Apple Watch subset is omitted from statistical testing because its sample size is small and the recordings are not pathologically diverse. We treat it as an out-of-distribution sanity check for acquisition shift (consumer single-lead, different electrode configuration and sampling rate), rather than as validation of wearable performance in clinical or high-stakes settings.
The reported errors on this subset are descriptive and exploratory, and should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical readiness on wearable devices. Both HeartPy and NeuroKit2 successfully produce RMSSD estimates for nearly all windows (48/50 and 49/50, respectively), whereas the discriminator-gated model is intentionally more selective (29/50).
Across all datasets, our model surpasses both classical baselines in average error and in distribution tails (Table 2). On the combined set, MAE decreases from 45.12 ms (HeartPy) and 27.93 ms (NeuroKit2) to 10.56 ms (ours), while large errors are curtailed (P95: 313.35 ms to 47.00 ms versus HeartPy; 167.84 ms to 47.00 ms versus NeuroKit2). The variability of absolute errors is also lower for the model (STD 26.3 ms combined; 14.2 ms LUDB; 26.7 ms PTB-XL) than for either HeartPy (STD about 104 to 107 ms on large ECG corpora) or NeuroKit2 (STD about 52 to 75 ms). These gains are consistent across LUDB and PTB-XL and carry over to the Apple Watch subset, where the model attains the lowest MAE (7.57 ms) despite operating under a selective gating regime.
To address real-time suitability, we profiled the end-to-end model on a single CUDA-capable GPU (TensorFlow 2.14.0), reporting latency, throughput, and peak memory usage (Table 4). The model is compact on disk (10.07 MB) with 2.62 M parameters (10.00 MB of weights in FP32). In steady-state inference, batch size 1 achieves a mean latency of 15.0 ms (66.5 windows/s), while throughput scales to about 4.49k windows/s at batch size 1024. Peak VRAM remains below 4 GB up to batch size 256 (2.24 GB), and fits within an 8 GB tier at batch size 512 (4.16 GB) and batch size 1024 (7.76 GB). Host (process) memory increased by 0.56 GB over the full benchmark run, consistent with TensorFlow runtime allocations and caching. Estimated compute (TF profiler, float ops): 0.795 GFLOPs per window at batch size 1, scaling approximately linearly to 814.540 GFLOPs at batch size 1024.

## Discussion

The results indicate that explicitly gating HRV estimation with a learned discriminator improves robustness in noisy and clinically heterogeneous ECG. Relative to rule-based pipelines, the proposed approach reduces catastrophic RMSSD outliers and yields more stable tail behavior, which is important because RMSSD can be strongly influenced by arrhythmias and morphologic variability. The improvement over NeuroKit2 suggests that the gain is not only due to stronger peak detection, but also due to the model learning representations that remain informative across rhythm regimes, noise conditions, and acquisition variability.
The proposed model operates in a selective prediction regime (with an explicit reject option via the discriminator).
Consequently, RMSSD error metrics should be interpreted jointly with coverage, as improved robustness may partially stem from rejecting low-quality or ambiguous windows. In contrast, classical baselines produce estimates for all windows that do not produce a numerical error, including severely corrupted segments, which can inflate tail errors.
At the system level, the end-to-end gated inference block operationalizes a mask-then-estimate pipeline within a single deployable graph. This design supports real-time operation by producing a direct processable or non-processable decision and, when appropriate, a metric estimate. The runtime profiling supports feasibility for streaming inference under typical GPU configurations and provides practical capacity guidance for batch processing.
```

##### [AI-enhanced approaches for personalized cardiac treatment: insights from ECG data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6)

```
## Abstract

The analysis of drug-induced alterations in the electrocardiogram (ECG) is essential in measuring cardiac safety, but manual analysis is not always accurate enough to identify subtle but important effects. This paper examines how machine learning (ML) models can be used to categorize various pharmacological treatments according to their distinct ECG patterns to establish a platform of individualized therapeutic evaluation. Using the public ECG Effects of Dofetilide, Moxifloxacin, Dofetilide+Mexiletine, Dofetilide+Lidocaine and Moxifloxacin+Diltiazem (ECGDMMLD) database, key electrophysiological features were extracted—including heart rate variability (HRV) and standard cardiac intervals (RR, PR, QT, QRS) to train and compare three different classifiers: XGBoost, Random Forest, and a Support Vector Machine (SVM). The analysis showed that tree-based ensemble techniques were very useful in this task. The XGBoost model had a better classification accuracy of 98.1%, which was closely followed by the random forest at 97.3%. Conversely, the SVM had much lower accuracy, implying that it was not as well adapted to the complexity of the high-dimensional ECG data. These results establish that ML models, particularly XGBoost, can accurately decode complex drug-induced cardiac signatures from ECG data. This work is a powerful demonstration of the proof-of-concept of automated and data-driven analytics integration into clinical processes to enhance drug safety and promote personalized medicine.

## Introduction

Clinical cardiology would not be the same without the electrocardiogram (ECG), which allows the diagnosis of many cardiac diseases, such as arrhythmias and ischemic heart disease, by examination of its special waveforms[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR1 "de Roos, A. & Nikolaou, K. in CT and MRI in Suspected Ischemic Heart Disease. 179–187 (Springer International Publishing, Cham, 2019)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR2 "Ashley, E. A. & Niebauer, J. Cardiology Explained London: Remedica; Chapter 3, Conquering the ECG. Available from: 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2214/
(2004)."). Its use is, however, not limited to routine diagnostics, but also to the imperative area of pharmacological safety surveillance, in which one formidable obstacle continues to exist, namely, the identification of drug-induced cardiotoxicity. This problem is idealized by the prolongation of the QT interval due to the use of drugs, a highly recognized antecedent of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), a fatal arrhythmia that has inspired the pulling out of drugs in the market in large numbers[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR3 "Johannesen, L. et al. Improving the assessment of heart toxicity for all new drugs through translational regulatory science. Clin. Pharmacol. Therapeut. 95, 501–508 (2014).").

The key issue is the complicated electrophysiology of drug-induced arrhythmias. Although blockage of the hERG potassium channel is an established mechanism, interactions with other ion channels, including calcium or other ion channels, of a given drug, sodium currents, may lead to a significant change in its pro-arrhythmic potential, occasionally in a protective manner[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR3 "Johannesen, L. et al. Improving the assessment of heart toxicity for all new drugs through translational regulatory science. Clin. Pharmacol. Therapeut. 95, 501–508 (2014)."). This causes the QT interval alone to be an inadequate and, in most cases, unstable indicator of the actual cardiac risk. This uncertainty is enhanced by the fact that manual interpretation of ECG is prone to error due to inter-observer variability and is not trustworthy to detect the subtle multi-parameter as such, there exists a differentiation between safe and dangerous compounds, as signatures[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR4 "Lyon, A., Mincholé, A., Martínez, J. P., Laguna, P. & Rodriguez, B. Computational techniques for ECG analysis and interpretation in light of their contribution to medical advances. J. R. Soc. Interface 15, 20170821 (2018)."). Therefore, there is a compelling need for more precise and objective risk stratification methodologies.

Machine learning (ML) can be used to fill this gap by deploying a disruptive solution to cardiac[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR5 "Adasuriya, G. & Haldar, S. Next generation ECG: The impact of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Curr. Cardiovasc. Risk Rep. 17, 1–12 (2023)."). In comparison to manual analysis, ML algorithms will be able to analyze high-dimensional data in order to discover the complex, non-linear relationships that define complex biological systems. This characteristic acts as a crucial ability as it supports the switch from simple biomarkers to the customized and trusted way of assessing cardiac risk, which leads to quicker and much more consistent outputs[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR6 "Attia, Z. I. & Friedman, P. A. Explainable AI for ECG-based prediction of cardiac resynchronization therapy outcomes: learning from machine learning?. Eur. Heart J. 44, 693–695 (2022).").

This study was carried out with the aim of finding the precision of machine learning models in predicting the difference between the effects of drugs on the heart and the raw ECG signals. Figure [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Fig1) can be used to summarize the complete research. The dataset used comes with a well-designed drug trial on healthy volunteers and also with public access as the Electrocardiogram Drug-Mediated Multi-Lead Database (ECGDMMLD)[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR7 "Johannesen, L. et al. Late sodium current block for drug-induced long QT syndrome: Results from a prospective clinical trial. Clin. Pharmacol. Therapeut. 99, 214–223 (2016)."). The multi-lead ECG recordings obtained from this database are used to create a list of sensitive features like heart rate variability (HRV), RR, PR, and QT intervals, and QRS duration, which were later used to train and evaluate three classifiers, i.e., Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and XGBoost. The outcomes display that models following a tree-based structure are advantageous for this task. The order of highest accuracy starts with the XGBoost, which showcases 98.1% accuracy, followed by Random Forest and then SVM. This highlights the benefits of using powerful new stage computation methods to understand the complex patterns in ECG introduced by drug induction, which is barely understood with daily measurement techniques. This study proves the role of machine learning in making accurate predictions of heart-related activity from complex signals.

A single heartbeat consists of a complex pattern of electrical events, beginning with the contraction of the atria and ending with the relaxation of the ventricles. These events are displayed as P-wave, QRS complexity, and T-wave[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR4 "Lyon, A., Mincholé, A., Martínez, J. P., Laguna, P. & Rodriguez, B. Computational techniques for ECG analysis and interpretation in light of their contribution to medical advances. J. R. Soc. Interface 15, 20170821 (2018)."). For more than one-hundred years, doctors have observed the shape of these waveforms, along with their steepness, amplitudes, and time differences, to detect cardiovascular disease. Even though this method is important, it has its own difficulties. The difficulty in reading the ECG signal due to the variability of waves from person to person makes interpretation a time-consuming process and is also dependent on the expertise of the physician. Relying only on the manual interpretation can lead to error and results varying from doctor to doctor, especially when finding small issues or working with a large amount of data[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR8 "Rafie, N., Kashou, A. H. & Noseworthy, P. A. Ecg interpretation: clinical relevance, challenges, and advances. Hearts 2, 505–513 (2021)."). Early computation methods that used simple rules are effective but were too strict in handling complicated data and continuously changing ECG, which makes it less useful for heart diagnosis[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR9 "In Chou’s Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice (Sixth Edition) (eds. Surawicz, B. & Knilans,T.K.) (W.B. Saunders, Philadelphia, 2008). 
https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-141603774-3.50001-X
.").

With the introduction of the Machine Learning, ECG analysis has been transformed. This technology provided strong resources to address the shortcomings of the manual and rule-based approaches[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR10 "Ren, H., Jin, H., Chen, C., Ghayvat, H. & Chen, W. A novel cardiac auscultation monitoring system based on wireless sensing for healthcare. IEEE J. Transl. Eng. Health Med. 6, 1–12 (2018)."). proposes a heart monitoring system that is wireless, based on a Hilbert-Huang transformation, which has shown its application on ECG interpretations by using AI. There is a whole variety of ML models that have been experimented with in this area, and each of them has its advantages. Such models as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) were effective in simple classification, such as distinguishing between the normal and arrhythmia heartbeat[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR11 "Osowski, S., Siwek, K. & Markiewicz, T. MLP and SVM networks a comparative study. 46, 37– 40 
https://doi.org/10.1109/NORSIG.2004.250120
(2004)."). More complex computer techniques, like Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) can proceed with more complex tasks by being trained based on patterns of big data repositories[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR12 "Acharya, U. R. et al. A deep convolutional neural network model to classify heartbeats. Comput. Biol. Med. 89, 389–396 (2017)."). Deep Learning models, in particular Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), do a fantastic job at automatically finding meaningful features of the raw ECG waves[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR13 "Kiranyaz, S., Ince, T. & Gabbouj, M. Real-time patient-specific ECG classification by 1D convolutional neural networks. In IEEE Transactions on Bio-Medical Engineering. Vol. 63 (IEEE, 2015)."). In addition to these endeavors, more recent work has devoted attention to signal quality improvement, such as a sparse code shrinkage algorithm, which is based on empirical mode decomposition, to effectively denoise ECGs[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR14 "Tiwari, V. et al. An efficient sparse code shrinkage technique for ECG denoising using empirical mode decomposition. Technol. Health Care 33, 1773–1786 (2025).").

Central to the success of many traditional ML classifiers is the critical step of feature engineering. Model predictability is essentially determined by the quality of the feature (vector) on which each heartbeat is modeled. As a result, studies have aimed at deriving clinically meaningful attributes of the ECG signal.

Primary biomarkers resulting in deep insights into the heart activity and critical in the formation of powerful predictive patterns are such key parameters as heart rate variability (HRV) and precise RR, PR and QT intervals and QRS complex.

In this respect, ensemble learning methods have also emerged as a leader in terms of power and strength. One such example is the random Forest, which is a generalized model, admired because of its ability to learn non-linear and complex associations between ECG features and clinical outcomes. The primary advantage of the Random Forest model is that there is a built-in feature importance analysis mechanism in the model, which provides valuable clinical data regarding the underlying factors that affect its predictions, and this makes the model highly interpretable in clinical practice[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR15 "Asadi, S., Roshan, S. & Kattan, M. W. Random forest swarm optimization-based for heart diseases diagnosis. J. Biomed. Inform. 115, 103690 (2021).").

The other powerful approach is known as XGBoost, which is also an ensemble technique and employs gradient-boosted decision trees, and has become one of the best choice models in classification in healthcare. Its structure is very effective in the event of huge and complex data sets that are in frequent use in the ECG analysis task. Also, XGBoost employs sophisticated methods to avoid overfitting and handles missing data effectively, which is why it is a stable and effective tool to use in real-world medical tasks, where data is not always in an ideal form.

Conversely, despite being very good classifiers, SVMs can be somewhat tricky to apply to the analysis of complex ECGs. Tuning of parameters, scaling of data, and feature selection are important to the performance of an SVM. Moreover, their computational needs may be prohibitive with large data sets needed to thoroughly clinically validate them, and this may restrict their scalability in some applications[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR6 "Attia, Z. I. & Friedman, P. A. Explainable AI for ECG-based prediction of cardiac resynchronization therapy outcomes: learning from machine learning?. Eur. Heart J. 44, 693–695 (2022)."). The evident advantages of approaches like XGBoost and Random Forest in terms of performance, scalability, and the ability to work with complex data made them the first choice of models to be used in this study.

Although the current literature supports the overall effectiveness of such models in the classification of cardiac signals, there is a certain gap in their use in the prediction of the outcomes of the complex, drug-induced changes in cardiac activity. The intersection of AI, IoT, and biomedical engineering is transforming personalized medicine and real-time monitoring of cardiac activity[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR16 "Pokkuluri, K. S. et al. Bridging the gap between technology and medicine through the revolutionary impact of the healthcare Internet of Things on remote patient monitoring. J. Intell. Syst. Internet Things 2, 212–212 (2024)."). This research paper adds to the literature by comparatively assessing the performance of XGBoost, random forest, and SVM on the Electrocardiogram Drug-Mediated Multi-Lead Database(ECGDMMLD). This study specifically tackles the issue of predicting the effects of treatment through an emphasis on a rich set of features, such as HRV, QT intervals, and other important biomarkers, which can be seen as an approach to illustrate the potential of machine learning to improve personalized medicine and enhance real-time clinical decision-making within a pharmacological setting.

## Results

The models used in this study, such as **Random Forest,** **XGBoost**, and **Support Vector Machine (SVM)**, showed impressive results in identifying the order of drug doses with the help of ECG-derived parameters and other clinical features. This section highlights the main findings, including the models’ accuracy, precision, recall, F1-scores, feature importance, and an analysis of the confusion matrix.

### Model performance

Among the three models, XGBoost demonstrated the highest overall accuracy at 98.12%, followed by the Best Random Forest model with an accuracy of 97.63% and a mean accuracy of 96.97%. The accuracy of the SVM model was 45.90%. These results imply that while all models performed admirably in categorizing ECG signals, XGBoost outperformed the Best Random Forest by a small margin.

All models showed remarkable precision, recall, and F1-score outcomes. In particular, the weighted average F1-score of XGBoost was 0.98, that of Best Random Forest was 0.97, and that of SVM was 0.75. All models demonstrated high overall classification performance and the capacity to maintain a decent balance between precision and recall across different classes, as evidenced by the stable macro averages for precision, recall, and F1-score.

Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Tab7) compares the classification performance of all three models. **XGBoost** achieved perfect precision, recall, and F1-scores (1.00) for Class 0, while the other classes also maintained scores above **0.95**.

### Feature importance analysis

Feature importance analysis was carried out for both Random Forest and XGBoost models to identify those ECG features that played the most significant role in the model’s predictions. The feature importance rankings from each model are illustrated in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Fig3). It was revealed in the analysis that the QRS duration, T-wave amplitude, and PR interval consistently ranked as the most important predictors of treatment regimens in both of the models.

In the **Random Forest** model, the **QRS duration** and **PR interval** emerged as the top features, contributing approximately **16%** each to the predictions, respectively. Similarly, in the **XGBoost** model, these features demonstrated prominence of **16%** and **13%**, confirming their clinical relevance in reflecting the influence of treatment regimens on cardiac functions Figure [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Fig3) shows the comparative feature importance analysis across both models and in Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Tab7).

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of **Random Forest**,**XGBoost**, and **SVM** models for determining drug responses on cardiac signals. The high accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores, along with insightful feature importance analysis and confusion matrices, underscore the models’ potential for clinical application, optimizing treatment strategies based on ECG data.

### Confusion matrix analysis

To ensure high-fidelity visualization, all classification accuracy charts and confusion matrices have been standardized to a unified, high-resolution format, accompanying a high-quality 12-lead ECG example (utilized for feature extraction). The standardized confusion matrices for each model given in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Fig4) offer a detailed breakdown of their classification performance across the ten treatment regimens(Fig. [5).](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#Fig5)The matrices show the number of correct predictions (diagonal elements) versus misclassifications (off-diagonal elements) for each class. For the **Random Forest** model, the majority of predictions fell on the diagonal, indicating high accuracy in classification. Similarly, **XGBoost** exhibited minimal misclassifications, and **SVM** showed slightly more misclassifications, particularly between Class B-C-E-D-A and Class E-A-B-D-C, likely due to overlapping ECG features. The confusion matrix of the best-performing model, **XGBoost**, clearly indicates that most misclassifications involved classes with similar ECG characteristics. However, these misclassifications were rare, and the overall performance across all models demonstrated robust classification of ECG signals.

The number of accurate predictions for each class (true positives) was indicated by diagonal elements, whereas the off-diagonal elements illustrate the instances of misclassification. For instance, the Random Forest model predicted Class A-D-E-C-B and Class E-B-A-C-D accurately 85 times and 95 times, respectively. However, there were minor misclassifications in other classes. These findings highlight the effectiveness of machine learning models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM in classifying ECG signals. The impressive accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores, combined with valuable feature importance analysis and confusion matrices, emphasize the potential of these models for clinical use in enhancing treatment strategies informed by ECG data.

### External generalizability validation

To prove the robustness and generalizability of the findings, the machine learning pipeline was independently tested against an external dataset: PhysioNet’s ECGRDVQ (ECG Effects of Ranolazine, Dofetilide, Verapamil, and Quinidine). We streamed the raw .dat time-series data and corresponding clinical information through the identical preprocessing and feature extraction methodologies. The models achieved similarly high precision, recall, and F1 scores natively without retraining. These external validation results firmly establish the stability of the proposed approach on diverse patient populations.

## Discussion

This study reveals that the ensemble methods are the best fit for this type of task, and overall underlines the significance of using machine learning for this problem. The Random Forest, being the accurate model with an accuracy of about 97.63%, proves that the computational methods are good at understanding complex, non-linear relationships between ECG occupied features and specific drug effects[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR19 "Breiman, L. Random forests. Mach. Learn. 45, 5–32 (2001).").

In addition to overall accuracy, the models also demonstrate considerable results in other evaluation class metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score. This depicts that the models are reliable and can clearly distinguish treatment groups, even if their effects on ECG are minor.

Crucially, the model’s internal logic aligns with established clinical knowledge. The feature importance analysis consistently ranked the QT interval and T-wave amplitude as the most influential predictors for classification. These features are well-understood clinical markers of cardiac repolarization, a process known to be highly sensitive to pharmacological intervention[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR20 "Kligfield, P. et al. Recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the electrocardiogram. Circulation 115, 1306–1324 (2007)."). The fact that these models independently converged on these clinically validated features not only reinforces the physiological basis offindings of this study but also builds significant trust in the models’ decision-making processes.

This research achieves competitive results compared to earlier studies that used machine learning for ECG classification. Previous research mainly focused on identifying specific heart conditions, such as arrhythmias or ischemic events, using models like Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Neural Networks, or Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Although these models have achieved high accuracy, they would frequently lack interpretability, which is essential for clinical use[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00702-6#ref-CR12 "Acharya, U. R. et al. A deep convolutional neural network model to classify heartbeats. Comput. Biol. Med. 89, 389–396 (2017)."). In this study, the **Random Forest** and **XGBoost** models not only achieved similar accuracy levels but also highlighted the key ECG features that significantly impact treatment outcomes. This finding addresses a gap in earlier research and illustrates how these models can enable more personalized and precise treatment strategies using ECG data.

Many previous studies did not concentrate on classifying ECG signals according to treatment regimens. This research shows that machine learning models can successfully distinguish between different drug effects, thus filling the previous void and laying the groundwork for enhancing treatment protocols in the future.

The outcomes of this study demonstrate the potential to use it in medical settings. By correctly identifying the right treatment sequences and more tailored options, we can improve personalized healthcare. For instance, if some patients are sensitive towards a particular medicine that increases the QT interval, the model can help find these patients early on. This will allow doctors to modify treatment plans before, and this will result in lower chances of adverse effects. Moreover, the big advantage is that these models are easily understandable, which is very crucial for medical settings. Highlighting the parts that are most important to predict how well the treatment will work will help medical professionals make better decisions, leading to better outcomes for patients. Adding machine learning models like these into daily medical work will make monitoring of patients more efficient and effective, especially in cases of need for quick results.

Considering the identified limitations and the encouraging results achieved, a few future research directions are proposed. First, there is a need to broaden the dataset to inculcate a more varied patient population to confirm the models’ effectiveness across different demographics and validate their generalizability. This can involve gathering ECG data of patients from diverse age groups, comorbidities, and treatment histories. Second, investigating alternative machine learning models, such as gradient boosting machines or deep learning techniques, could provide comparative insights into their performance against the Random Forest and XGBoost models. Third, the development of a system that will help doctors to use these models in their daily clinical practices, which will enable them to analyze the ECG results as soon as they are obtained, allowing for faster results. Finally, keeping track of patients over a long time can demonstrate how well the model predictions are working, which will make them more useful in future operations.

The research carried out shows how different machine learning methods, such as SVM, Random Forest and XGBoost, can be used to classify ECG signals and detect therapy responses. The Random Forest model achieved an astonishing 97.63% accuracy rate, while the accuracy rate of XGBoost is better than that, i.e., 98.12%. Both models demonstrate the satisfying results in distinguishing the effects of drugs on cardiac electrical activity, illustrated by their high precision, recall and F1-score across various categories.

As seen in the analysis of important features, the QT interval and T-wave amplitude are the most dominant in predicting the treatment results. These features are proven important in cases of questions about heart recovery and the reactions of drugs on the body. With an approval to model’s predictions, the outputs also provide new insights into physical signs and treatment outcomes.

Although the results are promising, It persists some limitations. The primary one is the lack of diversity in our dataset, along with the need for more testing across a wider range of patients to validate the results of this study.

Notwithstanding these difficulties, this study advances the field of AI-assisted healthcare by applying machine learning-based techniques to increase the accuracy and effectiveness of ECG analysis, especially when it comes to categorizing medication regimens.

In conclusion, this study lays a strong foundation for applying machine learning in ECG-based treatment classification, paving the way for more personalized and data-driven approaches in clinical practice.
```
