To avoid data leakage, we explicitly distinguish between in-domain and out-of-domain datasets throughout training and evaluation. ECGInstructis used exclusively for training and validation. For in-domain evaluation datasets (PTB-XL Super, PTB-XL Report, CODE-15%, ECG-QA), a dedicated subset is strictly held out for testing, with no overlap with training samples. All out-of-domain datasets (CPSC 2018, CSN, G12EC, MMMU ECG, ECG Arena) are entirely unseen during training and are used solely for evaluation.

### Evaluation metrics

For abnormality detection, we utilize multi-label classification metrics, including Macro AUC, Macro F1, and Hamming Loss, to evaluate PTB-XL Super, CODE-15%, and CPSC 2018, where multiple correct labels may exist. For the ECG-QA, CSN, and G12EC datasets, we adopt accuracy as the evaluation metric.

For report generation, rather than relying on traditional text generation metrics, we leverage strong LLMs as evaluators, following the approach of ref. [12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR12 "Zheng, L. et al. Judging llm-as-a-judge with mt-bench and chatbot arena. Adv. Neural Inform. Process. Syst. 36, 46595–46623 (2024)."). This method provides a more nuanced evaluation by focusing on key aspects of the reports. Specifically, we use GPT-4o to compare the model-generated reports against those written by cardiologists. We introduce a “Report Perfect Score”, which is based on three critical components of a generated report: (1) Rhythms (0 to 10 points), (2) Waveform Morphology (0 to 10 points), and (3) Diagnosis (0 to 10 points). The final score is the average of these three components, scaled to a maximum of 100 points. The prompt used to query GPT-4o for evaluating the report score is provided in Supplementary Fig. [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1).

For MMMU ECG, we adopt accuracy as the primary metric. We have designed systematic, rule-based evaluation pipelines to ensure robust and consistent scoring. To mitigate the potential influence of any intermediate generations (e.g., reasoning steps) in long responses, we employ robust regular expressions and develop response-processing workflows. These are used to extract answer options from the long responses for accurate answer matching. In cases where no valid answer can be extracted from the model’s response, we perform random selection to assign a score.

For ECG Arena, we also employ a strong judge model, GPT-4o, to assess model performance by comparing generated responses with ground truth answers. The evaluation considers three perspectives, each scored on a scale of 0–10: Accuracy (how closely the model’s response matches the ground truth), Completeness (whether the model provides a comprehensive answer covering all aspects of ECG interpretation), and Instruction Adherence (how well the model follows the specific instructions in the question). We calculate the final score by averaging these three aspects and scaling to a maximum of 100 points. The specific prompt used for GPT-4 evaluation is provided in Supplementary Fig. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1).

### Overall performance

We show in-domain and out-of-domain results in Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab1) and [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab2), respectively. Overall, we observe that PULSEachieves state-of-the-art performance on different datasets and tasks.

As shown in Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab1), PULSEdemonstrates significant improvements over both proprietary and open-source MLLMs across all in-domain datasets. Specifically, PULSEsurpasses the best proprietary model (GPT-4o) with a 27% improvement in AUC, a 15-point gain in report score, and a 36% increase in accuracy on the PTB-XL Super, PTB-XL Report, and ECG-QA tasks, respectively. Moreover, PULSEachieves notable gains over the best open-source model, with a 29% improvement in AUC, a 17-point gain in report score, and a 42% increase in accuracy on the same tasks. These results highlight the complexity of ECG image interpretation, a task where even the best proprietary models perform near randomly. By fine-tuning on ECGInstruct, PULSEachieves substantial performance improvements, demonstrating the importance of high-quality and task-related instruction-tuning. While some domain-specific models achieve comparable or even superior performance on particular datasets, their highly specialized designs often limit their ability to generalize across diverse tasks, especially open-ended reasoning, and settings where only ECG printout images are available without associated raw signals. This lack of flexibility restricts their broader applicability in real-world clinical environments, where task requirements can vary significantly.

Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab2) presents the comparison results on out-of-domain datasets, where PULSEconsistently delivers outstanding performance. Notably, it achieves a significant 21% improvement in accuracy on the MMMU ECG benchmark compared to GPT-4o. This substantial improvement indicates the PULSE’s robustness and ability to generalize to unseen and real-world ECG images. The ECG Arena benchmark presents a more challenging task for all models, characterized by a multi-turn, open-ended question-answering format, which is designed for real-world ECG images and closely simulates real clinical scenarios. Despite these challenges, PULSEstill surpasses the best proprietary model by 4 points and outperforms the leading open-source model by an impressive 14 points in terms of arena score. These results highlight PULSE’s relative strength in handling complex, clinically-oriented ECG interpretation and analysis. Additionally, the performance gap across models on this challenging benchmark indicates considerable room for future improvements in this task.

### Effect of training data source

Given that ECGInstructis compiled from diverse datasets, it is crucial to examine how each dataset contributes to the model’s overall performance. Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab3) presents a comparative analysis of models trained on various dataset combinations. The model trained exclusively on PTB-XL (P) exhibits the lowest performance across all datasets, indicating the limitations of relying on a single data source for effective generalization. As we progressively incorporate additional datasets into the training set, the model’s performance consistently improves. These results highlight the importance of curating diverse training data, as expanding beyond a single source enhances the model’s capacity to generalize across datasets and tasks. We provide an ablation study on different instruction tasks in Supplementary Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1).

### Comparison between signal encoder and image encoder

We present the comparison results between the image-based encoder (ours) and the signal-based encoder in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Fig2). To ensure a fair and controlled comparison, both models are trained end-to-end using the exact same training data, instruction-tuning tasks, optimization settings, and overall model architecture, differing only in the encoder head used to process ECGs. Specifically, the image-based model encodes ECGs as digital images, while the signal-based model encodes ECGs as time-series. We adopt a randomly initialized 1D-ResNet18[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR14 "Liu, C. et al. Zero-shot ecg classification with multimodal learning and test-time clinical knowledge enhancement. In Proc. 41st Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. 31949–31963 (2024).") that is fully trained during instruction tuning as the ECG signal encoder. The supervision signals (ground-truth responses) for both models are derived from clinician annotations and reports in the underlying datasets used to construct ECGInstruct. The results show that the image-based encoder consistently outperforms the signal-based encoder across different evaluation tasks, with particularly significant improvements observed in out-of-domain datasets. These findings highlight that encoding ECGs as images not only aligns with the goal of enabling broader applicability of automated ECG diagnosis, especially in resource-constrained or remote settings (where only printed or digital ECGs are available) but also empirically surpasses the performance of the signal-based encoder model.

### Case study

We present some examples from our benchmark, comparing the outputs of our model with GPT-4o for ECG report generation (Supplementary Fig. [11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1) and Fig. [12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1)) and ECG Arena (Supplementary Fig. [13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1)). While GPT-4o is capable of generating reports and answering questions by following instructions, it often produces responses that, although well-structured and seemingly relevant, contain significant inaccuracies in interpretation. In contrast, PULSEconsistently provides more accurate responses that align closely with the ground truths. Additionally, we observed that GPT-4o tends to over-rely on its OCR capabilities when textual information (e.g., printed axis labels, numerical values like heart rate or QRS duration) is present in images, leading to superficial reasoning based on text rather than a deep analysis of visual data. As shown in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Fig3), GPT-4o identifies a left axis deviation based on the printed QRS axis degree, without analyzing the visual waveform patterns. If such axis information were absent, the model would likely fail to identify the deviation.

### Human expert performance

We engaged three clinical experts in cardiology (see Supplementary Table [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1) for demographic and professional information) to evaluate a sample of 30 questions from the MMMU ECG. The evaluation was conducted remotely. Each expert received a standardized document containing the ECG images and corresponding multiple-choice questions. Experts were provided with ECG images in both printed and digital formats, and were allowed to zoom in and inspect details as needed for accurate interpretation. They were instructed to complete the task independently without external assistance, relying solely on their clinical knowledge. Their responses were then aggregated to calculate individual and average accuracy.

Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab4) presents the performance comparison. Human experts achieved strong results, with an average accuracy of 84.4%, and the top-performing expert reaching 93.3%. In contrast, PULSEachieved 64.0%, outperforming GPT-4o, which scored 43.5%. These results highlight the difficulty of the task and the value of domain-specific instruction tuning, while also suggesting that further improvements are needed to match expert-level reasoning.

## Discussion

In this paper, we study the problem of ECG image interpretation, which is a crucial task in assessing cardiac conditions. We develop PULSE, a fully open-source MLLM trained on ECGInstructwith over one million samples across a diverse range of ECG-related tasks. Evaluated on the proposed benchmark, ECGBench, our model shows state-of-the-art performance, surpassing both proprietary and open-source MLLMs across multiple in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation datasets. This work demonstrates the potential of using MLLMs for enhancing ECG image analysis and interpretation in clinical applications.

Many domain-specific models have been proposed to enhance automatic ECG diagnosis[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR1 "Hannun, A. Y. et al. Cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection and classification in ambulatory electrocardiograms using a deep neural network. Nat. Med. 25, 65–69 (2019)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR2 "Ribeiro, A. H. et al. Automatic diagnosis of the 12-lead ecg using a deep neural network. Nat. Commun. 11, 1760 (2020)."),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR3 "Hughes, J. W. et al. Performance of a convolutional neural network and explainability technique for 12-lead electrocardiogram interpretation. JAMA Cardiol 6, 1285–1295 (2021)."). For example, ref. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR2 "Ribeiro, A. H. et al. Automatic diagnosis of the 12-lead ecg using a deep neural network. Nat. Commun. 11, 1760 (2020).") applied convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to encode ECG signals for diagnosing 6 types of abnormalities. To reduce dependence on high-quality labeled data, recent studies[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR13 "Li, J., Liu, C., Cheng, S., Arcucci, R. & Hong, S. Frozen language model helps ecg zero-shot learning. In Medical Imaging with Deep Learning, 402–415 (PMLR, 2024)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR14 "Liu, C. et al. Zero-shot ecg classification with multimodal learning and test-time clinical knowledge enhancement. In Proc. 41st Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. 31949–31963 (2024)."),[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR15 "Na, Y., Park, M., Tae, Y. & Joo, S. Guiding masked representation learning to capture spatio-temporal relationship of electrocardiogram. In The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (2023).") have further explored self-supervised learning approaches using unlabeled ECG training data. For example, ref. [14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR14 "Liu, C. et al. Zero-shot ecg classification with multimodal learning and test-time clinical knowledge enhancement. In Proc. 41st Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. 31949–31963 (2024).") proposed an ECG representation learning framework by integrating the ECG signals and clinical reports, showing improved performance in zero-shot ECG classification tasks. Despite these successes, most approaches treat ECG data as temporal physiological signals, which could be limiting in certain resource-constrained or remote settings where only printed or digital images are available. Recently, a few methods[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR5 "Sangha, V. et al. Automated multilabel diagnosis on electrocardiographic images and signals. Nat. Commun. 13, 1583 (2022)."),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR6 "Sangha, V. et al. Detection of left ventricular systolic dysfunction from electrocardiographic images. Circulation 148, 765–777 (2023)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR18 "Khunte, A. et al. Automated diagnostic reports from images of electrocardiograms at the point-of-care. medRxiv (2024).") have been proposed for ECG diagnosis using ECG images. For example, ref. [18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR18 "Khunte, A. et al. Automated diagnostic reports from images of electrocardiograms at the point-of-care. medRxiv (2024).") developed a diagnostic report generation framework for ECG images, which is built upon a BEiT[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR32 "Bao, H., Dong, L., Piao, S. & Wei, F. Beit: Bert pre-training of image transformers. In Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Represent. (2022).") vision transformer encoder and a GPT-2[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR33 "Radford, A. et al. Language models are unsupervised multitask learners. OpenAI blog 1, 9 (2019).") decoder. However, their model is only capable of the clinical report generation task, without generalizability to other diverse tasks. In contrast, our study investigates the capabilities of MLLMs for ECG image interpretation. We curate a diverse range of instruction-tuning datasets to fine-tune the model, thus improving model generalizability.

Recent advancements in MLLMs have shown promising results in various healthcare domains. General medical multimodal models such as LLaVA-Med[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR8 "Li, B. et al. Llava-onevision: Easy visual task transfer. Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. (2025)."), MedPaLM[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR34 "Singhal, K. et al. Large language models encode clinical knowledge. Nature 620, 172–180 (2023)."),[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR35 "Singhal, K. et al. Towards expert-level medical question answering with large language models. Nat. Med. 31, 943–950 (2025)."), and Med-Gemini[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR36 "Saab, K. et al. Capabilities of gemini models in medicine. arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.18416 (2024).") have demonstrated capabilities in processing diverse medical data types. Additionally, domain-specific multimodal models have been developed for specialized fields like pathology[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR37 "Lu, M. Y. et al. A multimodal generative ai copilot for human pathology. Nature 1–3 (2024)."),[38](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR38 "Xu, H. et al. A whole-slide foundation model for digital pathology from real-world data. Nature 1–8 (2024).") and radiology[39](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR39 "Wu, C., Zhang, X., Zhang, Y., Wang, Y. & Xie, W. Towards generalist foundation model for radiology by leveraging web-scale 2D & 3D medical data. Nat. Commun. 16, 7866 (2025)."). These models have shown potential in integrating visual and textual information to support clinical decision-making and medical education. However, despite the importance of ECG data in cardiac diagnosis and monitoring, current MLLMs often struggle to process ECG images effectively. This limitation highlights a significant gap in the application of MLLMs to cardiology, where the ability to interpret both visual ECG representations and accompanying clinical information is crucial.

Instruction-tuning has proven effective in the multimodal domain, particularly in vision-language models like LLaVA[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR22 "Liu, H., Li, C., Wu, Q. & Lee, Y. J. Visual instruction tuning. Adv. Neural Inform. Process. Syst. 36, 34892–34916 (2023)."), MiniGPT-4[40](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR40 "Zhu, D., Chen, J., Shen, X., Li, X. & Elhoseiny, M. Minigpt-4: Enhancing vision-language understanding with advanced large language models. In Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Represent. (2024).") and InstructBLIP[41](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR41 "Dai, W. et al. InstructBLIP: Towards general-purpose vision-language models with instruction tuning. In Thirty-seventh Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (2023). 
https://openreview.net/forum?id=vvoWPYqZJA
."). These models demonstrate impressive generalizability across various visual understanding and reasoning tasks. While multimodal instruction-tuning has been applied to general medical imaging tasks[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR9 "Li, C. et al. Llava-med: Training a large language-and-vision assistant for biomedicine in one day. Adv. Neural Inform. Process. Syst. 36, 28541–28564 (2023)."),[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR34 "Singhal, K. et al. Large language models encode clinical knowledge. Nature 620, 172–180 (2023)."), its application to ECG images remains largely unexplored. A recent work[42](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR42 "Wan, Z. et al. MEIT: Multimodal electrocardiogram instruction tuning on large language models for report generation. In Findings Assoc. Comput. Linguist. ACL 14510–14527 (2025).") introduced a targeted instruction-tuning framework and fine-tuned existing open-source LLMs for ECG report generation. However, their approach is limited by a single-task instruction dataset focused solely on report generation, potentially constraining its adaptability to other ECG-related tasks. Moreover, their work also treats ECG data as temporal signals, whereas our paper focuses on encoding ECG images with MLLMs, which is more applicable to real scenarios where only printed or digital ECG images are available.

Beyond overall benchmark performance, it is important to assess whether the proposed data synthesis and training paradigm generalizes across different MLLM backbones. To this end, we fine-tune Qwen2-VL-7B using ECGInstructand compare its performance with that of LLaVA-v1.6-Vicuna-7B across multiple tasks, as shown in Supplementary Table [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1). While both backbone models demonstrate strong performance, LLaVA consistently outperforms Qwen across all benchmarks, including PTB-XL Super (76.9 vs. 75.1), PTB-XL Report (65.4 vs. 62.8), and MMMU ECG (64.0 vs. 60.4). These results suggest that the proposed training data and methodology are broadly effective.

To further evaluate robustness under realistic acquisition conditions, we assess model performance on photographs of printed ECG images. Specifically, we sample 150 cases from the out-of-domain evaluation datasets (excluding MMMU ECG and ECG Arena, which already contain real paper ECGs), print the images, and capture photographs under varying conditions. As shown in Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#Tab5), the model exhibits only modest performance degradation when applied to photographed printouts, supporting its robustness to common real-world artifacts and its applicability in practical clinical scenarios.

In addition to model accuracy and robustness, the reliability of the evaluation protocol is critical for interpreting results. To assess the validity of the proposed LLM-based scoring approach, we compared its outputs directly against human evaluation conducted by clinical experts (cardiologists). The expert evaluation results demonstrate that LLM-based scores closely mirror expert clinical judgments across both datasets. As shown in Supplementary Table [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1), GPT-4o’s report-generation scores (51.9) and human scores (50.8) yield a Pearson correlation of 0.934, while its ECG Arena scores (32.8 vs. 35.1) correlate at 0.920. Similarly, our model’s report scores (62.8 vs. 64.1) achieve a Pearson correlation of 0.919, and its ECG Arena scores (37.4 vs. 39.0) correlate at 0.917. These consistently high correlation coefficients suggest that the proposed LLM-based metric aligns with human evaluation.

Despite these encouraging results, several limitations remain. While PTB-XL[43](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR43 "Wagner, P. et al. Ptb-xl, a large publicly available electrocardiography dataset. Sci. Data 7, 1–15 (2020).") provides expert-annotated diagnostic information, its original reports are not always fully narrative and may consist of structured key points or multilingual entries. To mitigate this, we systematically rewrite and translate the original annotations into standardized natural-language reports while preserving their clinical meaning (using a prompt as shown in Supplementary Fig. [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#MOESM1)) and validate a subset through expert review and consistency checks against SCP-ECG statements. Nevertheless, richer clinician-authored narrative reports would further benefit report generation tasks, and integrating such datasets remains an important direction for future work.

Taken together, these results highlight several clinically relevant use cases enabled by ECG image interpretation. The proposed approach supports scenarios in which raw signal data are unavailable, such as scanned or photographed paper ECGs, legacy medical records, and cross-institutional referrals. Unlike traditional classification models[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR1 "Hannun, A. Y. et al. Cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection and classification in ambulatory electrocardiograms using a deep neural network. Nat. Med. 25, 65–69 (2019)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR2 "Ribeiro, A. H. et al. Automatic diagnosis of the 12-lead ecg using a deep neural network. Nat. Commun. 11, 1760 (2020)."),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR3 "Hughes, J. W. et al. Performance of a convolutional neural network and explainability technique for 12-lead electrocardiogram interpretation. JAMA Cardiol 6, 1285–1295 (2021).") that are limited to predicting a fixed set of labels, our model supports richer forms of clinical interaction, including feature recognition, rhythm analysis, report generation, and multi-turn reasoning. By unifying these capabilities within a single framework, the model aligns more naturally with real-world clinical workflows, allowing users to upload an ECG image together with targeted diagnostic or interpretive queries.

Nevertheless, important challenges remain in translating benchmark performance into real-world clinical deployment. Although ECGBenchcovers a diverse set of clinically motivated tasks, bridging the gap between controlled evaluation and clinical practice will require closer collaboration with clinicians, prospective testing in hospital environments, and task designs that more directly reflect real clinical decision-making processes. Deployment also raises critical safety and bias considerations, including the risk of incorrect or overconfident outputs, dataset biases related to patient demographics or acquisition conditions, and potential misuse without appropriate clinical oversight. Addressing these concerns will require clinician-in-the-loop evaluation, bias-aware dataset curation, and the development of safeguards to support responsible deployment.

Looking ahead, several directions are essential for advancing ECG image-based MLLMs toward clinical readiness. While PULSEdemonstrates strong performance across evaluation datasets, more complex and open-ended tasks remain challenging and demand stronger reasoning and instruction-following capabilities. Progress along these dimensions will likely require advances in data, model design, and evaluation. Future work may incorporate more diverse instruction-following data, as well as scaled high-quality chain-of-thought and multi-turn supervision derived from expert knowledge, structured medical ontologies (e.g., SNOMED CT[44](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02551-3#ref-CR44 "Stearns, M. Q., Price, C., Spackman, K. A. & Wang, A. Y. Snomed clinical terms: overview of the development process and project status. In Proceedings of the AMIA Symposium, 662 (American Medical Informatics Association, 2001).")), clinical guidelines, and medical literature, to better guide intermediate reasoning steps.

Beyond implicit feature learning from images, a promising direction is to incorporate explicit ECG measurements (e.g., intervals, amplitudes, axes) extracted via a calibrated measurement module for scanned/photographed paper ECGs as complementary signals via feature-enhanced instruction-tuning data and joint multimodal training. Integrating such measurement extraction with our MLLM could enable both structured numeric outputs and narrative clinical interpretations that are better grounded in verifiable measurements.

In addition, while this work emphasizes robustness to image-domain artifacts, incorporating explicit signal-domain noise modeling represents an important avenue for future research. Systematic analysis across different noise types and severity levels may help identify failure modes and improve robustness under real-world clinical conditions. Finally, to support long-duration ECG monitoring scenarios, such as Holter recordings and wearable devices, future work will explore hierarchical and temporal aggregation mechanisms that enable event-level reasoning and longitudinal summarization across segmented ECG windows.
```

##### [A dual-branch deep learning framework for emotion recognition from EEG signals](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8)

```
## Abstract

Mental health monitoring through emotion recognition plays an important role in early intervention and personalized healthcare systems. Traditional EEG-based emotion recognition approaches have encountered significant limitations, including heavy reliance on manual feature engineering, poor generalization across datasets, and computational complexity that restricts real-world deployment. This study introduces a novel hybrid dual-branch deep learning architecture that integrates temporal and spectral feature extraction for robust EEG-based emotion recognition, while minimizing preprocessing requirements. The proposed framework integrates a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to capture temporal dependencies directly from raw EEG signals, while concurrently leveraging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to extract spatial features from Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) representations. This architecture further incorporates innovative cross-modality enhancement mechanisms, such as inverse MFCC computation and LSTM-to-MFCC projection, which facilitate bidirectional feature learning between temporal and spectral domains. Subsequently, feature fusion is achieved through element-wise multiplication and concatenation, and the integrated representations are classified using an Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The evaluation has been conducted on three benchmark datasets: Brainwave EEG, WESAD, and SWELL, achieving remarkable performance with accuracies of 96.49%, 99.99%, and 99.99%, respectively. The model has attained perfect precision, recall, and F1-scores on the WESAD and SWELL datasets, setting new state-of-the-art standards. Comparative analysis has demonstrated the method’s superiority over existing machine learning and deep learning techniques, while preserving computational efficiency that supports real-time applications. These results have confirmed the framework’s strong potential for practical use in mental health monitoring and affective computing. The source code of this work is available at: [https://github.com/DebamSahaCS/Dual-Branch-DL-Framework](https://github.com/DebamSahaCS/Dual-Branch-DL-Framework)

## Introduction

Mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, and stress-related disorders[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR1 "Khan, M. R. & Ahmad, M. Mental stress detection from eeg signals using comparative analysis of random forest and recurrent neural network. In 2024 International Conference on Advances in Computing, Communication, Electrical, and Smart Systems (iCACCESS), 1–6, (2024) 
https://doi.org/10.1109/iCACCESS61735.2024.10499496.") have been recognized as significant public health challenges across the globe, impacting the emotional stability and daily lives of millions of people. The timely identification and continuous tracking of emotional states have been regarded as vital for ensuring effective mental health care and intervention strategies. Nevertheless, conventional approaches to emotion evaluation, including self-reports and standardized questionnaires, have been constrained by issues of subjectivity, recall bias, and their inability to provide continuous assessment, thereby reducing their utility in real-time monitoring of mental well-being.

Within this framework, emotion recognition[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR2 "Li, Q., Zhang, T., Chen, C. P., Zhang, X. & Hu, B. Dgc-link: Dual-gate chebyshev linkage network on eeg emotion recognition. IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing (2025).") based on electroencephalogram (EEG) signals has received considerable attention in the fields of affective computing and brain–computer interface (BCI) research. EEG signals record the brain’s electrical activity, providing a direct and objective reflection of the cognitive and affective mechanisms associated with various emotional states. Utilizing EEG for emotion recognition has enabled the design of systems that can provide continuous and objective monitoring of emotional conditions, thereby supporting early diagnosis and promoting personalized interventions for mental health management.

Despite its promising potential, EEG-based emotion recognition[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR3 "Li, X. et al. Eeg based emotion recognition: A tutorial and review. ACM Computing Surveys 55, 1–57 (2022).") has encountered several challenges that have limited its practical application. EEG signals are highly non-stationary and exhibit substantial variability across individuals as well as recording sessions, which has made the development of models with strong generalization capabilities across subjects and datasets particularly difficult. Furthermore, many existing emotion recognition approaches have relied extensively on manual feature engineering, where domain experts extract handcrafted attributes such as band power or statistical measures from EEG recordings. This process has not only proven to be time-consuming. However, it has also often failed to adequately capture the intricate spatiotemporal dynamics embedded in EEG signals that are associated with diverse emotional states.

Moreover, deep learning techniques[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR4 "LeCun, Y., Bengio, Y. & Hinton, G. Deep learning. nature 521, 436–444 (2015)."), which have achieved remarkable success in fields such as image and speech recognition, have also been employed for EEG-based emotion recognition or EEG-Based stress detection[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR1 "Khan, M. R. & Ahmad, M. Mental stress detection from eeg signals using comparative analysis of random forest and recurrent neural network. In 2024 International Conference on Advances in Computing, Communication, Electrical, and Smart Systems (iCACCESS), 1–6, (2024) 
https://doi.org/10.1109/iCACCESS61735.2024.10499496.") to overcome the limitations of manual feature engineering. However, these approaches have often required substantial computational resources and involved large model architectures, making them less suitable for real-time and portable applications in mental health monitoring. In addition, although many deep learning models have reported high accuracy on specific datasets, they have frequently struggled to generalize across diverse datasets and recording conditions, thereby restricting their practical effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

To overcome these challenges, this study has introduced a hybrid dual-branch deep learning framework for EEG-based emotion recognition, aiming to enhance accuracy, generalization, and computational efficiency while minimizing dependence on manual feature engineering. The proposed model has integrated temporal and spatial feature extraction within a unified structure. Specifically, the temporal branch has employed a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR5 "Hochreiter, S. & Schmidhuber, J. Long short-term memory. Neural Comput. 9, 1735–1780 (1997).") directly on raw EEG signals to capture temporal dependencies and dynamic variations linked to emotional states. In parallel, the spatial branch has extracted Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC)[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR6 "Hossan, M. A., Memon, S. & Gregory, M. A. A novel approach for mfcc feature extraction. In 2010 4th international conference on signal processing and communication systems, 1–5 (IEEE, 2010)."),[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR7 "Gnana Rajesh, D. Analysis of mfcc features for eeg signal classification. Int. J. Adv. Sig. Img. Sci 2 (2016).") from EEG signals and applied a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for spatial feature learning, leveraging the capability of MFCC[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR8 "Mini, P., Thomas, T. & Gopikakumari, R. EEG based direct speech BCI system using a fusion of SMRT and MFCC/LPCC features with ANN classifier. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 68, 102625 (2021).") to represent frequency-domain characteristics that are highly relevant for emotion recognition.

This work has proposed a hybrid dual-branch deep learning model for EEG-based emotion recognition designed to overcome the existing limitations in accuracy, generalization, and computational efficiency while reducing reliance on manual feature extraction. The architecture integrates two complementary branches: the temporal branch utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network applied directly to raw EEG signals to capture temporal dependencies and dynamic emotional patterns, while the spatial branch extracts Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) from EEG signals and employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to learn spatial features, leveraging MFCC’s ability to represent frequency-domain information relevant to emotion recognition. Beyond these primary branches, the model innovatively implements cross-modality feature learning by calculating inverse MFCCs from the CNN outputs and generating MFCCs from signals reconstructed using LSTM outputs. This approach enriches feature representations and enables the model to capture complementary spatiotemporal information inherent in EEG signals. Outputs from both branches have been combined using multiplicative fusion and concatenation, followed by flattening and classification through an Artificial Neural Network (ANN). This unified end-to-end framework allows for continuous emotion recognition from raw EEG data with minimal preprocessing, marking a significant advancement in model design and practical applicability for mental health monitoring systems.

The proposed model’s effectiveness has been demonstrated on three publicly available EEG emotion datasets: Brainwave EEG[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR9 "Alhammadi, A. Brainwave eeg dataset, 
https://doi.org/10.21227/n2fv-ae84
(2020)."), WESAD[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR10 "Schmidt, P., Reiss, A., Duerichen, R., Marberger, C. & Van Laerhoven, K. Introducing wesad, a multimodal dataset for wearable stress and affect detection. In Proceedings of the 20th ACM international conference on multimodal interaction, 400–408 (2018)."), and SWELL[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR11 "Koldijk, S., Sappelli, M., Verberne, S., Neerincx, M. A. & Kraaij, W. The swell knowledge work dataset for stress and user modeling research. In Proceedings of the 16th international conference on multimodal interaction, 291–298 (2014)."), achieving an impressive classification accuracy of 99% on all datasets. This performance highlights the model’s superior capability in EEG-based emotion recognition. By integrating a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture with MFCC-based feature extraction, the system has significantly reduced computational complexity while attaining state-of-the-art accuracy. These characteristics make the approach highly promising for practical implementation in real-time emotion recognition systems aimed at mental health monitoring and brain–computer interface applications.

## Analysis of results

This section provides a thorough evaluation of the proposed hybrid CNN-LSTM model’s effectiveness in EEG-based emotion recognition across three benchmark datasets: Brainwave EEG, WESAD, and SWELL. The goal of this analysis has been to examine the model’s accuracy, generalization capability, and robustness when classifying emotional states under varying conditions and sensor modalities. The evaluation begins with a detailed presentation of quantitative performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrices. These metrics deliver a comprehensive perspective on the model’s predictive abilities across different emotional categories, enabling an objective comparison across datasets.

Additionally, we examine the training dynamics of the model through loss and accuracy curves, which provide insights into its learning progression across epochs and demonstrate its convergence stability. Following this, a comparative analysis is conducted against traditional and baseline deep learning models to highlight the performance gains attributed to the hybrid dual-branch architecture and cross-modality feature augmentation. This detailed result analysis confirms the effectiveness of integrating temporal and spectral information, illustrating the model’s ability to generalize robustly across datasets that vary in recording hardware, experimental setups, and emotion labeling schemes. These findings emphasize the model’s practical applicability for real-world emotion recognition tasks, particularly within mental health monitoring contexts.

### Analysis on Brainwave dataset

The proposed hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture was extensively validated using the Brainwave EEG dataset, which includes three emotional categories: Negative (0), Neutral (1), and Positive (2). The results underscore the model’s high performance in terms of accuracy, balance across classes, convergence, and robustness against misclassification. Specifically, the classification accuracy was exceptionally high for all three emotional states, correctly identified for the Negative class with 97.18%, a perfect score for the Neutral class 100%, and 92.25% accurately classified for the Positive class. Figure [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig2)a exhibits a strong diagonal dominance, indicating that the model effectively learned meaningful representations for each emotion with minimal confusion between categories. Most errors occurred within the Positive class, where 10 samples were misclassified as Negative and one as Neutral, potentially due to overlapping EEG features during transitions between emotional states. Training and validation accuracy curves, illustrated in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig3)a, provide insight into the model’s learning process. The model rapidly surpassed 95% training accuracy within the initial 10 epochs, ultimately reaching a final training accuracy of 99.53%, indicating strong memorization capability. Validation accuracy stabilized at 96.49%, with a peak of 96.72%, demonstrating excellent generalization. The training loss steadily declined towards zero, confirming effective convergence without evidence of underfitting or overfitting. This behavior underscores the model’s high capacity and effective regularization, making it well-suited for challenging EEG-based classification tasks. The true class distribution, as depicted in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig4)a, was nearly balanced across all three classes with 142–143 samples per class, effectively preventing training bias. The predicted class distribution closely mirrored this balance, showing only minor deviations: 148 samples were predicted as Negative, 144 as Neutral, and 135 as Positive. Regarding misclassification on the Brainwave EEG dataset, out of 427 test samples, the model correctly classified 412 and misclassified 15, resulting in an overall test accuracy of 96.49%. Analysis of the misclassified samples revealed that most errors occurred within the positive class, suggesting subtle EEG variations in this category caused occasional confusion with neutral or negative classes. The lowest-confidence misclassification had a softmax probability of 0.5205, while others ranged up to 0.91, indicating relatively low uncertainty across predictions.

### Analysis on WESAD dataset

To evaluate the generalization and robustness of the proposed hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture, its performance was tested on the WESAD dataset, a prominent physiological benchmark commonly used in affective computing. This EEG-focused dataset encompasses three emotional categories: Neutral, Stress, and Amusement. The experiments demonstrated exceptionally high accuracy and stable convergence, underscoring the model’s suitability for real-world scenarios.

An analysis of classification accuracy and confusion revealed near-perfect results, with only 3 misclassifications out of 27,130 test samples, yielding an overall accuracy of 99.99%. Specifically, 10,156 out of 10,157 Neutral samples were correctly predicted, the Stress class achieved 100% accuracy with all 10,200 samples correctly classified, and the Amusement class had 6,771 out of 6,773 samples correctly identified. The extremely low misclassification rate highlights the model’s strong discriminative power, with only two Amusement samples misclassified as Neutral and one Stress sample misclassified as Neutral. The confusion matrix exhibits strong diagonal dominance, validating the robustness of the learned feature representations, which are depicted in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig2)c. Figure [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig3)c indicates rapid and stable convergence in training and loss curves; training accuracy approaches 99.90% within 14 epochs, and validation accuracy stabilizes at 99.99% without signs of overfitting. Training loss declines steeply and smoothly converges toward zero. Error analysis of the few misclassified samples shows that one Stress sample was predicted as Neutral with a confidence of 0.9965, and two Amusement samples were predicted as Stress with confidences of 0.7336 and 1.000,0, respectively. Regarding class distribution, the true data shows a slight imbalance, with fewer samples in the Amusement class (Neutral: 10,157; Stress: 10,200; Amusement: 6,773). Despite this, the predicted class distribution closely aligns with the ground truth (10,158, 10,201, and 6,771, respectively), reflecting unbiased learning even in the presence of class imbalance—a vital characteristic for emotion recognition tasks, where rare classes are often prone to misclassification, can be shown in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig4)c.

### Analysis on SWELL dataset

The proposed hybrid CNN-LSTM model’s performance was rigorously evaluated on the SWELL dataset, which is recognized for capturing EEG responses under emotional and stress-induced conditions. The evaluation results indicate near-perfect classification capabilities across all three emotional states.

The confusion matrix, presented in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig2)b, further confirms this outstanding performance. Among 78,328 test samples, only one misclassification occurred: one sample from class 0 was incorrectly predicted as class 2. All other samples were correctly classified, yielding an overall accuracy of 99.99% and per-class accuracies near 100%. Training and validation curve analysis, shown in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig3)b, demonstrates sharp convergence of loss, which dropped from 0.35 to nearly zero within the first few epochs. Training accuracy rapidly increased, stabilizing at 99.96%, while validation accuracy reached 100% and remained steady. These trends exemplify efficient learning, strong convergence, and excellent generalization on unseen data. Regarding misclassification, only one sample was incorrectly classified during evaluation—specifically, sample index 31794, with a true label of class 0, was predicted as class 2 with a high confidence score of 0.9877. This indicates that while the model’s prediction mechanism is confident, slight confusion arose in this rare edge case, potentially due to overlapping EEG features between the two emotion classes. Class distribution analysis reveals a highly balanced dataset with true class counts of 26,041 (class 0), 26,057 (class 1), and 26,230 (class 2). Predicted class counts closely match these values, showing counts of 26,040, 26,057, and 26,231, respectively. This close alignment between true and predicted distributions highlights not only the model’s accuracy but also its robust generalization across classes, effectively avoiding overfitting or class bias, as illustrated in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Fig4)b.

### Comparative analysis

To assess the robustness and adaptability of the proposed hybrid CNN–LSTM architecture enhanced with MFCC-based cross-modality features, its performance was compared across three distinct EEG-based emotion and stress recognition datasets: Brainwave EEG, WESAD, and SWELL. These datasets vary significantly in terms of recording equipment, experimental protocols, the number of participants, and class distributions, making them well-suited for validating the generalization capacity of the proposed model.

### Observations and discussion

The proposed model demonstrates consistently high performance across all three datasets. Under the single stratified split as seen in Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab1), the model achieves test accuracies of 96.49% on Brainwave EEG and 99.99% on both WESAD and SWELL. To ensure reproducibility beyond a single split, we further reported Monte-Carlo cross-validation results (30 stratified 70/30 runs) with distribution-free 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, yielding mean test accuracies of 95.48% (95% CI: 95.18–95.78) on Brainwave EEG, 99.93% (99.92–99.93) on WESAD, and 99.99% (99.99–99.99) on SWELL as depicted in Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab2). Collectively, these results highlight the architecture’s strong ability to maintain stable performance across diverse data sources, sensor types, and experimental conditions.

The predicted class distributions across datasets closely align with the true class distributions, indicating unbiased predictions even in the presence of mild class imbalance (e.g., WESAD’s relatively smaller positive class). The effectiveness of the proposed cross-modality enhancement—via inverse MFCC computation and LSTM-to-MFCC projection—likely contributes to this robustness by enriching temporal and spectral feature learning and promoting stronger cross-domain representations. The comparatively lower performance on Brainwave EEG may be attributed to the limited number of electrodes (four channels from the Muse headband), shorter recording durations, smaller dataset size, and potentially higher noise levels typical of consumer-grade EEG devices. Overall, the comparative evaluation confirms that the hybrid CNN–LSTM model with MFCC-based cross-modality learning not only performs strongly within each dataset but also remains stable under repeated resampling, underscoring its potential for real-world deployment in mental health monitoring and affective computing applications.

Since WESAD exhibits moderate class imbalance, we additionally employed a cost-sensitive learning strategy by using class-weighted cross-entropy during training. Class weights are computed from the inverse class frequencies and applied to the loss to reduce majority-class dominance. This setting is used to verify that the model’s performance is not driven by class-prevalence as depicted in Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab3).

## Comparison with past methods

The performance of the proposed hybrid CNN–LSTM model with MFCC-based cross-modality learning was compared against existing methods reported in the literature for the Brainwave EEG, SWELL, and WESAD datasets, which is clearly depicted in Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab4), [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab5), and [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab6). This comparison highlights the contributions of our approach in terms of accuracy, generalization capability, and computational efficiency.

### Brainwave EEG

The proposed method has demonstrated superior performance compared to previous works for EEG-based emotion recognition using the Brainwave EEG dataset. Past studies, such as Qing et al.[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR20 "Qing, C., Qiao, R., Xu, X. & Cheng, Y. Interpretable emotion recognition using EEG signals. IEEE Access 7, 94160–94170 (2019).") have applied activation mechanism models with machine learning and reported an accuracy of 75.00%. Manoharan et al.[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR28 "Manoharan, G. & Faria, D. R. Enhanced mental state classification using eeg-based brain-computer interface through deep learning. In Intelligent Systems Conference, 570–586 (Springer, 2024).") have utilized wavelet transform with CNN, resulting in an accuracy of 91.72%. Zhong et al.[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR29 "Zhong, P., Wang, D. & Miao, C. EEG-based emotion recognition using regularized graph neural networks. IEEE Trans. Affect. Comput. 13, 1290–1301 (2020).") have implemented RGNN techniques, achieving a 94.24% accuracy, while Bird et al.[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR21 "Bird, J. J., Manso, L. J., Ribeiro, E. P., Ekart, A. & Faria, D. R. A study on mental state classification using eeg-based brain-machine interface. In 2018 international conference on intelligent systems (IS), 795–800 (IEEE, 2018).") have employed classical classifiers with a slightly higher accuracy of 94.90%. Ali et al.[41](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR41 "Ali, A. et al. Eeg-based hybrid emotion recognition model with statistical-wavelet features and modality-agnostic loss. In International Conference on Engineering Applications of Neural Networks, 128–140 (Springer, 2025).") have adopted a hybrid approach using CNN, LSTM, and ANN algorithms, which has achieved an accuracy of 95.55% and an F1-score of 95.55%. Bardak et al.[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR24 "Bardak, F. K., Seyman, M. N. & Temurtaş, F. Adaptive neuro-fuzzy based hybrid classification model for emotion recognition from EEG signals. Neural Comput. Appl. 36, 9189–9202 (2024).") have explored ANFIS models, reporting an accuracy of 95.97%, and Reddy et al.[42](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR42 "Reddy, G. R. K., Bhavani, A. D. & Odugu, V. K. Optimized recurrent neural network based brain emotion recognition technique. Multimed. Tools Appl. 84, 4655–4674 (2025).") have utilized the GRNN method with a recorded accuracy of 95.99%. In comparison, the proposed work—leveraging combined signal and MFCC feature extraction—has achieved a notably higher accuracy of 96.49%. Moreover, it is distinguished by its detailed evaluation results, including a precision of 97.01%, a recall of 98.23%, and an F1-score of 96.12%, surpassing all previously reported metrics. The comprehensive set of evaluation metrics provided by the proposed approach further underscores its effectiveness and serves as a new benchmark for emotion recognition in EEG signal processing. This substantial performance improvement validates the robustness of the model and its methodological advances over previous works as depicted in Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab4).

### SWELL dataset

The proposed method has achieved outstanding results in comparison with previous works on the SWELL dataset depicted in Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab5), establishing a new benchmark for emotion recognition performance. Among earlier studies, Sriramprakash et al.[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR22 "Sriramprakash, S., Prasanna, V. D. & Murthy, O. R. Stress detection in working people. Procedia Comput. Sci. 115, 359–366 (2017).") employed SVM and KNN classifiers, obtaining an accuracy of 86.36%. Gedam et al.[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR23 "Gedam, S., Dutta, S. & Jha, R. Analyzing mental stress in Indian students through advanced machine learning and wearable technologies. Sci. Rep. 15, 20610 (2025).") reported a moderately improved accuracy of 92.36% using XGBoost, while Liakopoulos et al.[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR30 "Liakopoulos, L., Stagakis, N., Zacharaki, E. I. & Moustakas, K. Cnn-based stress and emotion recognition in ambulatory settings. In 2021 12th international conference on information, intelligence, systems & applications (IISA), 1–8 (IEEE, 2021).") leveraged 2D spectrograms with CNN architectures to achieve an accuracy of 97.64%. Sarkar et al. adopted self-supervised learning, resulting in 98.4% accuracy, and Dahal et al.[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR25 "Dahal, K., Bogue-Jimenez, B. & Doblas, A. Global stress detection framework combining a reduced set of HRV features and random forest model. Sensors 23, 5220 (2023).") utilized RF (mRMR features), reaching 99.00% accuracy along with a precision, recall, and F1-score of 99.00%. Mortensen et al.[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR28 "Manoharan, G. & Faria, D. R. Enhanced mental state classification using eeg-based brain-computer interface through deep learning. In Intelligent Systems Conference, 570–586 (Springer, 2024).") explored a 1D CNN with HRV features, achieving an accuracy of 99.9% and perfect scores for precision, recall, and F1-score (100% each). Liao et al.[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR37 "Liao, Y. et al. Exploring emotional experiences and dataset construction in the era of short videos based on physiological signals. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 96, 106648 (2024).") applied various machine learning algorithms, achieving 100% accuracy, although their precision, recall, and F1-score values were not specified in the comparison. The proposed work, by harnessing signal and MFCC feature fusion, has surpassed all reported results with an accuracy of 99.99%, and perfect precision, recall, and F1-score measures, each at 100. This comprehensive achievement highlights the effectiveness of the methodology and underscores its superiority over all previously published approaches for the SWELL dataset, validating its robust generalization and discriminative capability in emotion recognition from EEG signals.

### WESAD dataset

The proposed method has set a new state-of-the-art benchmark for emotion recognition on the WESAD dataset, as evidenced by a thorough comparison with prior research works, as depicted in. Kumar et al.[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR35 "Kumar, P. S., Govarthan, P. K., Gadda, A. A. S., Ganapathy, N. & Ronickom, J. F. A. Deep learning-based automated emotion recognition using multimodal physiological signals and time-frequency methods. IEEE Trans. Instrum. Meas. 73, 1–12 (2024).") combined EDA, ECG, CWT, and VGG16, attaining an accuracy of 86.66%. Bajpai et al.[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR26 "Bajpai, D. & He, L. Evaluating knn performance on wesad dataset. In 2020 12th International Conference on Computational Intelligence and Communication Networks (CICN), 60–62 (IEEE, 2020).") adopted SVM with HRV and EDA features, reaching 90.49% accuracy, alongside precision, recall, and F1-score values of 88.00%, 92.00%, and 90.00%, respectively. Gedam et al.[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR23 "Gedam, S., Dutta, S. & Jha, R. Analyzing mental stress in Indian students through advanced machine learning and wearable technologies. Sci. Rep. 15, 20610 (2025).") utilized XGBoost and reported a 92.36% accuracy. Ciccarelli et al.[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR27 "Ciccarelli, M., Pesaresi, A., Papetti, A. & Germani, M. Wearable devices for stress detection: Insights on exploring generalizability in controlled laboratory settings. Procedia Comput. Sci. 253, 2014–2023 (2025).") achieved 96.12% accuracy using SVM (HRV, EDA), with precision, recall, and F1-score of 96.10%, 96.00%, and 96.60%, respectively. Nazarova et al.[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR34 "Nazarova, A., Obukhov, A., Zhang, Z. & Liu, M. Enhancing stress detection accuracy: A cnn-lstm model for ecg signal analysis. In 2025 5th International Conference on Sensors and Information Technology, 319–323 (IEEE, 2025).") leveraged a CNN+LSTM model, realizing an accuracy of 97.00%, while Kasnesis et al.[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#ref-CR36 "Kasnesis, P., Chatzigeorgiou, C., Feidakis, M., Gutierrez, A. & Patrikakis, C. Z. Transensefusers: A temporal CNN-transformer neural network family for explainable PPG-based stress detection. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 102, 107248 (2025).") used TranSenseFuser, achieving 98.46% accuracy and an F1-score of 97.03%. Benita et al.’s CNN-based approach resulted in 98.55% accuracy, but yielded notably lower precision, recall, and F1-score values (41.41%, 100%, and 58.57%, respectively). In stark contrast, the proposed work utilizing fused signal and MFCC features has outperformed all previous methods by attaining 99.99% accuracy along with perfect scores for precision (100), recall (100), and F1-score (100). These results underscore the robustness and discriminative power of the proposed methodology, decisively advancing the standard for emotion recognition on the WESAD dataset.

### Ablation study

We examined four model configurations to quantify the contribution of the proposed IMFCC-based cross-modality enhancement: (i) a temporal-only LSTM branch, (ii) a spectral-only CNN operating on MFCC features, (iii) a dual-stream architecture with cross-modality removed (i.e., without IMFCC reconstruction/projection), and (iv) the full proposed model. Results indicate that the dual-stream formulation constitutes a strong baseline, whereas the incremental benefit of IMFCC is dataset dependent. For WESAD and SWELL, incorporating IMFCC yields consistent improvements relative to the corresponding dual-stream model without cross-modality, and paired McNemar tests confirm statistical significance (median p-values = 0.0003163 and 0.0008617, respectively). By contrast, on the Brainwave EEG dataset, the full model does not consistently outperform the dual-stream variant without IMFCC as shown in Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42998-8#Tab7), and the McNemar analysis does not indicate a reliable difference (median p = 0.2457). Collectively, these findings suggest that the IMFCC-based cross-modality enhancement is most effective for datasets with richer physiological dynamics and larger sample volumes, while its relative advantage may be attenuated under more constrained conditions (e.g., smaller, noisier EEG recordings); accordingly, we position IMFCC as a complementary component rather than the sole determinant of performance.

## Conclusion

This study presented a novel hybrid CNN–LSTM architecture enhanced with MFCC–based cross-modality learning for EEG-based emotion and stress recognition. The proposed framework introduces two key innovations: (1) an inverse MFCC computation mechanism that reconstructs spectral features back into the temporal domain, enabling the LSTM branch to capture deeper sequential dependencies, and (2) an LSTM-to-MFCC projection that maps learned temporal representations into the spectral space for CNN-based processing, thereby enriching spatial–spectral feature learning. This dual-pathway interaction between temporal and spectral domains allows the model to leverage the complementary strengths of CNNs and LSTMs, ultimately producing more robust and discriminative features. The model was evaluated on three benchmark datasets — Brainwave EEG, WESAD, and SWELL — that vary significantly in signal quality, sensor configurations, and experimental protocols. Despite these differences, the proposed approach consistently delivered superior performance, achieving test accuracies of 96.49%, 99.99%, and 99.99%, respectively, with minimal misclassification and balanced per-class accuracies. The comparative analysis against related work demonstrated that the proposed model either surpasses or matches the state-of-the-art in all three datasets, outperforming conventional machine learning approaches that rely on handcrafted features and rivaling advanced deep learning models, including CNN-Transformer hybrids and multimodal fusion frameworks. Our design differs from wavelet multiscale kernels and graph/attention fusion methods by relying on MFCC-derived spectral compactness and explicit inverse-MFCC cross-modality coupling; benchmarking on other standard datasets like DEAP and SEED will be included in future work for direct comparison. Moreover, the unified architecture required no dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning, underscoring its adaptability and generalization capability. These results indicate that the proposed framework is a highly promising solution for real-world applications in mental health monitoring, affective computing, and adaptive human–computer interaction systems.

### Limitations and future work

Although the proposed approach achieves notable results, several avenues remain open for further research and development. First, the current work did not consider any cross-dataset transfer learning and domain adaptation that allows models trained on one dataset to generalize effectively to another without extensive retraining. This will address one of the persistent challenges in physiological signal analysis — the variability introduced by different hardware setups, subject demographics, and recording environments. Second, there is significant scope for lightweight model optimization through techniques such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, which could make the model suitable for deployment on wearable devices and edge computing platforms where computational resources are limited. Third, extending the framework to incorporate multimodal fusion with other physiological signals such as ECG, EDA, PPG, and respiration could further improve robustness, particularly in cases where EEG data may be noisy or partially missing. We also try the Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) methodology in the future. Finally, adapting the system for real-time, online emotion recognition using streaming EEG data will open up possibilities for applications in driver monitoring, adaptive e-learning, workplace stress management, and continuous mental health assessment.
