These associations indicate that ECG measures combined with Killip grade could enhance real-time triage and early intervention in the emergency or primary environment. These exploratory results indicate that individual risk prediction can be enhanced further by incorporating demographic and electrophysiological variables. Further multicenter validation will be used to identify whether such extended parameters can be used to improve robustness and clinical applicability of the existing model.

Future research can be enhanced by new multifidelity learning approaches that can merge small high-fidelity cohorts with bigger routine-care data to improve the generalizability. Moreover, incorporating geometric measurements of cardiac imaging input, including myocardial strain or shape measures, and ECG variables would potentially further augment the representation of myocardial structure and mechanics[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR29 "Mehdi, R. R. et al. Non-invasive diagnosis of chronic myocardial infarction via composite in-silico-human data learning. Adv. Sci. (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany) 12, e06933 (2025)."),[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR30 "Mehdi, R. R. et al. Comparison of Three Machine Learning Methods To Estimate Myocardial Stiffness (Chap. 19) 363–382 (Elsevier Science Ltd, 2023)."),[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR31 "Naeini, V. et al. A computational journey toward an optimal design for metamaterial epicardial passive sleeves. Adv. Healthc. Mater. 15, e01369 (2026)."). Such methods would be helpful to augment the current ECG-based framework and enable more robust risk modelling in externally valid populations.

### Limitations and future prospects

For example, the study was retrospective and single-center. The relatively small sample size may limit the generalizability of the results. First, the proportion of female participants was relatively low, so there is potential sex-related bias. the relatively low proportion of female participants may introduce gender-related prediction biases, and future research should aim to achieve better gender balance.” In addition, the model stability was confirmed by this internal validation, but this needs to be validated across external multicenter populations before it should be taken as reliable or be used in practice. Second, some valuable ECG features, such as ST-segment resolution, the Tp-e interval and the Tp-e/QT ratio, were not included due to retrospective dataset availability. Future work may involve these and other dynamic ECG parameters; for example, we might use AI systems to assist or automate ECG analysis to obtain more accurate predictions of prognosis. Finally, we are planning to cooperate with several regional hospitals throughout the country so that we can collect a larger and more diverse cohort for prospective validation; this should allow us greater opportunities to integrate demographic and electrophysiological indicators into personalized risk prediction models, hence improving outcomes in theory as more factors are accounted for before decisions are made. Although continuous modeling with non-linear terms may offer greater statistical efficiency, we adopted guideline-based categorization to balance interpretability and usability. Future externally validated studies may benefit from spline-based approaches to further refine risk estimation. While sex emerged as an independent predictor, the relatively small proportion of women limited the robustness of sex-specific performanceassessment; future externally validated studies with balanced sex representation are needed to evaluate potential effect modification.

## Conclusion

In summary, we created an ECG-based model for predicting AHF in patients with AMI that was both practical and interpretable. This model was demonstrated to have good discrimination and calibration after internal validation with 2000 bootstrapping iterations. Hence, by relying mainly on routine ECG parameters for visible diagnosis with a simple and inexpensive tool, early risk identification is realizable, especially for primary care physicians and hospitals. For resource-limited hospitals, we hope with more multicenter validation, and if factors such as ST segment resolution and the Tp-e/QT ratio, which are also ECG indicators, can be included, the model will be even more powerful and practical at the bedside.
```
##### [Empowering genetic discoveries and cardiovascular risk assessment by predicting electrocardiograms from genotype](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3)

```
## Abstract

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death worldwide. To interpret disease mechanisms and warn CVDs in early life, biobanks have emerged to collect genotype and electrocardiogram (ECG) data. However, only 10% of samples contain both genotype data and ECG data in UK-Biobank (UKB), limiting the utility of the biobanks. Here, we have developed an attention-based Capsule Network (CapECG), to predict ECG traits from genotype. CapECG has mapped high dimensional genotype to low dimensional ECG traits and improved the CVDs prediction from genotype. CapECG achieved an average Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.62 for 7422 individuals in the internal test set from UKB. The model was used to predict 169 ECG traits for 388,284 individuals containing only genotype data in UKB. The predicted 169 ECG traits were used to assess risks of six types of CVDs, and achieved average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.80, higher than 0.71 provided by the polygenic risk score-based method. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) on the predicted spatial QRS-T angle (spQRSTa) identified 133 significant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), including 33 overlapping with a published GWAS on 118,780 individuals, surpassing 13 overlaps from observed spQRSTa of 29,692 individuals. Thus, this study proposed a new way to predict ECG traits from genotype and bridge the early prediction of diseases.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death, and the warning in early life is critical[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR1 "Marijon, E., Garcia, R., Narayanan, K., Karam, N. & Jouven, X. Fighting against sudden cardiac death: need for a paradigm shift-Adding near-term prevention and pre-emptive action to long-term prevention. Eur. Heart J. 43, 1457–1464 (2022)."). To identify the variants that modulate CVD risks, many genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been performed in recent years. Towards one of the most frequently occurring CVDs, atrial fibrillation, 150 genetic loci were detected by GWAS on 77,690 cases[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR2 "Miyazawa, K. et al. Cross-ancestry genome-wide analysis of atrial fibrillation unveils disease biology and enables cardioembolic risk prediction. Nat. Genet. 55, 187–197 (2023)."), and a recent GWAS meta-analysis for atrial fibrillation identified additional 91 associated loci[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR3 "Yuan, S. et al. Deciphering the genetic architecture of atrial fibrillation offers insights into disease prediction, pathophysiology and downstream sequelae. medRxiv, 
https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.07.20.23292938
(2023)."). Another large-scale GWAS for CVDs incorporating a quarter of a million cases has identified 95 novel loci[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR4 "Tcheandjieu, C. et al. Large-scale genome-wide association study of coronary artery disease in genetically diverse populations. Nat. Med. 28, 1679–1692 (2022)."). However, the associated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are still limited to accurately predicting disease risks due to the challenge of collecting large numbers of patients for GWAS[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR5 "Chatterjee, N., Shi, J. & García-Closas, M. Developing and evaluating polygenic risk prediction models for stratified disease prevention. Nat. Rev. Genet. 17, 392–406 (2016).").

Alternatively, many GWAS were proposed to identify variants associated with electrocardiogram (ECG) traits since ECG is the simplest clinical method to assess cardiac abnormality[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR6 "AlGhatrif, M. & Lindsay, J. A brief review: history to understand fundamentals of electrocardiography. J. Commun. Hosp. Intern. Med. Perspect. 2, 14383 (2012).") and many ECG traits have been indicated as risk factors of CVDs[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR1 "Marijon, E., Garcia, R., Narayanan, K., Karam, N. & Jouven, X. Fighting against sudden cardiac death: need for a paradigm shift-Adding near-term prevention and pre-emptive action to long-term prevention. Eur. Heart J. 43, 1457–1464 (2022)."). Essentially, such GWAS are not limited to patients and easy to be accumulated to enlarge sample size, and recent studies have identified variants associated with ECG risk factors of cardiac disorders, such as QT interval[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR7 "Arking, D. E. et al. Genetic association study of QT interval highlights role for calcium signaling pathways in myocardial repolarization. Nat. Genet. 46, 826–836 (2014)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR8 "Young, W. J. et al. Genetic analyses of the electrocardiographic QT interval and its components identify additional loci and pathways. Nat. Commun. 13, 5144 (2022)."), PR interval[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR9 "Van Setten, J. et al. PR interval genome-wide association meta-analysis identifies 50 loci associated with atrial and atrioventricular electrical activity. Nat. Commun. 9, 2904 (2018)."),[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR10 "Ntalla, I. et al. Multi-ancestry GWAS of the electrocardiographic PR interval identifies 202 loci underlying cardiac conduction. Nat. Commun. 11, 2542 (2020)."), QRS interval[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR11 "Prins, B. P. et al. Exome-chip meta-analysis identifies novel loci associated with cardiac conduction, including ADAMTS6. Genome Biol. 19, 1–17 (2018)."), and long-QT syndrome (LQTS)[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR12 "Crotti, L. et al. NOS1AP is a genetic modifier of the long-QT syndrome. Circulation 120, 1657–1663 (2009)."),[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR13 "Kolder, I. C. et al. Analysis for genetic modifiers of disease severity in patients with long-QT syndrome type 2. Circul. Cardiovasc. Genet. 8, 447–456 (2015)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR14 "Nauffal, V. et al. Monogenic and polygenic contributions to QTc prolongation in the population. Circulation 145, 1524–1533 (2022)."). As expected, many significant associations of genetic variants were identified harbored in genes encoding proteins that have been implicated in cardiac electrophysiology. For example, _KCDN3_ gene encodes Kv4.3 that is responsible for the transient outward potassium current, and is important for the early phase of repolarization in heart[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR15 "Verweij, N. et al. The genetic makeup of the electrocardiogram. Cell Syst. 11, 229–238.e225 (2020)."). _SCN5A_ is another gene, encoding the cardiac sodium-channel NaV1.5, and was identified to contain variants critical for regulation of cardiac electrophysiological function[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR15 "Verweij, N. et al. The genetic makeup of the electrocardiogram. Cell Syst. 11, 229–238.e225 (2020)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR16 "Glinge, C., Lahrouchi, N., Jabbari, R., Tfelt-Hansen, J. & Bezzina, C. R. Genome-wide association studies of cardiac electrical phenotypes. Cardiovasc. Res. 116, 1620–1634 (2020).").

Although promising, the identified genes are still limited because it’s not easy to collect samples containing both ECG and genotype data. For example, the UK Biobank (UKB) released genotype data for ~400 thousand individuals of European ancestry with only 10% of them also containing ECG data. Previous studies have established that a substantial portion of the inter-individual differences in ECG data is genetically determined, with heritability ranging from 40% to 70%[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR17 "Nolte, I. M. et al. A comparison of heritability estimates by classical twin modeling and based on genome-wide genetic relatedness for cardiac conduction traits. Twin Res. Hum. Genet. 20, 489–498 (2017)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR18 "Jamshidi, Y., Nolte, I. M., Spector, T. D. & Snieder, H. Novel genes for QTc interval. How much heritability is explained, and how much is left to find? Genome Med. 2, 35 (2010)."). A twin study has shown that R-R and QT intervals demonstrated significant heritable components, accounting for 77% and 36%, respectively[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR19 "Russell, M. W., Law, I., Sholinsky, P. & Fabsitz, R. R. Heritability of ECG measurements in adult male twins. J. Electrocardiol. 30, 64–68 (1998)."). In individuals of European descent, the heritability of QT interval, PR interval, and QRS duration is estimated as 29.3%, 18.2%, and 15.0%, respectively[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR8 "Young, W. J. et al. Genetic analyses of the electrocardiographic QT interval and its components identify additional loci and pathways. Nat. Commun. 13, 5144 (2022)."),[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR10 "Ntalla, I. et al. Multi-ancestry GWAS of the electrocardiographic PR interval identifies 202 loci underlying cardiac conduction. Nat. Commun. 11, 2542 (2020)."). This raises a natural question that whether we can leverage both genetic and ECG data of individuals in UKB to construct a model for predicting ECG traits through genotype data, which is useful to map high-dimensional genotype data to low-dimensional ECG traits, and to further accurately predict risks of CVDs.

Classical approaches for predicting phenotypes from genotype data mainly rely on linear models. For example, traits of wheat were predicted from genotype through the Bayesian Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) ß[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR20 "Ornella, L. et al. Genomic-enabled prediction with classification algorithms. Heredity 112, 616–626 (2014)."). Liang et al. predicted brain MRI image derived phenotypes through a linear regression model[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR21 "Liang, Y., Melia, O., Brettin, T., Brown, A. & Im, H. K. BrainXcan identifies brain features associated with behavioral and psychiatric traits using large scale genetic and imaging data. medRxiv, 2021.2006. 2001.21258159 (2021)."). Unfortunately, the linear models are hard to capture non-linear effects like epistasis[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR22 "Mackay, T. F. Epistasis and quantitative traits: using model organisms to study gene–gene interactions. Nat. Rev. Genet. 15, 22–33 (2014).") and complicated SNP interactions[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR23 "Prabhu, S. & Pe’er, I. Ultrafast genome-wide scan for SNP–SNP interactions in common complex disease. Genome Res. 22, 2230–2240 (2012)."). To address these issues, deep learning model was recently used to accurately predict phenotype from genotype data by capturing the non-linear relationships between variants and disease[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR24 "Luo, X., Kang, X. & Schönhuth, A. Predicting the prevalence of complex genetic diseases from individual genotype profiles using capsule networks. Nat. Mach. Intell. 5, 114–125 (2023)."),[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR25 "van Hilten, A. et al. GenNet framework: interpretable deep learning for predicting phenotypes from genetic data. Commun. Biol. 4, 1094 (2021)."). For example, van Hilten employed fully connected neural network to infer schizophrenia from individual genotype[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR25 "van Hilten, A. et al. GenNet framework: interpretable deep learning for predicting phenotypes from genetic data. Commun. Biol. 4, 1094 (2021)."). However, they did not consider the non-linear interactions across linkage disequilibrium (LD) blocks, which play an important role in understanding how LD blocks collectively influence phenotypic outcomes[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR26 "Slatkin, M. Linkage disequilibrium—understanding the evolutionary past and mapping the medical future. Nat. Rev. Genet. 9, 477–485 (2008)."). Thus, it is promising to deeply mine the UKB through integrating whole-genome-wide SNPs, and non-linear interactions across LD blocks to predict ECG traits from genotype.

To capture the non-linear interactions across LD blocks, it is necessary to model hierarchical structures of genotype data. Capsule network (CapsNet) is a representation of a deep neural network as a set of capsules, which allow each of the capsules to interact with other capsules by dynamic routing, thereby enabling the model to learn complex hierarchical structures of data[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR27 "Hinton, G. E., Sabour, S. & Frosst, N. Matrix capsules with EM routing. International conference on learning representations, 2018."). Recent studies indicate that the potential of CapsNet to learn complex hierarchical structures can indeed be leveraged also for biomedical data[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR28 "Camacho, D. M., Collins, K. M., Powers, R. K., Costello, J. C. & Collins, J. J. Next-generation machine learning for biological networks. Cell 173, 1581–1592 (2018)."). For example, Wang et al. used CapsNet to identify groups of genes encoding different subcellular types[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR29 "Wang, L. et al. An interpretable deep-learning architecture of capsule networks for identifying cell-type gene expression programs from single-cell RNA-sequencing data. Nat. Mach. Intell. 2, 693–703 (2020)."). Zhang et al. employed CapsNet to predict ncRNA-disease associations (LDAs)[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR30 "Zhang, Z. et al. CapsNet-LDA: predicting lncRNA-disease associations using attention mechanism and capsule network based on multi-view data. Brief. Bioinforma. 24, bbac531 (2023)."). Thus, CapsNet is ripe for application in biomedical data.

In this study, we proposed the attention-based Capsule Network to predict ECG traits from genotype (CapECG). CapECG was developed to enlarge the sample size of ECG by predicting ECG traits from genotype, and to further improve the accuracy of early warning CVD risks through using genotype data. CapECG used attention mechanism to weigh the LD block, and captured whole-genome wide and non-additive interactions among SNPs, which is different from the commonly used capsule network model[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR31 "Sabour, S., Frosst, N. & Hinton, G. E. Dynamic routing between capsules. Adv. Neural Inform. Process. Syst. 30 (2017)."). The weighted features were input into self-attention routing to train a model for identifying complex patterns of the ECG traits-genotype associations. Applications of CapECG have mapped high dimension genotype data to 169 ECG traits, and improved the accuracy of CVD risk prediction from genotype. Moreover, CapECG captured the non-linear relationships between ECG and genotype, and improved the power of identifying ECG-associated SNPs. Thus, this study represents a new paradigm to associate genotype and phenotype for detecting novel genetic factors of ECG, and to predict CVDs in earlier life only using genotype data.

## Results

### Overview of this study

Figure [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig1) depicts the overall workflow of this study. From UK-Biobank (UKB), we obtained 37,114 European individuals containing both ECG and genotype data (namely UKB-ECG dataset), and 388,284 European individuals containing only genotype data but no ECG data (namely UKB-noECG dataset, Supplementary Fig. [S1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). We further obtained the ECG and genotype data from 1929 individuals of non-European ancestry to construct the Non-European test set. From ECG data, 169 ECG traits were extracted, which include 168 two-dimensional (2D) ECG traits (Supplementary Fig. [S2A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1), Supplementary Table [S1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)) and one three-dimensional (3D) ECG trait called spatial QRS-T angle (spQRSTa, Supplementary Fig. [S2B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)).

These ECG traits and the genotype data in UKB-ECG dataset were used to construct an attention-based Capsule Network (CapECG) model for predicting ECG traits from genotype (SNPs). To reduce the high dimensional SNP features, SNPs were assigned to linkage disequilibrium (LD) blocks, and principle component analysis (PCA) was performed to select the top 10 components in each block. Each LD block was weighted according to the LD block-based attention mechanism, and the weighted features were used to train a self-attention-based capsule network for predicting ECG traits. The CapECG trained by UKB-ECG dataset was finally applied to UKB-noECG dataset. The predicted ECG traits were used to identify SNPs associated with ECG through genome-wide association studies (GWAS), and to predict CVD risks and CVD diagnosis age by deep-learning models, DeepCVD and DeepCVD-Age. DeepCVD is an auto-encoder based deep neural network model that only requires genotype, sex and age as input to predict risks of CVDs. DeepCVD has invoked CapECG to predict 169 ECG traits, and integrates these ECG traits with sex and age in the prediction. DeepCVD-Age was modified from DeepCVD by replacing the final softmax activation layer with a linear activation layer, thus adapting the model for diagnosis age prediction.

### Predicting ECG traits from genotype by CapECG

To investigate the ability of CapECG for predicting ECG traits from genotype, the UKB-ECG dataset was randomly split into the training set (29,692 individuals) and test set (7422 individuals). In predicting 102 ECG traits with significant heritability (_h_2) (_P_ < 0.05/169 = 2.96 × 10−4), CapECG achieved average PCC of 0.64 (PCC ranging from 0.38 to 0.82, standard error (SE) ranging from 0.01 to 0.05, _P_ < 5.62×10−33) and _R_2 of 0.40 (_R_2 ranging from 0.15 to 0.68, SE ranging from 0.01 to 0.08). The best prediction is achieved in predicting the difference between R start and S end in voltage on V6 lead (_h__2_ = 0.19, PCC = 0.82). In the test set, the model achieved average PCC of 0.62 (ranging from 0.35 to 0.82, _P_ < 8.12 × 10−31) and average _R_2 of 0.37 (ranging from 0.12 to 0.66) in predicting 102 ECG traits.

In predicting spQRSTa, CapECG achieved average PCC of 0.66 (ranging from 0.62 to 0.69, SE = 0.02 and _P_ < 3.71 × 10−86) and average _R_2 of 0.44 (ranging from 0.41 to 0.48, SE = 0.03) for five-fold cross-validation, and it achieved PCC of 0.65 (_P_ = 6.33 × 10−93) and _R_2 of 0.42 in the test set (Fig. [2A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig2)). The predicted spQRSTa is not significantly different from the observed one as indicated by Bland Altman analysis[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR32 "Bland, J. M. & Altman, D. G. Measuring agreement in method comparison studies. Stat. methods Med. Res. 8, 135–160 (1999).") (Bland Altman analysis _P_ = 0.18). Besides, the changed prediction performances of CapECG for various ECG traits are partly due to different heritability since the prediction performances of ECG traits show significantly positive (_R__2_ = 0.58, _P_ = 4.73 × 10−21) correlation with the heritability (Fig. [2B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig2)), indicating that ECG traits with higher proportion of phenotypic variance from genetic factors are easy to be predicted through genotype.

CapECG was further compared to other six state-of-the-art methods: CapsNet[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR31 "Sabour, S., Frosst, N. & Hinton, G. E. Dynamic routing between capsules. Adv. Neural Inform. Process. Syst. 30 (2017)."), multi-layer perceptron (MLP)[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR25 "van Hilten, A. et al. GenNet framework: interpretable deep learning for predicting phenotypes from genetic data. Commun. Biol. 4, 1094 (2021)."), Transformer[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR33 "Vaswani, A. et al. Attention is all you need. Adv. Neural Inform. Process. Syst. 30, 5998–6008 (2017)."), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR34 "Wang, W. & Li, B. A novel model based on a 1D-ResCNN and transfer learning for processing EEG attenuation. Comput. Methods Biomech. Biomed. Eng. 26, 1980–1993 (2023)."), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR35 "Chen, T. & Guestrin, C. in Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining. 785–794.") and ridge regression model. As shown in Fig. [2C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig2), CapECG achieved significantly (two-sided _t_-test _P_ < 2.17 × 10−4) better predictions (average PCC of 0.62, ranging from 0.35 to 0.82) for 102 ECG traits, relative to the 2nd best technique CapsNet (average PCC of 0.49, ranging from 0.32 to 0.64) when the model was trained by the features with reduced dimension through LD-PCA.

When the dimensions of features in CapECG model were reduced by genome-scale PCA (All-PCA) rather than the PCA performed in each LD block, CapECG has significantly dropped in the average PCC from 0.62 to 0.27 (two-sided _t_-test _P_ = 3.66 × 10−18). When the dimensions of features were reduced by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE)[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR36 "Sakaue, S. et al. Dimensionality reduction reveals fine-scale structure in the Japanese population with consequences for polygenic risk prediction. Nat. Commun. 11, 1569 (2020).") instead of LD-PCA, the PCC achieved by CapECG dropped to 0.29 in the test set, which is significantly lower than the method using LD-PCA (two-sided _t_-test _P_ = 7.87 × 10−15). The drops were also observed in other benchmark models (Fig. [2C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig2)). All these results indicated the effectiveness of LD-PCA in predicting ECG traits from genotype.

### Identifying SNP associations by using CapECG-predicted ECG traits

To investigate how well the predicted ECG traits in identifying SNP associations, we performed GWAS for the predicted ECG traits of 29,692 individuals in the UKB-ECG training dataset through five-fold cross-validation. Since ECG traits are not independent, the 169 ECG traits were clustered into 11 clusters by K-means (Supplementary Fig. [S3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). By using the predicted ECG traits from CapECG, GWAS have identified totally 347 independent SNPs (iSNPs) (_P_ < 5 × 10−8 and LD _r_2 < 0.01) for 11 representative ECG traits, covering the iSNPs identified by the observed ECG traits with an average precision of 0.837 (ranging from 0.742 to 0.955) and recall of 0.900 (ranging from 0.819 to 0.977) (Fig. [2D](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig2), Supplementary Fig. [S6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). The average precision and recall of CapECG are both superior to CapsNet (0.751 and 0.829), MLP (0.757 and 0.781), Transformer (0.720 and 0.723), CNN (0.797 and 0.527), XGBoost (0.689 and 0.636) and ridge regression model (0.831 and 0.635). When these methods were examined on their true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) in recovering iSNPs using different SNP _P-_value thresholds, CapECG achieved higher average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.95 that is higher than other methods (Fig. [2E](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig2)). Specifically, GWAS for the spQRSTa predicted by CapECG has achieved AUC 0.95 that is higher than the GWAS for spQRSTa predicted by other methods (Supplementary Fig. [S7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). The genetic correlation between the GWAS of observed spQRSTa and the predicted spQRSTa was estimated by LD score regression (LDSC)[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR37 "Ni, G. et al. Estimation of genetic correlation via linkage disequilibrium score regression and genomic restricted maximum likelihood. Am. J. Hum. Genet. 102, 1185–1194 (2018)."), and achieved _r__g_ of 0.70 (_P_ = 2.91 × 10−11). This result indicates that the genetic architecture of the predicted spQRSTa is highly correlated with that of the observed spQRSTa both at individual GWAS loci. We also examined the correlations between the polygenic risk score (PRS) for predicted spQRSTa and observed spQRSTa in UKB-ECG test set. As shown in Supplementary Fig. [S9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1), the regression shows that the PRS for spQRSTa predicted by CapECG are in significant correlation (FDR < 0.05) with the observed spQRSTa when employing six different _P-_value cutoffs (i.e., 5 × 10−8, 1 × 10−5, 1 × 10−3, 0.01, 0.1 and 1).

To ensure that the genetic associations identified by CapECG were not confounded by systematic bias, we estimated the genomic inflation factor (_λ_) for 11 representative ECG traits. GWAS of the predicted ECG traits achieved a mean _λ_ of 1.056 (ranging from 1.047 to 1.096), which was not significantly different from the mean _λ_ of 1.048 (ranging from 1.000 to 1.106) for the observed traits (difference = 0.008, _t_-test _P_ = 0.24; Supplementary Table [S7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). This result demonstrates that CapECG maintains the integrity of GWAS and does not introduce substantial inflation.

### Discovering genetic variants associated with ECG traits

Application of CapECG to 388,284 European individuals in the UKB-noECG dataset has enlarged the sample size of ECG, and improved the power of GWAS. A recent multi-ancestry GWAS was performed for the spQRSTa based on 118,780 individuals[38](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR38 "Young, W. J. et al. Genetic architecture of spatial electrical biomarkers for cardiac arrhythmia and relationship with cardiovascular disease. Nat. Commun. 14, 1411 (2023)."), a cohort larger than UKB-ECG dataset but smaller than UKB-noECG dataset, and identified 52 associated independent SNPs (iSNPs) (_P_ < 5×10−8, LD _r_2 < 0.01, Supplementary Table [S8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). These 52 iSNPs were used as a golden standard for evaluating the GWAS for the predicted spQRSTa. By using the spQRSTa predicted by CapECG for individuals from UKB-noECG dataset (388,284 individuals), GWAS identified 133 iSNPs (_P_ < 5 × 10−8, LD _r_2 < 0.01, Supplementary Table [S9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)), which covered 33 (63.4%) out of 52 iSNPs with overlap or within ±250 kb (Fig. [3A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3)). A Quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot of GWAS for the predicted spQRSTa indicated an early separation of the observed _P-_value from the expected _P-_value (Supplementary Fig. [S10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). By comparison, GWAS for the observed spQRSTa from the UKB-ECG training set (29,692 individuals) only identified 4 out of 8 SNPs (_P_ < 5 × 10−8, LD _r_2 < 0.01) or 13 out of 133 top significant SNPs (_P_ < 6.4 × 10−5, LD _r_2 < 0.01) with overlap or within ±250 kb for the 52 iSNPs (Supplementary Fig. [S11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). When the GWAS was performed for predicted spQRSTa by reducing the sample size to 29,692 individuals, it still identified 18 out of 133 top significant SNPs (_P_ < 7.3 × 10−6, LD _r_2 < 0.01) overlapped with the published GWAS (Fig. [3B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3)).

CapECG enables us to potentially uncover intricate relationships and patterns between ECG traits and genotype, which potentially improves the power of GWAS. To evaluate the effect of the CapECG model in capturing genetic factors of ECG traits and further improving GWAS power, we simulated genotype through HAPNEST[39](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR39 "Wharrie, S. et al. HAPNEST: efficient, large-scale generation and evaluation of synthetic datasets for genotypes and phenotypes. bioinformatics 39, btad535 (2023).") using the 1000 Genomes Project European as reference[40](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR40 "Consortium, G. P. A map of human genome variation from population scale sequencing. Nature 467, 1061 (2010)."). The simulated genotype data was used to predict spQRSTa. For the predicted spQRSTa using the simulated genotype data, the GWAS identified 16 iSNPs out of 133 top significant SNPs (LD _r_2 < 0.01) overlapped with the published spQRSTa GWAS (Fig. [3B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3)). This is higher than the 13 overlapped iSNPs out of 133 top significant SNPs (LD _r_2 < 0.01) identified by the GWAS for the observed ECG traits, indicating CapECG has captured non-linear associations between ECG traits and genotype in the training process using the UKB-ECG dataset (Fig. [3B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3)).

CapECG was further used to predict QT interval that is another critical marker of cardiac repolarization, associated with arrhythmias and sudden cardiac events[41](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR41 "Hoffmann, T. J. et al. A large genome-wide association study of QT interval length utilizing electronic health records. Genetics 222, 
https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyac157
(2022)."). A recent multi-ancestry GWAS for the QT interval was performed for 117,532 individuals (including 86,165 Europeans)[41](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR41 "Hoffmann, T. J. et al. A large genome-wide association study of QT interval length utilizing electronic health records. Genetics 222, 
https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyac157
(2022)."), a cohort larger than UKB-ECG dataset but smaller than UKB-noECG dataset, and identified 73 associated independent SNPs (iSNPs) (_P_ < 5 × 10−8, LD _r__2_ < 0.01, Supplementary Fig. [S12A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). In predicting QT interval, CapECG achieved PCC values of 0.56 (SE = 0.02) and 0.53 for the five-fold cross-validation and held-out test set, respectively (Supplementary Fig. [S12B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). CapECG was then employed to predict QT interval for 388,284 European individuals in the UKB-noECG dataset, and the predicted QT interval were used for GWAS. For the QT interval predicted by CapECG for individuals from UKB-noECG dataset (388,284 individuals), GWAS identified 186 iSNPs (_P_ < 5 × 10−8, LD _r__2_ < 0.01, Supplementary Table [S10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)), which included 41 (56.2%) overlapped or within ±250 kb to the iSNPs identified by the published GWAS for QT interval (Supplementary Fig. [S12A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). When the GWAS was performed for predicting QT interval from the simulated genotype, it identified 29 out of 186 top significant SNPs (_P_ < 4.6 × 10−5, LD _r__2_ < 0.01) overlapped with the published GWAS. In comparison, the GWAS for the observed QT interval of 29,692 individuals from UKB-ECG dataset has identified 11 significant (_P_ < 5 × 10−8, LD _r__2_ < 0.01) SNPs (Supplementary Fig. [S12A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). Out of the top 186 most significant SNPs, 24 are overlapped or within ±250 kb to the iSNPs identified by the published GWAS for QT interval, which is lower than 29 overlapped SNPs obtained by the GWAS for the predicted QT interval from the simulated genotype data. This finding further indicated the potential of CapECG in capturing complex relationships between genotype and trait and improved the power of GWAS.

### Discovering candidate genes associated with spQRSTa

The GWAS summary data for the predicted spQRSTa was used to perform gene-level GWAS through MAGMA[42](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR42 "De Leeuw, C. A., Mooij, J. M., Heskes, T. & Posthuma, D. MAGMA: generalized gene-set analysis of GWAS data. PLoS Comput. Biol. 11, e1004219 (2015)."). Based on the predicted spQRSTa from UKB-noECG, 62 significant genes (_P_ < 0.05/18762 = ~2.66 × 10−6) were identified (Supplementary Table [S11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)), where 12 genes were overlapped with the genes (21 genes, Supplementary Table [S12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)) identified by the published multi-ancestry GWAS, indicating a significant (Fisher’s exact test _P_ = 1.51 × 10−126) overlap of gene associations between two GWAS. Out of the remaining 50 newly identified genes, 28 genes have been reported to be associated with at least one type of heart functions, such as electrocardiogram morphology, QRS duration, PR interval, and 19 genes were found by previous studies to be associated with CVDs, such as atrial fibrillation, rheumatic heart disease and heart failure (Supplementary Fig. [S13B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). In total, 18 genes had not been previously reported as being associated with heart functions or heart diseases. The gene, CDH13, was most significantly associated with spQRSTa in MAGMA analysis (_P_ = 3.85 × 10−29). As shown in previous studies, CDH13 is a putative mediator of cell-cell interactions in the heart[43](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR43 "Edwards, J. J. et al. Impact of fetal hypoxia on myocardial molecular profile in the lamb extra-uterine environment for neonatal development. Circulation 146, A11646–A11646 (2022)."), and has been proven to be correlated with myocardial infarction[44](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR44 "Hartiala, J. A. et al. Genome-wide analysis identifies novel susceptibility loci for myocardial infarction. Eur. Heart J. 42, 919–933 (2021).") and PR interval[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR10 "Ntalla, I. et al. Multi-ancestry GWAS of the electrocardiographic PR interval identifies 202 loci underlying cardiac conduction. Nat. Commun. 11, 2542 (2020).").

For the 50 newly identified genes, the gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis by g: Profiler[45](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR45 "Reimand, J. et al. g: Profiler—a web server for functional interpretation of gene lists (2016 update). Nucleic Acids Res. 44, W83–W89 (2016).") indicated these genes are enriched in the biological process (BP) of atrioventricular (AV) node cell action potential (FDR = 4.56 × 10−3), AV node cell to bundle of His cell signaling (FDR = 4.56 × 10−3), and AV node cell to bundle of His cell communication (FDR = 4.95 × 10−3), which are related with the regulation of heart rate[46](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR46 "van der Maarel, L. E., Postma, A. V. & Christoffels, V. M. Genetics of sinoatrial node function and heart rate disorders. Dis. Models Mech. 16, dmm050101 (2023).") (Fig. [3C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3), Supplementary Fig. [S15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1), Supplementary Table [S13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). Thus, these new genes identified by GWAS using the predicted spQRSTa are potentially associated with heart functions.

### Predicting cardiovascular disease risks from genotype

The predicted ECG traits were used to predict six types of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) risks and their diagnosis age by deep-learning models. The deep-learning model for predicting risks of CVDs is termed as DeepCVD that is an auto-encoder based deep neural network model integrating the 169 predicted ECG traits with sex and age. DeepCVD is formed by two parts. The first part is an auto-encoder (AE) that is used to denoise and extract compressed representations of ECG traits. The second part is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that is employed to predict risk of CVD from the compressed representation and original representation of ECG traits with sex and age. DeepCVD was tested by 7422 individuals (Supplementary Table [S5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)) from UKB-ECG test set. By training the DeepCVD using the predicted ECG traits for samples in UKB-noECG dataset (DeepCVDpred), it achieved average AUC of 0.80 (ranging from 0.76 to 0.86) (Fig. [4A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4) and Supplementary Fig. [S16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)) in the test set (UKB-ECG test set). By comparison, the PRS regression model integrated with sex and age achieved average AUC of 0.71 (ranging from 0.69 to 0.74) (Fig. [4A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4) and Supplementary Fig. [S16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)).

DeepCVDobs model trained on the observed ECG traits from 29,692 individuals in UKB-ECG training set achieved a significantly (_P__t-test_ = 3.24 × 10−4) lower AUC (averagely 0.77, ranging from 0.74 to 0.83) than the DeepCVDpred model (AUC = 0.80) trained on the predicted ECG traits of 388,284 individuals from UKB-noECG dataset when these two models were tested on the 7422 individuals in UKB-ECG test set (Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Tab1), Fig. [4A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4) and Supplementary Fig. [S16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). When DeepCVDpred was trained in a smaller dataset containing 29,692 individuals randomly selected from the UKB-noECG dataset, the model (DeepCVDpred-s) achieved average AUC of 0.76 in predicting CVD risks for 7422 individuals in UKB-ECG test set. This result is only slightly lower than the DeepCVDobs model (Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Tab1)). This result indicated that the ECG traits predicted by CapECG have a comparable ability to predict disease risks as the observed ECG traits. Figure [4B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4) shows the ROC for predicting risks of angina pectoris and myocardial infarction by DeepCVDpred model trained on the predicted ECG traits of 388,284 individuals from UKB-noECG dataset.

DeepCVD-Age is developed to predict the diagnosis age of CVDs, which was constructed by adapting the output layer and loss function of DeepCVD through preserving the original architecture. Specifically, the output layer of the DeepCVD-Age was modified by replacing the final softmax activation layer with a linear activation layer, thus adapting the model for diagnosis age prediction. The model was trained using the CapECG-predicted ECG traits for individuals in UKB-noECG dataset, and was tested by individuals from UKB-ECG test set. In the test set (Supplementary Table [S5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)), the predicted age for the occurring of CVDs is significantly correlated with the observed diagnosis age with average PCC of 0.74 ranging from 0.68 to 0.84 (Fig. [4C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4)), indicating the potential of the method in early warning of CVDs. By comparison, the model trained by using the observed ECG traits of the individuals in UKB-ECG training set achieved average PCC of 0.72 (Supplementary Fig. [S17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)).

The importance of the 169 ECG traits in DeepCVD for predicting risks of CVDs are evaluated through integrated gradients[47](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR47 "Cheung, C. Y. et al. A deep-learning system for the assessment of cardiovascular disease risk via the measurement of retinal-vessel calibre. Nat. Biomed. Eng. 5, 498–508 (2021)."). The top 5 most important ECG traits are T-wave amplitude on V6 lead (V6_T), R-wave amplitude on V5 lead (V5_R), R peak area on V3 lead (V3_inteR), R-wave amplitude on V4 lead (V4_R), and S-wave amplitude on V4 lead (V4_S) (Supplementary Fig. [S18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1)). As shown in Supplementary Fig. [S18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#MOESM1), V6_T is the most important ECG trait for predicting risks of ischemic heart disease, angina pectoris and coronary atherosclerosis. Besides, V5_R and V3_inteR are the top 5 most important features for more than three CVDs. This finding is consistent with previous studies that have indicated that myocardial infarction and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are correlated with high amplitude R wave and T wave inversion on the left precordial leads[48](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR48 "Vitale, G. et al. Standard ECG for differential diagnosis between Anderson-Fabry disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Heart 108, 54–60 (2022)."),[49](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR49 "Koechlin, L. et al. Hyperacute T wave in the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. Ann. Emerg. Med 82, 194–202 (2023).").

### Applications of CapECG in predicting risks of CVDs in multiethnicity

The CapECG was also tested by Non-European test set, Asian-ECG test set and African-ECG test set, respectively. The individuals in the Non-European test set are those not of European ancestry, and individuals in the Asian-ECG test set and African-ECG test set are those who are of Asian ancestry and African ancestry, respectively. The samples in these three datasets have both ECG and genotype data, and do not take part in training CapECG.

CapECG has achieved average PCC of 0.51, 0.52 and 0.50 for predicting 102 ECG traits with significant heritability (_P_ < 0.05/169 = 2.96 × 10−4) in the Non-European test set, Asian-ECG test set and African-ECG test set, respectively. Specifically, CapECG has achieved PCC of 0.52, 0.52 and 0.51 in predicting spQRSTa for individuals in Non-European test set, Asian-ECG test set and African-ECG test set, respectively (Fig. [4D](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4)).

When the predicted ECG traits were used to predict the risks of six types of CVDs, the DeepCVD achieved average AUC of 0.73, 0.74 and 0.73 in Non-European test set, Asian-ECG test set and African-ECG test set, respectively (Fig. [4E](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4)), which is close to the DeepCVD model trained using genotype data of individuals with European Ancestry (average AUC = 0.80). In comparison, the PRS-based method has achieved average AUC of 0.66, 0.68 and 0.66 in predicting risks of CVDs for individuals in Non-European test set, Asian-ECG test set and African-ECG test set, respectively (Fig. [4E](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig4)).

## Discussion

Electrocardiogram (ECG) is important for cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) diagnosis. Sau et al. have developed a deep-learning model for predicting cardiovascular diseases and mortality using ECG information, and have shown that the predicted risks are significantly correlated with risks of cardiovascular diseases and mortality[50](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR50 "Sau, A. et al. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram for mortality and cardiovascular risk estimation: a model development and validation study. Lancet Digit Health 6, e791–e802 (2024)."). However, the missing ECG in population-scale biobank is an obstacle to effectively utilizing both genotype and phenotype data.

In this study, we have used Capsule Network to construct the ECG trait prediction model (CapECG). CapECG has shown the potential to capture the complex relationship of SNPs. The relationship of these SNPs in each LD block was characterized by a self-attention based capsule network in the prediction. The self-attention routing algorithm is further used to route active capsules to the whole capsules. Comparing CapECG to CapsNet, it has achieved much better performance in predicting ECG traits, indicating LD block-based self-attention is an efficient approach to describe genotype and ECG traits relationships.

Moreover, the advantages of CapECG have also been identified in comparison to other machine-learning methods, such as MLP, Transformer, CNN, XGBoost and ridge regression model. This study has taken spQRSTa as an example to evaluate the performance of CapECG. Recent studies have reported associations of the spQRSTa with risk for arrhythmogenesis, sudden cardiac death and cardiac-related mortality[51](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR51 "Jensen, K. et al. Bringing critical race praxis into the study of electrophysiological substrate of sudden cardiac death: the ARIC study. J. Am. Heart Assoc. 9, e015012 (2020)."),[52](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR52 "Zhang, X. et al. Spatial/frontal QRS-T angle predicts all-cause mortality and cardiac mortality: a meta-analysis. PloS One 10, e0136174 (2015)."). Thus, spQRSTa is an important electrocardiographic feature associated with specific cardiac conditions and pathologies, making it crucial for understanding underlying genetic determinants. A recent study has provided GWAS results on spQRSTa, which is one of the GWAS with the largest samples for electrocardiography analysis[38](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR38 "Young, W. J. et al. Genetic architecture of spatial electrical biomarkers for cardiac arrhythmia and relationship with cardiovascular disease. Nat. Commun. 14, 1411 (2023)."). Using this GWAS result as part of external validation helps us to verify the accuracy and reliability of our method in predicting genetic correlations. Besides, we also demonstrated that CapECG is accurate and efficient, and the predicted ECG traits have improved the prediction (average AUC = 0.80) of CVD risks by using genotype data compared to the polygenic risk-based method (average AUC = 0.71) developed by Tanigawa[53](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR53 "Tanigawa, Y. et al. Significant sparse polygenic risk scores across 813 traits in UK Biobank. PLoS Genet 18, e1010105 (2022)."), indicating a key application of CapECG in early warning of CVDs.

CapECG has improved the accuracy of the prediction of ECG traits from genotype in comparison to the linear model and the commonly used capsule network. The genotype and phenotype may not be correlated linearly[54](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR54 "An, U. et al. Deep learning-based phenotype imputation on population-scale biobank data increases genetic discoveries. Nat. Genet 55, 2269–2276 (2023)."). Although it is possible to build a non-linear model considering all possible genotypic data, this approach is limited by potential overfitting from adding highly interacted genetic variants. CapECG developed in this study is capable of capturing complex patterns in the phenotype-genotype associations and SNP-SNP interactions in LD blocks by leveraging multiple capsule layers of non-linear transformations and attention mechanism. Comparing to the traditional CapsNet and other machine learning models, CapECG has achieved better performance in predicating ECG traits (>6% improvement in PCC between the predicted and observed ECG traits compared to other methods). This ability to learn high-level representations of genetic information can be advantageous in tasks with large and complex datasets, where traditional machine learning methods may struggle to capture intricate patterns. Thus, CapECG can handle high-dimensional genotype data efficiently, and to learn representations or embeddings that capture the most informative aspects of the genotype data.

The advantages of CapECG are partly contributed by the LD-PCA. The LD-PCA is developed to reduce the dimensionality of genotype data by leveraging Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and LD information. LD can be used to segment genome-wide information into disjoint substructures through quantifying the correlation between SNPs. High or complete LD between SNP pairs is often pointed out as the source of redundancy in large-scale genomic data and removing loci based on their pairwise correlation is a prevalent practice called LD pruning[55](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR55 "Calus, M. P. & Vandenplas, J. SNPrune: an efficient algorithm to prune large SNP array and sequence datasets based on high linkage disequilibrium. Genet. Select. Evol. 50, 1–11 (2018)."). Hibar et al. summarized correlated SNPs within each gene into principal components that explain 95% of the variance per gene[56](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR56 "Hibar, D. P. et al. Voxelwise gene-wide association study (vGeneWAS): multivariate gene-based association testing in 731 elderly subjects. Neuroimage 56, 1875–1891 (2011)."). LD-PCA addresses two fundamental challenges in genomic prediction: (1) the high-dimensionality problem of genomic data, by transforming highly correlated SNPs within an LD block into a small set of principal components; and (2) the limitation of single-SNP models in capturing haplotype-based effects and epistatic interactions, as the principal components effectively represent common haplotypes, enabling the model to learn from aggregated genetic information. The LD-PCA is the first approach to combine LD-based dimensionality reduction and enable CapECG to capture interactions between LD blocks across the whole genome, and further identify significant SNPs in LD blocks.

Although the average heritability of ECG traits is low, our prediction model has achieved good performance. The ~15% estimate of ECG traits refers to the SNP-based heritability (_h²_) estimated from all common SNPs across the genome. This is a measure of the total phenotypic variance attributable to common genetic variants captured by the GWAS. While the overall SNP-based heritability of ECG traits is moderate, our model specifically targets the heritable genetic architecture that is both stable and predictive. The LD-PCA increases the effective heritability captured by our model by aggregating all associated SNPs and focusing on the principal components that explain the majority of population genetic covariance. These SNPs have the potential to represent greater heritability enrichment of ECG traits[57](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR57 "He, D. et al. Accurate identification of genes associated with brain disorders by integrating heterogeneous genomic data into a Bayesian framework. EBioMedicine 107, 105286 (2024)."). By concentrating on this effective genetic signal, our model achieves meaningful predictive accuracy. Moreover, the sample size for ECG GWAS is limited, which may reduce the power for estimating the heritability.

The GWAS for the predicted spQRSTa have identified more significant SNPs overlapped with the published GWAS comparing to the GWAS for the observed spQRSTa. The underlying reason is from two respects. First, by predicting ECG traits from genotype data, CapECG has enlarged the sample size of the ECG. Secondly, CapECG has captured the non-linear relationship between genotype and ECG traits, which have improved the power of the GWAS. The contributions of CapECG in improving power of GWAS were measured using the simulated genotype. For the predicted spQRSTa using the simulated genotype data, the GWAS identified 16 iSNPs out of 133 top significant SNPs (LD _r__2_ < 0.01) overlapped with the published spQRSTa GWAS (Fig. [3B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3)). This is higher than 13 overlapped iSNPs out of 133 top significant SNPs (LD _r__2_ < 0.01) identified by the GWAS for the observed ECG traits, indicating CapECG has captured non-linear associations between ECG traits and genotype in the training process using the UKB-ECG dataset (Fig. [3B](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#Fig3)).

Additionally, MAGMA analysis of the GWAS for the CapECG-predicted spQRSTa has identified many novel genes that are not identified as associated with the observed ECG traits. For example, _ALPK3_ is indicated to be associated with “interval of R-wave begin to R-wave end at I lead” (I_t_R) (MAGMA _P_ = 2.34 × 10−9). Indeed, _ALPK3_ encodes a nuclear kinase that plays an essential role in early differentiation of cardiomyocytes, and has been proven to be correlated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)[58](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR58 "Lopes, L. R. et al. Alpha-protein kinase 3 (ALPK3) truncating variants are a cause of autosomal dominant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Eur. Heart J. 42, 3063–3073 (2021).") and electrocardiogram (ECG)[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR10 "Ntalla, I. et al. Multi-ancestry GWAS of the electrocardiographic PR interval identifies 202 loci underlying cardiac conduction. Nat. Commun. 11, 2542 (2020)."). Besides, the MAGMA analysis for the GWAS of CapECG-predicted “the difference between R and S amplitude at V3 lead” (V3_RS) identified _FHOD3_ gene (MAGMA _P_ = 1.75 × 10−25) that is known to play a crucial role in early heart development and maintenance of the heart function in adults by contributing to sarcomere organization[59](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR59 "Kan-o, M. et al. Mammalian formin Fhod3 plays an essential role in cardiogenesis by organizing myofibrillogenesis. Biol. Open 1, 889–896 (2012)."),[60](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR60 "Fujimoto, N. et al. Transgenic expression of the formin protein fhod3 selectively in the embryonic heart: role of actin-binding activity of fhod3 and its sarcomeric localization during myofibrillogenesis. PLoS One 11, e0148472 (2016).").

CapECG has mapped the high dimensional SNPs to a few ECG traits and has improved the prediction of CVD risks in early life from genotype. The genotype is an important factor for the occurring of CVDs in individuals[61](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR61 "Li, C. et al. Genomic innovation in early life cardiovascular disease prevention and treatment. Circ. Res 132, 1628–1647 (2023)."). However, most of the current methods for predicting CVDs using the genotype data achieved limited accuracy. The underlying reason is that these methods are unable to capture the non-linear relationships between genotype and phenotype. When we applied CapECG to predict ECG traits for 388,284 UKB European individuals without ECG information, the predicted ECG traits have achieved average AUC of 0.80 (ranging from 0.76 to 0.86) in predicting CVDs, which is much better than the model using the genotype information (average AUC = 0.71), suggesting the importance of predicting ECG traits using the deep-learning model from genotype data rather than only the genotype data. Using the CapECG-predicted ECG traits, we have trained a model to predict the occurring age of CVDs. The predicted age is highly correlated with the observed age with PCC > 0.6. These results have supported an important application of CapECG in early warning the risk of CVDs only using the genotype data.

This study has several limitations. First, we performed PCA for dimensionality reduction in the LD block. Despite its usefulness in disposing of the redundancy in sparse data, PCA is only able to preserve variance as long as the SNPs can be assumed to interact linearly[62](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR62 "Alanis-Lobato, G., Cannistraci, C. V., Eriksson, A., Manica, A. & Ravasi, T. Highlighting nonlinear patterns in population genetics datasets. Sci. Rep. 5, 8140 (2015)."). Non-linear feature extractor, such as auto-encoder[63](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02438-3#ref-CR63 "Taş, G. et al. Computing linkage disequilibrium aware genome embeddings using autoencoders. Bioinformatics btae, 326 (2024)."), is required in the future for phenotype prediction. Second, the identification of the SNPs associated with ECG traits is influenced by the accuracy of the predicted ECG traits. Thirdly, due to the limitation of obtaining an external validation dataset that includes genotype data, ECG and disease diagnoses, it is impractical to conduct the related experiments out of the UK-Biobank, currently. While we employed internal train-validation-test splits to ensure robustness of CapECG and DeepCVD within the UKB population, the generalizability of CapECG and DeepCVD needs to be confirmed in future studies using the dataset out of UKB.

In conclusion, we have developed CapECG for predicting ECG traits from genotype, which has significantly improved the early prediction of CVDs for participants only having genotype data. Moreover, we have demonstrated that this method can capture the non-linear relationship between SNP and ECG traits, and to identify more SNPs showing significant associations with ECG traits. Thus, we anticipate this method to have wide applications for uncovering novel insights into the genetic factors associated with ECG.
```

##### [A deep learning model integrating structured data and clinical text for predicting atrial fibrillation recurrence](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5)

```
## Abstract

Multimodal perioperative data from patients undergoing atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation offer valuable insights for stratifying recurrence risk, yet remain underutilized in prediction models. This multicenter retrospective study included 2508 patients who underwent AF ablation at five Chinese centers: The Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine (Jan 2016–Mar 2024; Training Cohort), Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province (Jan 2015–Jan 2024; Training Cohort), The Affiliated Hospital of Yunnan University (Jan 2016–Jan 2024; Validation Cohort), Jinhua People’s Hospital (Jan 2020–Jan 2024; Test Cohort), and Ningbo Beilun Hospital (Jan 2020–Jan 2024; Test Cohort). We developed a dual-branch deep learning model to predict AF recurrence, in which structured data were processed via a 1D ResNet and textual data were encoded using four large language models (LLaMA-7B, Phi2-2.7B, Mistral-7B, and MedGemma-27B). The model incorporating MedGemma for text feature extraction performed best, achieving areas under the curve of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.921–0.946), 0.928 (95% CI: 0.904–0.950), and 0.911 (95% CI: 0.878–0.941) on the training, validation, and test sets, respectively. Our model integrates multimodal perioperative data from AF ablation patients, effectively identifies high-risk individuals, and may facilitate targeted interventions to reduce relapse.

## Introduction

Catheter ablation is a rhythm control strategy endorsed by guidelines for patients with atrial fibrillation (AF)[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR1 "Writing Committee Members et al 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 83, 109–279 (2024)."). Nonetheless, long-term freedom from atrial arrhythmias remains unsatisfactory, with 30–50% of patients experiencing recurrence within 1 year and requiring repeat ablation[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR2 "Zink, M. D. et al. Predictors of recurrence of atrial fibrillation within the first 3 months after ablation. Europace. 22, 1337–1344 (2020)."). The identification of populations at high risk for AF recurrence facilitates the development of post-ablation preventive strategies and rhythm control regimens[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR2 "Zink, M. D. et al. Predictors of recurrence of atrial fibrillation within the first 3 months after ablation. Europace. 22, 1337–1344 (2020).").

Established predictors, including AF type, left atrial diameter (LAD), AF duration, machine learning models based on structured preoperative data, and clinical risk scores such as APPLE and CAAP-AF, have demonstrated efficacy in forecasting recurrence[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR3 "Dretzke, J. et al. Predicting recurrent atrial fibrillation after catheter ablation: a systematic review of prognostic models. Europace. 22, 748–760 (2020)."),[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR4 "Jia, S. et al. Association between triglyceride-glucose index trajectories and radiofrequency ablation outcomes in patients with stage 3D atrial fibrillation. Cardiovasc. Diabetol. 23, 121 (2024)."),[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR5 "Black-Maier, E. et al. Predicting atrial fibrillation recurrence after ablation in patients with heart failure: validity of the APPLE and CAAP-AF risk scoring systems. Pacing Clin. Electrophysiol. 42, 1440–1447 (2019)."). However, they remain constrained by their reliance on pre-procedural information and fail to capture the impact of individualized treatment strategies and procedural specifics on outcomes. The clinical management of AF generates extensive multimodal textual records that encapsulate valuable information beyond the structured data. Echocardiography reports provide quantitative and qualitative assessments of the cardiac structure and function, incorporating interpreter-specific insights. Pre-procedural 24-h Holter monitoring captures the dynamic arrhythmia burden and heart rate variability. Crucially, electrophysiologists document detailed procedural notes, including the ablation strategy, lesion set design, and real-time parameters, which are often lost in structured data systems. The semantic depth of these texts represents a critical and underutilized source of prognostic information.

Large language models (LLMs) provide a transformative approach to clinical text mining through advanced semantic understanding[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR6 "Shool, S. et al. A systematic review of large language model (LLM) evaluations in clinical medicine. BMC Med. Inform. Decis. Mak. 25, 117 (2025)."). This study innovatively applied four state-of-the-art LLMs—MedGemma, Phi2, Llama, and Mistral—to derive high-dimensional features from clinical texts such as echocardiography reports, Holter interpretations, and ablation notes[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR7 "Google. MedGemma. GitHub repository, 
https://github.com/Google-Health/medgemma
(2025)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR8 "Microsoft. Phi-2: The surprising power of small language models. Microsoft Research Blog, 
https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/phi-2-the-surprising-power-of-small-language-models/
(2023)."),[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR9 "Touvron, H. et al. Llama 2: open foundation and fine-tuned chat models. Preprint at arXiv 
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2307.09288
(2023)."),[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR10 "Jiang, A. Q. et al. Mistral 7B. Preprint at arXiv 
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2310.06825
(2023)."). By evaluating the proficiency of each model in medical language comprehension, we identified the most predictive LLM for textual representation. We further propose a deep learning framework that combines LLM-based text features with structured clinical data. Using peri-procedural text extracted from hospital systems for patients with AF undergoing ablation, we aimed to develop a precise and individualized AF recurrence prediction model tailored to personalized treatment.

## Results

### Participant baseline

This study retrospectively analyzed data from patients who underwent AF ablation at five Chinese AF centers: the Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine (ZJU4th; January 2016–March 2024), Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province (ZJTZH; January 2015–January 2024), the Affiliated Hospital of Yunnan University (YNH; January 2016–January 2024), Jinhua People’s Hospital (JHPH; January 2020–January 2024), and Ningbo Beilun Hospital (NBH; January 2020–January 2024). As shown in Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Tab1) (the missing structured data is shown in Supplementary Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)), a total of 2,508 participants were enrolled in this study, with a median age of 65.00 (interquartile range [IQR] 58.00–71.00) years. Among them, 1,572 (62.68%) were men. The overall median follow-up duration was 31.00 (IQR 17.00–48.00) months, and the overall recurrence rate was 22.57%. Significant differences (_p_ < 0.05) were observed across centers in the following variables: age, systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), AF duration, CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, HAS-BLED score, LAD, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), survival time, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), albumin, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), APPLE score, CAAP-AF score, gender, hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, AF type, and use of class I/III or class II antiarrhythmic drugs.

### Model development and validation

Before model development, patient data from the five centers were assigned to a training set (ZJU4th and ZJTZH), a validation set (YNH), and a test set (JHPH and NBH). Detailed data distributions are provided in Supplementary Tables [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)–[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1). Within the architecture of the dual-branch deep learning network, we fine-tuned different LLMs (LLaMA-7B, Phi2-2.7B, Mistral-7B, and MedGemma-27B) as the base for the textual feature extraction branch (Clinical text examples are presented in Supplementary [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)), while keeping the structured data branch and late fusion pathway identical across experiments. As shown in Fig. [1A–C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Fig1), the model incorporating the MedGemma-27B module for text processing, followed by late fusion with structured data (MedGemma-Fusion), yielded the best performance. It achieved an area under the curve of 0.934 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.921–0.946) in the training set, 0.928 (95% CI: 0.904–0.950) in the validation set, and 0.911 (95% CI: 0.878–0.941) in the test set. Additionally, we assessed the impact of sample size on the performance of the MedGemma-Fusion model (Supplementary Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)). To evaluate the generalization performance of the model, we used each center as the test set, with the remaining centers constituting the training and validation sets (Supplementary Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)). To further validate the rationale for late fusion, we conducted additional ablation experiments, including predictions of AF recurrence based solely on structured data and predictions based on text features extracted using the optimal LLM (MedGemma) (Supplementary Table [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1), Supplementary Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)). Moreover, we conducted a series of ablation studies to rigorously substantiate the design of MedGemma-Fusion network for predicting AF recurrence. We adopted a two-stage fine-tuning strategy for the text feature extraction branch: domain-adaptive pre-training, followed by supervised contrastive fine-tuning (Supplementary Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1), Supplementary Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)). During this process, the weights of the structured data channel in MedGemma-Fusion were frozen. In the structured data-processing branch, given that recurrence represents a relatively minor class, we implemented a conditional tabular generative adversarial network (GAN) within the training fold to perform data augmentation and balance the class distribution. Specifically, a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty‌ (WGAN-GP) variant tailored to tabular data was employed, where the generator was conditioned on class labels and encoded categorical features to produce synthetic positive samples consistent with the real joint distribution. After freezing the weights of the text feature channel in the optimally trained MedGemma-Fusion model, we compared different data augmentation techniques (synthetic minority oversampling technique [SMOTE] and adaptive synthetic sampling [ADASYN]) to demonstrate the advantages of using the WGAN-GP (Supplementary Table [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1), Supplementary Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)). We further compared the MedGemma-Fusion model against conventional AF recurrence risk factors (including AF type and LAD) and established clinical risk scores (CHA₂DS₂-VASc, CAAP-AF, and APPLE). As summarized in Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Tab2) and depicted in Fig. [1D–L](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Fig1), MedGemma-Fusion outperformed all reference models across all three datasets. Moreover, decision curve analysis (DCA) consistently demonstrated the superior clinical utility of MedGemma-Fusion across datasets, as shown in Fig. [1G–I](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Fig1). We also benchmarked our novel AF recurrence risk model against models derived from the original variables of the APPLE and CAAP-AF scores (Supplementary Tables [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)–[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#MOESM1)).

### Kaplan–Meier (K–M) survival analysis

Based on the optimal MedGemma-Fusion model, we generated K–M survival curves to evaluate its ability to discriminate recurrence risk across different datasets. As shown in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Fig2), the model exhibited a strong discriminative ability for recurrence risk, with a concordance index of 0.874 in the training set, 0.860 in the validation set, and 0.870 in the test set.

### SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based interpretability analysis of the model

In Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Fig3), AF duration, LAD, and AF type emerged as the primary weighted variables within the structured data, whereas text-derived features such as “pulmonary vein,” “potential,” and “motion” were identified as key vectors contributing to the model’s decision-making process.

### Sensitivity analysis

A sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the stability of the model with and without early AF recurrence (Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#Fig4)).

## Discussion

We developed a dual-branch deep learning network that integrates unstructured medical texts and structured data features based on perioperative data from patients undergoing AF ablation. In the text feature extraction module, a comparative evaluation of the four LLMs within an invariant fusion framework identified MedGemma-Fusion as optimal. This demonstrated robust predictive performance and generalizability in external validation.

In clinical practice, patients undergoing AF ablation generate multimodal medical data during the perioperative period, including unstructured medical texts and structured data. Textual modalities capture physicians’ clinical interpretations and reflect patients’ current AF progression. However, conventional machine learning models remain limited in their ability to comprehend the underlying logical relationships within medical services, which was corroborated by the models we built by employing clinical variables from the APPLE and CAAP-AF scores. In contrast, LLMs trained through extensive parameter iterations demonstrate superior performance in processing textual data. This study designed a dual-channel deep learning architecture that prevents structured data vectors from inducing hallucinatory interference during textual feature extraction. Furthermore, to fine-tune the LLMs, we employed a weakly supervised training strategy (recurrence risk classification) to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during text feature learning. The rationality of our network architecture was verified through a series of ablation studies.

The MedGemma-Fusion framework achieved the best predictive performance, indicating that MedGemma effectively learned more discriminative feature representations from the multimodal medical text data of patients with AF. MedGemma, developed by Google (Mountain View, CA, USA) based on the Gemma-3 architecture, is a domain-specific LLM optimized for multimodal medical comprehension[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR7 "Google. MedGemma. GitHub repository, 
https://github.com/Google-Health/medgemma
(2025)."). Its medical background knowledge enhances its utility in supporting clinical decision-making. Therefore, MedGemma performed optimally in this study, given that its pre-training corpus was derived from medical domains. Because LLMs operate through semantic segmentation, we conducted a keyword analysis on the best-performing model to identify semantically salient features[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR11 "Bedi, S. et al. Testing and evaluation of health care applications of large language models: a systematic review. JAMA. 333, 319–328 (2025)."). Terms such as “pulmonary vein” and “potential,” which are key concepts documented during ablation procedures, emerged as critical tokens. This aligns with the semantic compression mechanism of transformer-based models, where attention mechanisms and subword tokenization condense core semantic information into highly informative tokens, such as the aggregated representation of “pulmonary vein” or the verbal center of “ablation,” causing attribution to focus on these tokens. These terms correspond to essential steps in electrophysiological procedures, including pulmonary vein isolation, which is the cornerstone of AF ablation, and the elimination of fractionated or additional potentials to disrupt rotor formation and terminate re-entrant circuits[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR12 "Parameswaran, R., Al-Kaisey, A.
