M. & Kalman, J. M. Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation: current indications and evolving technologies. Nat. Rev. Cardiol. 18, 210–225 (2021)."). This confirms that the model successfully captured clinically relevant feature vectors.

The token “Vein” reflects the necessity of femoral vein puncture for catheter insertion during AF ablation, increasing its frequency in clinical narratives. Furthermore, the token “Motion” likely originates from the model’s interpretation of preoperative echocardiography reports and carries significant weight in feature importance. Different types of AF exhibit distinct atrial motion patterns, potentially related to atrial fibrosis[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR13 "Brundel, B. J. J. M. et al. Atrial fibrillation. Nat. Rev. Dis. Primers 8, 21 (2022)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR14 "Hu, Y. F., Chen, Y. J., Lin, Y. J. & Chen, S. A. Inflammation and the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation. Nat. Rev. Cardiol. 12, 230–243 (2015)."). Although echocardiography is operator-dependent, we mitigated this heterogeneity by incorporating multicenter datasets, thereby enhancing the robustness of the model. By leveraging textual reports from echocardiograms, we input functional and kinematic descriptors of cardiac chambers based on the sonographers’ expertise, circumventing the variability in imaging parameters or machine differences. Interestingly, tokens from Holter reports contributed relatively little to the model, likely because paroxysmal AF, which was the predominant subtype in our cohort, often resulted in normal Holter findings. While previous studies by Krasteva and Zhang highlighted the predictive value of Holter monitoring for AF detection, its limited influence may be attributable to the loss of granular electrographic features in textual representations[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR15 "Krasteva, V. et al. Detection of atrial fibrillation in Holter ECG recordings by ECHOView images: a deep transfer learning study. Diagnostics 15, 865 (2025)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR16 "Zhang, P. et al. Automatic screening of patients with atrial fibrillation from 24-h Holter recording using deep learning. Eur. Heart J. Digit. Health 4, 216–224 (2023).").

In the structured data analysis, factors such as the duration of AF, AF type, and LAD were identified as the most significant predictors of AF recurrence, which was consistent with our previous findings[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR17 "Jia, S. et al. A simple logistic regression model for predicting the likelihood of recurrence of atrial fibrillation within 1 year after initial radio-frequency catheter ablation therapy. Front. Cardiovasc. Med. 8, 819341 (2022)."). These factors contribute to the deterioration of the atrial substrate to varying degrees, thereby perpetuating arrhythmia[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR14 "Hu, Y. F., Chen, Y. J., Lin, Y. J. & Chen, S. A. Inflammation and the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation. Nat. Rev. Cardiol. 12, 230–243 (2015)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02436-5#ref-CR18 "Sohns, C. & Marrouche, N. F. Atrial fibrillation and cardiac fibrosis. Eur. Heart J. 41, 1123–1131 (2020)."). These results validate the efficacy of our approach, which combines sample augmentation with a ResNet-based architecture within a structured data pipeline.

In this study, the rationale behind adopting a center-based split into training/validation/test sets was to ensure, without introducing data leakage, sufficient sample size and relatively balanced class distribution during the training phase. This approach enables stable and reproducible training and hyperparameter tuning for both our model and all comparator baselines, while also allowing a genuine assessment of cross-center generalization during testing. The ZJU4th and ZJTZ cohorts were used for training: together they provide a larger overall sample size with a more balanced ratio of positive to negative cases. Their combination offers richer learning signals for the model and baseline methods, thereby reducing instability and randomness caused by insufficient training data or severe class imbalance. The YNH cohort served for external validation (hyperparameter tuning and model selection): an independent center not involved in training was reserved for early stopping, hyperparameter selection, and final model determination. This prevents “implicit tuning” from repeated experimentation on the test set and ensures objectivity in the evaluation pipeline. The JHPH and NBH cohorts were held out for external testing. The remaining centers were entirely reserved for final performance assessment to evaluate cross-center generalization. In particular, JHPH, a center with fewer positive samples and a skewed distribution, is more suitable as an external test set representing a challenging “real-world” scenario. Including it in training could introduce severe class imbalance, compromise training stability, and hinder a conservative and credible estimation of generalization performance. To further verify the robustness of our deep learning model, we also performed additional leave-one-center-out validation.

Our study had some inherent limitations. First, although the model was validated across multiple centers, the sample size remained limited, and further validation with larger cohorts is warranted. Second, while we incorporated multimodal medical text data, including echocardiography, Holter electrocardiography (ECG), and procedural records, variability in reporting styles and levels of detail among physicians may have introduced heterogeneity into the text-based features. Although personalized ablation strategies (e.g., intraoperative energy settings and ablation sites) have been tailored to patients with AF across different centers, their impact on feature extraction using LLMs from templated procedural notes remains elusive. In the structured data domain, we incorporated both routine preoperative laboratory tests and basic patient information. While exporting these structured data from the Hospital Information System reflects real-world clinical practice, it inevitably introduces variables unrelated to AF recurrence that may influence the model’s decision-making. Moreover, it is unavoidable that certain risk factors relevant to AF recurrence are omitted due to their unavailability in current real-world settings or within the Hospital Information System. Finally, the LLMs used in this study were based on the most recent versions available at the time of research; however, given the rapid iteration of LLMs, the impact of future updates on model performance remains uncertain. Additionally, the substantial computational resources required to deploy such models may impede their implementation in resource-limited healthcare settings.

We developed a dual-branch deep learning network that integrates feature representations extracted from medical texts using MedGemma, a specialized LLM, with structured data features derived from the perioperative records of AF ablation patients. This integrated approach provides novel clinical insights into risk prognosis and enhances strategies for the post-procedural management of AF ablation.
```
##### [Evaluation and application of electrocardiographic age model for children](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3)

```
## Abstract

ECG-age, derived from ECG signals using deep neural networks (DNNs), correlates with health status but has been predominantly studied in adults, neglecting the unique development trajectories of pediatric hearts. This study evaluates and proposes a pediatric-specific ECG-age model for clinical application. Validated on 58,672 ECGs from healthy children, three approaches were assessed: a pre-trained adult model, the same model retrained on pediatric data, and feature-enhanced models which was used to enhance the interpretability of the model. Results demonstrate limited applicability of adult-derived models, while dedicated pediatric models achieved accurate age assessment (MAE: 7.878 ± 6.658 months, R²=0.821), further confirmed on external data. Analysis of 209,644 ECGs across 21 pediatric diseases and 102,441 ECGs with 20 abnormalities revealed that an large ECG-age gap between chronological age indicates stronger associations with diseases or abnormalities. In a specific scenario study, ECG-age significantly correlated with postoperative complications in tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) surgery children. These findings indicate that pediatric-specific ECG-age models can effectively measure children’s cardiac development and signal pathological conditions, supporting their potential as a widely applicable clinical digital biomarker in pediatrics.

## Introduction

Invented by Dutch scientist W. Einthoven in 1895, electrocardiogram (ECG) has become indispensable in clinical usage and is now widely used in both adults and pediatric populations. Computerized ECG analysis, developed 50 years ago to aid clinics/research, still faces accuracy/interference limits[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR1 "Shah, A. P. & Rubin, S. A. Errors in the computerized electrocardiogram interpretation of cardiac rhythm. J. Electrocardiol. 40, 385–390 (2007)."), particularly in pediatric contexts due to rapidly changing ECG characteristics during childhood development, especially in infancy[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR2 "O’Connor, M., McDaniel, N. & Brady, W. J. The pediatric electrocardiogram. Am. J. Emerg. Med. 26, 221–228 (2008).").

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep neural networks (DNNs), have demonstrated significant potential for automated ECG interpretation, achieving exceptional performance in preliminary studies[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR3 "Ribeiro, A. H. et al. Automatic diagnosis of the 12-lead ECG using a deep neural network. Nat. Commun. 11, 1760 (2020)."),[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR4 "Hannun, A. Y. et al. Cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection and classification in ambulatory electrocardiograms using a deep neural network. Nat. Med. 25, 65–69 (2019)."). DNNs represent a paradigm shift from traditional ECG automated analysis methods[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR5 "Liu, Y. et al. Y-Net-ECG: A Multi-Lead informed and interpretable architecture for ECG segmentation across diverse rhythms. Expert Syst. Appl. 283, 127955 (2025)."). Unlike conventional approaches, DNN-derived characteristics do not always possess explicit electrocardiographic meaning[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR6 "Tao, R., Wang, L., Xiong, Y. & Zeng, Y. R. IM-ECG: an interpretable framework for arrhythmia detection using multi-lead ECG. Expert Syst. Appl. 237, 121497 (2024)."). While, this also indicates that DNN models may identify novel biomarkers with practical clinical utility. However, the “black-box” nature of DNNs also presents substantial challenges for clinical translation.

One promising application of ECG-based AI is ECG-age estimation, where neural network derive age prediction from ECG signals[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR7 "Attia, Z. I. et al. Age and sex Estimation using artificial intelligence from standard 12-Lead ECGs. Circ Arrhythmia Electrophysiol 12, (2019)."). ECG age extends the concept of “biological age”[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR8 "Hamczyk, M. R., Nevado, R. M., Barettino, A., Fuster, V. & Andrés, V. Biological versus chronological aging. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 75, 919–930 (2020)."), which reflects how specific physiological systems may age at rate different from chronological age. Since aging is a risk factor for numerous diseases-including cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR9 "Savji, N. et al. Association between advanced age and vascular disease in different arterial territories. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 61, 1736–1743 (2013).")-and since biological aging is influenced by diseases, environmental variables, inherited and acquired disorders, and lifestyle choices, ECG-age may serve as a predictor of such health determinants. Recent studies have established ECG-age as a scalable biomarker of cardiovascular risk and have associated it with various pathologies and mortality[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR10 "Toya, T. et al. Vascular aging detected by peripheral endothelial dysfunction is associated with ECG-Derived physiological aging. J Am. Heart Assoc 10, (2021)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR11 "Lima, E. M. et al. Deep neural network-estimated electrocardiographic age as a mortality predictor. Nat. Commun. 12, 5117 (2021)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR12 "Brant, L. C. C. et al. Association between electrocardiographic age and cardiovascular events in community settings: the Framingham heart study. Circ Cardiovasc. Qual. Outcomes 16, (2023)."). However, those ECG-age models often lack interpretability, posing challenges for performance validation and generalizability across diverse populations[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR13 "Sadeghi, Z. et al. A review of explainable artificial intelligence in healthcare. Comput. Electr. Eng. 118, 109370 (2024).").

Critically, while ‘age’ encompasses both aging in adults and developmental maturation in children, existing ECG-age research has overlooked the impact of continuous cardiac development in pediatric populations. Neonatal ECGs resemble right ventricular hypertrophy patterns seen in adults. Infant ECGs exhibit shorter conduction intervals (e.g. PR interval, QRS duration) due to smaller heart size, and postnatal cardiomyocyte growth transitions from fetal hyperplasia to hypertrophy—with cell volume increasing approximately 30-fold in early infancy[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR14 "Tan, C. M. J. & Lewandowski, A. J. The transitional heart: from early embryonic and fetal development to neonatal life. Fetal Diagn. Ther. 47, 373–386 (2020)."). As child age, ECGs shift toward left ventricular dominance, with heart rate, axis, intervals, and voltage criteria all evolving dynamically[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR15 "Rijnbeek, P. New normal limits for the paediatric electrocardiogram. Eur. Heart J. 22, 702–711 (2001)."). Given these profound developmental changes, the applicability of adult-derived ECG-age model to children remains unestablished.

In pediatric populations, ECG-age could serve as a low-cost and non-invasive biomarker of cardiac maturation. Furthermore, correlations between ECG-age deviations and clinical diagnoses or ECG abnormalities might offer valuable clinical insights. This study therefore aims to: (1) validate existing DNN-based ECG-age model in pediatric dataset; (2) develop and train dedicated pediatric ECG-age models with enhanced interpretability; and (3) investigate associations between ECG-age and pediatric diseases/ECG abnormalities.

## Methods

### Internal and external datasets and preprocessing

The primary dataset comprised 339,568 standards 12-lead ECGs retrospectively collected from the Children’s Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine (January 2019–June 2023). All ECGs were digital recorded at 500 Hz sampling rate with 10-second durations and clinically interpreted by pediatric cardiologists. Expert-annotated ECG features (e.g., heart rate, PR interval, QTc interval; full list in Supplementary Table [S1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#MOESM1)) were extracted from hospital reporting systems for subsequent feature selection. Chronological age (in months) was calculated from the difference between ECG acquisition time and birthdate.

For model development and validation, we identified 58,672 normal ECGs from children age < 84 months (mean age = 41.69 ± 24.44 months, neonates [< 1 month]: _n_ = 1,509) without clinical diagnoses. The cohort was sex-balanced (56.21% males).

External validation utilized a public pediatric ECG database from the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR16 "Tan, J. et al. A pediatric ECG database with disease diagnosis covering 11643 children. Sci. Data. 12, 867 (2025)."). After standardizing record length to 10 s with 500 Hz sampling rate, 584 ECGs interpreted as normal were selected from this cohort.

This retrospective study received approval from the Institutional Review Board/Ethics Committee of Children’s Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine (approval No. 2023-IRB-0108-P-01; May 3, 2023). Informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board/Ethics Committee of Children’s Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine for de-identified retrospective data. All procedures adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki principles.

### Architecture and feature selection of ECG-age models

#### The pre-trained Adult-derived ECG-age model

We utilized a pre-trained DNN-based ECG-age model developed by Lima et al.[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR11 "Lima, E. M. et al. Deep neural network-estimated electrocardiographic age as a mortality predictor. Nat. Commun. 12, 5117 (2021)."), which employs a ResNet-inspired architecture adapted for one-dimensional signals. This model incorporates skip connections to enhance training efficiency and was originally trained on the Clinical Outcomes in Digital Electrocardiography (CODE) cohort[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR17 "Ribeiro, A. L. P. et al. Tele-electrocardiography and bigdata: the CODE (Clinical outcomes in digital Electrocardiography) study. J. Electrocardiol. 57, S75–S78 (2019)."), comprising 15,584,415 adult patients ( age 16–85 years; 40.2% male). This pre-trained model (publicly available at Zenodo: [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4892365](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4892365)) served as our baseline for validation in pediatric populations, though it was not explicitly optimized for developmental nuances in children.

#### Dedicated pediatric ECG-age model

To address this limitation, we implemented an identically structured DNN architecture trained exclusively on pediatric ECG data. This model shares the same residual network design as the pre-trained adult model but was developed de novo using our pediatric dataset to capture age-specific electrophysiological patterns.

#### Feature-enhanced interpretable ECG age model

To bridge the “black-box” limitation of end-to-end DNNs and incorporate pediatric-specific electrocardiographic knowledge, we proposed and developed a dual-branch feature-enhanced architecture. This model processes:

- Raw signal branch: Original 12-lead ECG signals;
    
- Feature branch: Clinical relevant characteristics (e.g., heart rate, intervals, amplitudes, sex) derived from expert annotations (Supplementary Table [S1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#MOESM1)).
    

Three feature selection methods were employed to optimize input to the feature branch. As illustrated in Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Fig1), the architecture combines:

- A residual network for raw signal processing.
    
- A two-layer DNN (512 nodes/layer) for engineered features.
    
- Integration via fully connected layers for the final age prediction.
    

This design enables identification of developmentally salient features while maintaining the representational power of deep learning. Source code is available at [https://github.com/Healthink/ECG-age-predictor/](https://github.com/Healthink/ECG-age-predictor/).

### Model training

We partitioned the 58,672 pediatric ECGs into training (85%) and test (15%) sets. The training set was further subdivided into model training (80% of total data) and validation (5% of total data) subsets. To account for rapid cardiac development in children, both pediatric-specific models predicted age in months rather than years.

All models were trained on a workstation with an Intel Xeon W5-3423 processor, 128GB RAM, and NVIDIA RTX 4090D GPU. The feature-enhanced ECG-age model completed training in 3937.76 s (≈ 1 h and 5 min), demonstrating computational efficiency given model complexity.

### Internal evaluation

All models underwent internal evaluation using a dedicated test data set comprising 15% of the pediatric normal ECGs (_n_ = 8801). Supplementary Figure S3-S4 confirm matched age and sex distributions between training and test sets. Performance was assessed using:

- Pearson correlation (r).
    
- Coefficient of Determination (R2).
    
- Mean absolute error (MAE).
    

These metrics quantified both the linear relationship between predicted ECG-age and chronological age, and absolute prediction accuracy. These evaluation indicators were also used in the assessment of previous studies on adult ECG age models.

### External evaluation

To evaluate generalizability, the dedicated pediatric-specific ECG-Age model were test against the external Zhengzhou University dataset (_n_ = 584 normal ECGs from hospitalized children). This independent cohort served to validate model robustness beyond the primary institution.

### Exploring ECG-age utility in clinical practice

To investigate associations between ECG-age and pediatric diseases, we analyzed 209,644 clinical 12-lead ECGs with corresponding ICD-10 diagnostic codes. Additionally, 102,441 abnormal ECGs (defined by report interpretations) were examined to assess relationships with electrocardiographic abnormalities. This real-world dataset captured diverse diseases states, signal quality, demographics, and arrhythmias, enabling robust evaluation of ECG-age’s clinical applicability.

In order to explore the application of ECG-age in actual clinical scenarios, we collected ECG-age of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) children before and after the surgery and evaluated the association between the predicted ECG-age and the postoperative complications. Based on the statistical difference analysis between the two groups with and without postoperative complications, to determine whether ECG-age could be used as a biomarker for prediction postoperative complications.

## Results

### Performance of ECG-Age models in internal and external validations

As detailed in Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Tab1) and visualized in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Fig2) (a-e), model performance was rigorously evaluated across development phases. The pretrained model developed on adult populations proved entirely unsuitable for pediatric applications, exhibiting an unacceptably high MAE of 48.814 ± 26.644 years. In stark contrast, the pediatric-specific ECG age model markedly improved accuracy with an MAE of 8.395 ± 7.245 months, along with strong correlation (_r_ = 0.893), and goodness-of-fit (R2 = 0.793) between predicted ECG-age and chronological age.

Feature-enhanced model via Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) yielded further improvements, achieving the lowest MAE of 7.878 ± 6.658 months and highest correlation metrics (R2 = 0.821, _r_ = 0.908) among all tested approaches.

External validation using an independent pediatric cohrot confirmed model robustness as shown in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Fig2)f, maintaining clinically relevant accuracy (MAE = 9.87 ± 8.71 months) and strong correlation (_r_ = 0.843) despite a moderate decrease in explained variance (R² = 0.571). The slight increase in error might be due to the fact that all these independent data are from hospitalized children. This comprehensive validation demonstrates that pediatric-specific modeling reduces prediction error by approximately 60-fold compared to adult-derived models, with the RFE-optimized approach achieving the highest precision for tracking cardiac maturation in children.

### Interpretability of feature-enhanced ECG-age model

Interpretability analyses were performed on the feature-enhanced ECG-age model using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR18 "Lundberg, S. M. & Lee, S. I. A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (eds Guyon, I. et al.) 30, (Curran Associates, Inc., (2017).") and Score-CAM[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR19 "Wang, H. et al. IEEE,. Score-CAM: Score-Weighted Visual Explanations for Convolutional Neural Networks. in 2020 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW) 111–119 (2020). 
https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPRW50498.2020.00020") techniques to elucidate the contributions of the eight RFE-selected features and underlying ECG waveforms. As illustrated in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Fig3), atrial rate emerged as the most influential feature, with elevated rates correlating inversely with predicted ECG-age, reflecting the natural decline in heart rate during childhood development. Conversely, prolongation of QT and PR intervals showed positive associations with higher ECG-age predictions. The model demonstrated divergent patterns for depolarization and repolarization metrics: QRS complex widening (indicating prolonged ventricular depolarization) predicted increased ECG-age, while T-wave widening (reflecting slower ventricular repolarization) paradoxically corresponded with younger predictions. Morphological features revealed clinically coherent patterns, with heightened R-wave amplitude in V1 – characteristic of pediatric cardiac anatomy due to thinner chest walls and ventricular dominance patterns – being appropriately recognized. However, different results were given in the analysis of S-waves. The reason might be that the R/S ratio in V1 proved particularly informative, capturing the physiological transition from right to left ventricular dominance during maturation. Technical factors were also incorporated, as ECG quality scores were inversely related to predicted age – a finding consistent with the practical challenge of obtaining clean tracings in uncooperative infants. Complementary waveform analysis via Score-CAM heatmaps, though not providing discrete feature explanations, consistently highlighted QRS complexes and T-waves as focal regions for age prediction, with illustrative examples available in supplemental materials. Collectively, these interpretability methods demonstrate the model’s ability to extract physiologically meaningful patterns from pediatric ECGs while accounting for technical acquisition factors.

### Associations between ECG-Age and pediatric disease

Previous studies have demonstrated a clear association between ECG-age and cardiovascular health. The Framingham Heart Study found that in community-dwelling people, the risk of death, infarction, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure increased when the ECG age was found to be older than the actual age[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR12 "Brant, L. C. C. et al. Association between electrocardiographic age and cardiovascular events in community settings: the Framingham heart study. Circ Cardiovasc. Qual. Outcomes 16, (2023)."). Attia et al. discovered that individuals whose ECG age was 7 years older than their actual age had a greater risk of low ejection fraction, hypertension, and coronary heart disease[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR7 "Attia, Z. I. et al. Age and sex Estimation using artificial intelligence from standard 12-Lead ECGs. Circ Arrhythmia Electrophysiol 12, (2019)."). Even with apparently normal ECGs, the estimated ECG-age gap from the chronological age remains a statistically significant mortality risk predictor[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR11 "Lima, E. M. et al. Deep neural network-estimated electrocardiographic age as a mortality predictor. Nat. Commun. 12, 5117 (2021)."). However, there is a lack of evidence to support whether this correlation holds true in children, when the heart is developing and maturing.

This study investigated disease association using 209,644 ECGs from children under 84 months, categorizing diagnoses into 21 ICD-10 chapters. As shown in Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Tab2) and visualized in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Fig4)a and supplementary Figure S5a, most disease states exhibited a distinct pattern of lower predicted ECG-age relative to chronological age. This phenomenon is largely attributable to elevated heart rates in common pediatric conditions such as fever and pain, where each 1 °C temperature increase elevates heart rate by approximately 10 bpm[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR20 "Davies, P. & I, M. The relationship between body temperature, heart rate and respiratory rate in children. Emerg. Med. J. 26, 641–643 (2009)."). Given the inverse relationship between heart rate and ECG-age established in our model, such physiological responses naturally bias predictions toward younger values. Notable exceptions emerged in neoplasms (II), diseases of the circulatory system (IX) and certain conditions originating in the perinatal period (XVI), which demonstrated older ECG-age predictions. The discrepancy in neoplasm patients likely reflects treatment-related cardiotoxicity (e.g., anthracycline-induced QTc prolongation and T-wave abnormalities), while circulatory diseases directly alter cardiac development and electrophysiology. The obvious unbalanced distribution of ECG age in class XVI (certain conditions originating in the perinatal period) and XV (pregnancy, childbirth and the puerperium) is because the neonatal period is on the verge of age prediction. Another outlier class is injury, poisoning and certain other consequences of external causes (XIX) which showed younger predictions consistent with stress-induced tachycardia. Most significantly, the external causes of morbidity and mortality (XX) exhibited the largest MAE with a pronounced skew toward elder ECG age predictions, suggesting this gap may serve as a biomarker for critical illness severity in pediatric populations. These findings collectively demonstrate that ECG-age deviations reflect both physiological responses to common childhood illnesses and pathological cardiac alterations in specific disease states.

### Associations between ECG-Age and ECG abnormalities

Analysis of 102,441 ECGs labelled with 20 common ECG abnormalities revealed distinct patterns in ECG-age prediction accuracy relate to normal pediatric tracings. As demonstrated in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Fig4)b, supplementary Figure S5b and Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Tab3), all abnormality groups exhibited larger prediction errors compare compared to normal ECGs, consistent with disease-associated patterns observed earlier. While, by comparing Figure S5a and S5b in supplemental material, the distribution of prediction errors showed a notable increase in cases where ECG-age exceeded chronological age among children with abnormalities. There are two examples, sinus bradycardia (SBRAD), which is mainly characterized by a slowing of the heart rhythm, and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), which represents a higher wall thickness of the left ventricle than at the same age. These two pathologic changes also correspond to physiological changes in the development and maturation of the heart in children (some ECG samples with Score-CAM heatmap were shown in the supplemental material). Conversely, sinus tachycardia (STACH) consistently yielded younger predictions due to its characteristic heart rate elevation, while right-axis deviation (RAD) – a finding that may be physiological in infants but pathological in older children – similarly skewed toward younger ECG-age values, demonstrating the model’s ability to capture developmentally appropriate electrophysiological patterns. The most substantial prediction errors emerged in groups with prolonged QT interval (LNGQT), ventricular preexcitation (WPW), and intraventricular conduction block (ICB), reflecting the additional complexity these severe conduction abnormalities introduce to age estimation. Importantly, these findings suggest that significant discrepancies between predicted ECG-age and chronological age may serve as indicators of underlying rhythm disturbances, with larger gaps potentially signaling more serious electrophysiological pathology in pediatric patients.

### ECG-age as a prognostic index for tetralogy of fallot repair

To evaluation whether ECG-age could enhance CHD surgical assessment beyond chronological age, we applied our model to 570 perioperative ECGs from 176 children undergoing TOF repair (rTOF) —a representative congenital heart surgery where age traditionally informs intervention timing. While most TOF patients survive initial repair, many develop post-operative complications.

As shown in Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#Tab4), Our analysis revealed that preoperative ECG-age predictions showed a mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.81 ± 9.38 months. Postoperatively, we observed a clinically significant divergence: the complication group demonstrated increased ΔAge (16.51 ± 12.45 months), while the non-complication group showed improved accuracy (9.96 ± 7.94 months). There was a statistically significant difference in postoperative ECG-age (_p_ = 0.001) as well as ΔAge (_p_ = 0.013) in patients with/without postoperative complications. When ΔAge > 16.51 months, the positive predictive value of postoperative complications reaches 83.33% (30 true positive cases in total 36 cases). These findings indicate that ECG-age not only reflects preoperative cardiac maturation status but also serves as a quantitative index of postoperative recovery, potentially offering superior prognostic insight compared to chronological age alone for managing rTOF patients.

## Discussion

### ECG AI model applicability in children

ECG presents an ideal substrate for AI applications due to its low-cost, widespread availability, reproducibility, and digital format suitability[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR21 "Siontis, K. C., Noseworthy, P. A., Attia, Z. I. & Friedman, P. A. Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography in cardiovascular disease management. Nat. Rev. Cardiol. 18, 465–478 (2021)."). While AI-enhanced ECG analysis has demonstrated capability in detecting subtle patterns imperceptible to human observers[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR22 "Adedinsewo, D. et al. Artificial Intelligence-Enabled ECG algorithm to identify patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction presenting to the emergency department with dyspnea. Circ Arrhythmia Electrophysiol 13, (2020)."),[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR23 "Galloway, C. D. et al. Development and validation of a Deep-Learning model to screen for hyperkalemia from the electrocardiogram. JAMA Cardiol. 4, 428 (2019)."),[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR24 "Kwon, J. et al. Artificial intelligence assessment for early detection and prediction of renal impairment using electrocardiography. Int. Urol. Nephrol. 54, 2733–2744 (2022)."), its applicability to pediatric populations has been largely overlooked. This is a critical gap, as ECGs undergo rapid developmental changes from birth through childhood, differing significantly from adult tracings. Our study addresses this by demonstrating that adult-derived ECG-age models are unsuitable for children, while a model specifically trained on pediatric data achieves substantially greater accuracy (MAE = 7.88 months vs. 8.38 years in adults[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-38704-3#ref-CR11 "Lima, E. M. et al. Deep neural network-estimated electrocardiographic age as a mortality predictor. Nat. Commun. 12, 5117 (2021)."). The enhanced accuracy in children ECG age is physiologically grounded, primarily reflecting age-dependent decreases in heart rate due to autonomic nervous system maturation, increased cardiac size, and stroke volume. Feature selection consistently prioritized heart rate parameters (especially atrial rate) and QT interval duration, with R- and S-wave amplitudes also contributing—aligning with known developmental electrophysiology. This finding suggests a broader need for age-tailored development and validation of ECG-AI tools. The interpretability of the model can also assist in identifying and reducing the risk of such AI models being incompatible. Crucially, the balance between model performance and interpretability depends on the clinical context: high-stakes applications necessitate intrinsic interpretability or robust post-hoc explanations, while performance-critical tasks may tolerate less transparent models. Until sufficient interpretability is achieved, every ECG-AI model requires explicit definition of its intended population to ensure safe clinical application, underscoring the importance of pediatric-specific models like the one presented here.

### Clinical applications and implementation considerations of pediatric ECG-age

The demonstrated accuracy of our pediatric ECG-age model supports its utility as a biomarker for assessing cardiac development during routine health screenings. Notably, observed discrepancies between ECG-age and chronological age across various pediatric conditions reveal distinct patterns: unlike adults where accelerated ECG-age typically indicates pathology, pediatric cases often show younger ECG-age predictions. This divergence may reflect delayed cardiac maturation relative to healthy peers, with significant implications for clinical decision-making. Given that chronological age guides critical interventions like surgical timing in congenital heart disease, ECG-age offers a physiologically grounded alternative for assessing cardiac development status. Our findings specifically demonstrate its prognostic value in TOFr outcomes, though multicenter validation remains essential before standalone clinical deployment. The technique’s non-invasive nature and low resource requirements make it particularly promising for improving pediatric cardiac assessment in resource-limited settings.

Implementation pathways include integration into ECG interpretation systems to flag significant age discrepancies automatically, alerting clinicians to potential developmental delays or occult conditions. However, deploying such AI tools in pediatric care introduces complex challenges: heightened regulatory scrutiny requires rigorous validation across diverse populations and pathologies; liability frameworks must address diagnostic accountability given pediatric ECG variability; and workflow integration necessitates careful design to maintain clinician oversight while avoiding protocol disruption. Equitable access, pediatric data privacy, and prevention of algorithmic over-reliance demand robust governance structures with ongoing performance monitoring.

### Limitations

Several important limitations warrant consideration. First, while the ECG-Age model was externally validated, all training data and clinical correlation analyses originated from a single center. This restricts generalizability across diverse populations, ECG acquisition technologies, and sampling frequencies. To facilitate broader validation, we have made the relevant code and pre-trained model publicly available at [https://github.com/Healthink/ECG-age-predictor/](https://github.com/Healthink/ECG-age-predictor/). Second, reliance on real-world clinical data introduces inherent noise from suboptimal ECG signals, potential annotation inconsistencies, and diagnostic variability that may impact model performance and clinical associations. Further investigations targeting specific clinical questions will require carefully curated datasets. Finally, current post-hoc interpretability methods remain insufficient to fully elucidate the model’s decision-making processes or extract clinically actionable rule-based knowledge, presenting barriers to clinical translation in pediatric cardiology. These limitations underscore the need for rigorous multicenter validation and enhanced interpretability frameworks before widespread clinical implementation.

## Conclusion

The development of clinically applicable ECG AI models necessitates deliberate age stratification, as demonstrated by the fundamental physiological differences between pediatric and adult electrocardiograms. Our findings establish that adult-derived ECG-age models are unsuitable for pediatric applications, while dedicated pediatric models show significant promise as quantitative biomarkers for cardiac maturation. These pediatric-specific models not only achieve substantially higher accuracy (MAE = 7.88 months) than their adult counterparts but also demonstrate clinical utility in detecting developmental deviations associated with various health conditions. Crucially, in numerous clinical scenarios – particularly those involving cardiac surgical timing decisions or prognostic assessments after interventions like TOFr repair – ECG-age may serve as a superior indicator of true cardiac development status compared to chronological age. Future work should prioritize multicenter validation across diverse populations, enhanced model interpretability, and exploration of specific clinical correlations to realize the full potential of this accessible, low-cost technology in pediatric cardiology.
```
##### [A large language model for complex cardiology care](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9)

```
## Abstract

The scarcity of subspecialist medical expertise poses a considerable challenge for healthcare delivery. This issue is particularly acute in cardiology, where timely, accurate management determines outcomes. We explored the potential of Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE), a large language model-based experimental medical artificial intelligence system, to augment clinical decision-making in this challenging context. We conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing large language model-assisted care with the usual care of complex patients suspected of having a genetic cardiomyopathy, and we curated a real-world dataset of complex cases from a subspecialist cardiology practice. Nine participating general cardiologists were provided with access to both clinical text reports and raw diagnostic data—including electrocardiograms, echocardiograms, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging scans and cardiopulmonary exercise testing—and were randomized to manage these cases, either with or without assistance from AMIE. We developed a ten-domain evaluation rubric used by three blinded subspecialists to evaluate the quality of triage, diagnosis and management. In our randomized controlled trial with retrospective patient data, subspecialists favored large language model-assisted responses overall, and for the management plan and diagnostic testing domains, with the remaining domains considered a tie. Overall, subspecialists preferred AMIE-assisted cardiology assessments 46.7% of the time, compared with 32.7% for cardiologists alone (_P_ = 0.02), with 20.6% rated as a tie. Subspecialists also quantified errors, extra and missing content, reasoning and potential bias. Cardiologists alone had more clinically significant errors (24.3% versus 13.1%, _P_ = 0.033) and more missing content (37.4% versus 17.8%, _P_ = 0.0021) than cardiologists assisted by AMIE. Lastly, cardiologists who used AMIE reported that AMIE helped their assessment more than half the time (57.0%) and saved time in 50.5% of cases.

## Main

Globally, there is a substantial shortage of specialized medical expertise[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR1 "Health Workforce Requirements for Universal Health Coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. Human Resources for Health Observer Series No. 17 (World Health Organization, 2016)."). The World Health Organization predicts a deficit of 18 million providers by 2030, with shortages being most acute in resource-limited and rural areas[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR2 "Charlton, M., Schlichting, J., Chioreso, C., Ward, M. & Vikas, P. Challenges of rural cancer care in the united states. Oncology (Williston Park) 29, 633–640 (2015)."). This disparity is exacerbated for rarer and more complex conditions, particularly those for which timely treatment prevents morbidity and mortality. For instance, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is one of the leading causes of sudden cardiac death in young adults[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR3 "Writing Committee Members et al. 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: a report of the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines. JACC CardioOncol. 83, 2324–2405 (2024)."), yet more than half of US states do not have an HCM subspecialist center[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR4 "HCMA recognized centers of excellence. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Association 
https://4hcm.org/center-of-excellence/
(2024)."). This lack of subspecialist access has led to 60% of patients with HCM being undiagnosed in the USA[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR5 "Massera, D., Sherrid, M. V., Maron, M. S., Rowin, E. J. & Maron, B. J. How common is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy… really?: disease prevalence revisited 27 years after cardia. Int. J. Cardiol. 382, 64–67 (2023)."). Given that premature mortality is highly preventable with implanted cardiac defibrillators[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR3 "Writing Committee Members et al. 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: a report of the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines. JACC CardioOncol. 83, 2324–2405 (2024)."), cardiac conditions such as HCM exemplify an urgent unmet need in healthcare delivery, namely timely and widely available access to subspecialist expertise[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR6 "Maddox, T. M., Fry, Edward T. A. & Wilson, B. H. The cardiovascular workforce crisis: navigating the present, planning for the future. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 83, 466–469 (2024)."). While cardiac conditions serve as an indicative example, the consequences of delayed access to subspecialist care are profound across all specialties, often resulting in increased morbidity and mortality, as patients miss critical diagnostic and treatment windows. Navigating the cascade of referrals required to access subspecialist expertise creates undue stress and anxiety while presenting a time-consuming and resource-intensive process for both patients and healthcare providers.

Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential assistive tools for an array of healthcare issues[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR7 "Clusmann, J. et al. The future landscape of large language models in medicine. Commun. Med. 3, 141 (2023)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR8 "Van Veen, D. et al. Adapted large language models can outperform medical experts in clinical text summarization. Nat. Med. 30, 1134–1142 (2024)."). LLMs can rapidly synthesize data from multiple sources and suggest differential diagnoses and management plans[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR9 "Tu, T. et al. Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence. Nature 642, 442–450 (2025)."),[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR10 "McDuff, D. et al. Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models. Nature 642, 451–457 (2025)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR11 "Saab, K. et al. Capabilities of gemini models in medicine. Preprint at 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18416
(2024)."). Some LLMs have already been integrated into electronic medical record software[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR12 "Jennings, K. Why $4.6 billion health records giant epic is betting big on generative AI. Forbes (18 March 2024)."),[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR13 "Turner, B. E. W. Epic, microsoft bring GPT-4 to EHRs. Modern Healthcare (17 April 2023).") as assistive tools for summarization and communication. Despite the potential of LLMs to enhance medical expertise, rigorous assessment of their performance remains scarce in medical specialties, with few openly available datasets for model evaluation and almost no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) performed. It remains unclear whether LLMs possess the nuanced understanding and intricate knowledge base required to effectively replicate the decision-making process of experts in highly specialized medical fields[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR14 "Hager, P. et al. Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making. Nat. Med. 30, 2613–2622 (2024).").

This study probes the potential of LLMs to democratize subspecialist-level expertise by focusing on an indicative example: the domain of genetic cardiomyopathies like HCM. We conducted an RCT in which cardiologists clinically assessed patients using comprehensive real-world clinical data with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance. This included both physician text reports and data for electrocardiograms (ECGs), transthoracic echocardiograms (TTEs), cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) scans and cardiopulmonary stress tests (CPX). Compared to earlier studies relying on simulated or text-only data, our design represents a substantial advancement toward real-world clinical applicability. We introduce an open-source dataset encompassing cardiac testing and genetic information from real-world patients at the Stanford Center for Inherited Cardiovascular Disease (SCICD), enabling further research in this specialized field. We use Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE)[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR9 "Tu, T. et al. Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence. Nature 642, 442–450 (2025)."), an LLM-based system built upon Gemini 2.0 Flash, to generate detailed assessments of patients with suspected complex cardiovascular disease. We propose detailed rubrics that subspecialists used to compare and evaluate the quality of diagnosis, triage and clinical management proposals for complex cardiology cases. Finally, we explore the potential of LLMs to upskill general cardiologists by evaluating whether interaction with AMIE improves their clinical decision-making. In our RCT, general cardiologists’ clinical assessments aided by AMIE were preferred overall, saved time in 50.5% of cases and had fewer clinically significant errors and fewer omissions of important content.

## Results

Figure [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig1) shows the study overview in which 107 consecutive patients were assessed by two general cardiologists, one with and one without AMIE assistance, using the interface shown in Extended Data Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig4). Details of the AMIE system are presented in Supplementary Section [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1).

The median age of the patients was 59 years (range 18–96 years). The number and percentage of patients with available clinical text data for each test were as follows: CMR 64 (59.8%), CPX 65 (60.7%), resting TTE 90 (84.1%), exercise TTE 69 (64.5%), ECG 99 (92.5%), ambulatory Holter monitor 79 (73.8%) and genetic testing 77 (72.0%) (Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Tab1)). Of the 107 patients, 39 (36.4%) had a variant adjudicated to be pathogenic or likely pathogenic as per the interpretation of variant criteria by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR15 "Richards, S. et al. Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants: a joint consensus recommendation of the american college of medical genetics and genomics and the association for molecular pathology. Genet. Med. 17, 405–423 (2015).").

### General cardiologists’ perspectives on LLM use in clinical care

As shown in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig2), general cardiologists responding to the questions in Extended Data Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig5) expressed a favorable view of LLM integration into their clinical workflows. In a majority (57.0%) of cases, cardiologists reported that the AI improved their clinical assessments (16.8% “definitely” and 40.2% “probably”), while only 12.1% indicated it was unlikely to be helpful. Similarly, in 52.3% of cases, the general cardiologists stated that the AI increased their confidence in decision-making (15.9% “definitely” and 36.4% “probably”), while only 14.9% reported any decrease in confidence. With respect to efficiency, the general cardiologists indicated time savings by the AI in 50.5% of cases; notably, they reported saving more than 50% of their time in 23.4% of these cases. Only 18.7% of the cases noted any delays attributable to AI use, and the incidence of AI hallucinations was low. In 91.6% of cases, there were no reported hallucinations, while in 6.5% of cases, a likely clinically significant hallucination was observed. Similarly, in 93.5% of cases, the general cardiologists reported that the LLM did not miss anything (Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig2)). Supplementary Section [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1) presents the results for each cardiologist, and we further analyzed the free-text comments left by the general cardiologists in ‘Analysis of general cardiologist feedback’.

### Direct preference comparing general cardiologists with and without AMIE

A blinded evaluation by subspecialist cardiologists, responding to the questions in Extended Data Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig6), demonstrated a consistent pattern favoring LLM-assisted responses across several key clinical domains. For the entire clinical response, AMIE-assisted outputs were significantly preferred, with subspecialists preferring 46.7% of all cases compared to 32.7% for unassisted cardiologists (_P_ = 0.02). For overall management, AMIE-assisted assessments were preferred for 45.8% of the cases compared to 29.9% for unassisted cardiologists (_P_ = 0.008). Similarly, for the diagnosis domain related to further testing, AMIE-assisted responses were preferred for 43.9% of the cases compared with 30.8% for the unassisted (_P_ = 0.03). General cardiologist responses alone were not preferred across any of the domains, although their responses were considered equivalent to the AMIE-assisted responses across the remaining domains, including consult question, triage, diagnosis and further diagnostic questions for the patient (Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig3)).

### Individual assessment of general cardiologists’ responses with and without AMIE

The subspecialist cardiologists found that AMIE-assisted responses were either better or equivalent across clinically significant errors, extra content, missing content, clinical reasoning and bias.

The subspecialists also found that AMIE-assisted general cardiologist responses had significantly fewer errors: 13.1% of AMIE-assisted responses contained errors compared with 24.3% for unassisted responses (11.2% difference, _P_ = 0.033). Similarly, there was significantly less missing content for AMIE-assisted responses: 17.8%, compared with 37.4% for unassisted responses (19.6% difference, _P_ = 0.0021). There was no statistically significant difference in extra content between the responses, and both responses contained equivalent clinical reasoning steps and a lack of demographic bias (Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig3)). The ‘Analysis of specialist feedback’ section shows an analysis of the free-text comments left by the subspecialists.

### Qualitative analysis

In Extended Data Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#Fig7), we provide an example of AMIE’s standalone assessment. We also include several examples of how general cardiologists chose to interact with AMIE to aid in the production of their final assessments in Supplementary Section [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1). These interactions with AMIE ranged from targeted querying for specific knowledge to more extensive engagement to work through disparate test results and build arguments for and against potential diagnoses and management plans.

During the study, general cardiologists were asked to provide comments on their use of AMIE, while subspecialists left comments on the quality of AI-assisted and unassisted cardiologist assessments. In addition to having a subspecialist cardiologist summarize this feedback, we used Gemini 2.5 Pro to analyze the feedback from the general cardiologists (summary in ‘Analysis of general cardiologist feedback’, automated report in Supplementary Section [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1)) and subspecialists (summary in ‘Analysis of specialist feedback’, automated report in Supplementary Section [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1)).

#### Analysis of general cardiologist feedback

The general cardiologists provided additional comments regarding their AI use for 41 out of the 107 cases. We used Gemini 2.5 Pro to categorize and summarize this feedback, with the prompt and full generated report shown in Supplementary Section [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1). The described benefits include providing detailed information on rare conditions, provoking critical thinking and reconsideration of initial assessments, and saving time. Observed errors include the AI outputs being overly verbose, overconfident and/or dogmatic and occasionally lacking clinical nuance, and the inability to interpret temporal data properly.

The general cardiologists also documented instances of LLM hallucinations across eight cases, which fell into several categories: diagnostic assertions that contradicted the general cardiologist’s opinions, fabrication of imaging findings absent from source reports (for example, ‘left ventricular hypertrabeculation’), unwarranted assumptions regarding patient demographics, such as gender when such information was not provided, and misinterpretation of quantitative measurements, including confusion between exercise and resting aortic parameters. The identified errors ranged from subtle misinterpretations to more significant hallucinations, wherein AMIE generated medical information unsupported by the original text-imaging reports. Notably, these hallucinations were often amenable to correction when challenged by the cardiologists. For instance, when AMIE initially fabricated the presence of left ventricular hypertrabeculation, direct questioning by the general cardiologist prompted the system to self-correct and acknowledge that no abnormal trabeculation was present in the imaging report data.

The general cardiologists provided qualitative feedback on seven examples where the LLM missed clinical information (‘omissions’). These comments highlighted AMIE’s tendency to sometimes overlook or inadequately process existing diagnostic information, including failing to recognize that CMR and stress echocardiography had already been completed, providing insufficient detail about important findings such as regional wall motion abnormalities and trabeculations on echo, and missing critical historical information such as prior myocardial infarction mentioned in stress tests. Certain omissions resulted from AMIE’s lack of access to imaging test dates, leading to erroneous clinical interpretations. For instance, AMIE incorrectly concluded that discrepancies existed between left ventricular ejection fraction measurements obtained via CMR and TTE, asserting that one dataset contained errors. However, chart review by the general cardiologists revealed that both left ventricular ejection fraction measurements were accurate, with the apparent discrepancy attributable to a therapeutic intervention that occurred between the two studies—information that was not accessible to AMIE. Lastly, AMIE made redundant recommendations for tests already completed (such as ambulatory event monitoring). Overall, omissions were considered mild and minimal, in line with systematic quantitative feedback that showed AMIE did not miss anything in 93.4% of cases.

#### Analysis of specialist feedback

The subspecialist cardiologists provided 138 comments regarding their preference ratings between the assisted and unassisted responses, spanning 43 of the 107 cases. They also left specific comments on 55 of the 107 assessments where cardiologists had AMIE assistance and 69 of the 107 assessments without assistance, giving a total of 184 informative comments across the individual assessments. We used Gemini 2.5 Pro to categorize and summarize this feedback, with the prompt and full generated report shown in Supplementary Section [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#MOESM1).

In summary, the AI-assisted cardiologists were preferred more often, seemingly driven by their more comprehensive responses, fewer omissions and incorporation of modern diagnostics and advanced treatments. However, some responses were also flagged due to excessive detail, diagnostic overreach and occasional leaps in logic. The unassisted cardiologists were often praised for clear and concise reasoning but tended to have clinically significant omissions and errors related to key management decisions. Many of the cited types of errors, such as missing and/or incorrect diagnoses or screening and/or testing errors, were seen with similar frequencies in both study arms, suggesting that AI assistance did not have a consistent impact in those areas.

## Discussion

In this study, we probe the ability of LLMs to provide additive support to generalists in the assessment of rare, life-threatening cardiac diseases that typically require subspecialty cardiac care. Further, we address the unmet need for the randomized evaluation of LLMs for challenging medical applications. To this end, we curate an open-source, de-identified, real-world clinical dataset for patients suspected to have inherited cardiomyopathies and propose an evaluation rubric for the quality of diagnosis, triage and clinical management of such patients. Blinded subspecialists employed this evaluation rubric to assess clinical assessments performed by general cardiologists, both with and without LLM assistance. The blinded evaluation by the subspecialist cardiologists demonstrated an overall preference for LLM-assisted clinical assessments. Specifically, the subspecialty cardiologists found that AMIE-assisted clinical assessments demonstrated fewer clinically significant errors (11.2% reduction) and missed less important content (19.6% reduction) while maintaining equivalent clinical reasoning quality and not introducing erroneous extraneous information. Furthermore, general cardiologists who utilized AMIE reported that the system helped their assessments in more than half of cases (57.0%), did not miss clinically significant findings in 93.5% of cases and reduced assessment time in over half of cases (50.5%).

Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using LLMs to assess patients with rare and life-threatening cardiac conditions. Adapting AMIE to this subspecialist and rarified domain was highly data-efficient, leveraging iterative feedback from subspecialist experts to enhance the quality of AMIE’s responses using just nine cases. This iterative process, combined with a self-critique and the incorporation of search functionality, enabled AMIE to assist general cardiologists in upskilling their clinical assessments to a preferred level. This contrasts with earlier studies using generic, nonspecialized LLMs, which did not achieve comparable clinical performance[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR14 "Hager, P. et al. Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making. Nat. Med. 30, 2613–2622 (2024).").

Our RCT results indicate that LLMs can assist general cardiologists in diagnosing and managing complex cardiac patients. Our evidence suggests that LLMs could help bridge unmet needs in genetic cardiovascular disease and possibly in cardiac care more broadly. While further research could extrapolate our approach to a broader group of specialties, cardiology is a useful indicative example because it features (a) highly preventable morbidity and mortality, (b) a reliance on an array of clinical investigations (for example, TTEs, ECGs, ambulatory Holter monitors, CMRs, CPXs and, when appropriate, genetic testing) and (c) a substantial deficit in the cardiology workforce. Our findings are particularly noteworthy because access to subspecialist care is a global challenge. The American College of Cardiology has identified a "cardiology workforce crisis," with the lack of access to subspecialty cardiologists an acute concern[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR6 "Maddox, T. M., Fry, Edward T. A. & Wilson, B. H. The cardiovascular workforce crisis: navigating the present, planning for the future. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 83, 466–469 (2024)."). In the USA, despite five HCM centers of excellence in both California and New York, there are none across 27 states[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR4 "HCMA recognized centers of excellence. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Association 
https://4hcm.org/center-of-excellence/
(2024)."). This has led to more than 60% of patients with HCM in the USA being undiagnosed, with estimates higher globally[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR5 "Massera, D., Sherrid, M. V., Maron, M. S., Rowin, E. J. & Maron, B. J. How common is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy… really?: disease prevalence revisited 27 years after cardia. Int. J. Cardiol. 382, 64–67 (2023)."). The propensity of inherited cardiomyopathy to cause sudden cardiac death (the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR3 "Writing Committee Members et al. 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: a report of the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines. JACC CardioOncol. 83, 2324–2405 (2024).")), exacerbates the problem. Lack of access to appropriate care and long wait times can lead to preventable, premature mortality. LLMs may help identify undiagnosed cases, assist with the triage and prioritization of urgent cases, and streamline management. In this way, LLMs could improve access to specific care by assisting generalists.

For researchers, our results have a number of implications. First, we have made our data openly available, facilitating the rigorous evaluation of our results and providing data for other models to use in their tests. We have also created and validated a 10-domain evaluation rubric that may be used for future studies. More broadly, this study demonstrates the feasibility of conducting RCTs to evaluate LLMs, establishing a gold-standard evidence framework that should guide future research in this domain. Currently, LLMs are being used in many US health systems via their implementation in electronic medical records software[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR13 "Turner, B. E. W. Epic, microsoft bring GPT-4 to EHRs. Modern Healthcare (17 April 2023)."). This implementation has occurred without a similar scale of scientific evaluation; the benefits and the possible harms are only partially known[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR16 "Schoonbeek, R. et al. Completeness, correctness and conciseness of physician-written versus large language model generated patient summaries integrated in electronic health records. Preprint at SSRN 
https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4835935
(2024)."). These results represent a major step toward demonstrating the real-world utility of LLMs in subspecialty care.

The implications for clinicians are twofold. First, our results show a clear, albeit modest, improvement in overall clinical assessment quality. The significantly fewer errors and extra content, as well as the significant improvement in management plan quality, gives insights into how LLMs can assist clinically. The general cardiologists demonstrated high precision in diagnostic accuracy and triage decisions; however, the nuanced clinical management of complex patients was associated with increased omission errors compared to the AMIE-assisted assessments. These clinical improvements were accompanied by enhanced efficiency and increased clinician confidence. As such, we present RCT-level evidence for LLMs improving clinical care overall, specifically driven by improvements in management and a reduction in clinical errors and erroneous extra content, with simultaneous improvements in the time and confidence of providers.

It seems premature to deploy LLMs autonomously, and our RCT did not address this design directly, as general cardiologists reported that 6.5% of AMIE’s responses contained clinically significant hallucinations. Reassuringly, we showed that when LLMs are deployed with cardiologist oversight, hallucinations are most often identified, and this combination results in overall fewer errors and more preferred assessments. We qualitatively explored the nature of these hallucinations and found that the general cardiologists often described them as ‘mild’, ranging from assuming the patient’s sex to hallucinating the presence of a CMR feature (for example, “LLM stated left ventricular hypertrabeculation on CMR, but this is not explicitly stated”). Notably, the general cardiologists found that when asked about the hallucination, AMIE would correct itself.

Our study addresses a meaningful wider gap in earlier literature. Prior research has evaluated LLMs in a number of different settings in medicine, from assessing quality in question-answering (spanning medical license examinations as well as open-ended medical questions) to clinical image and complex diagnostic challenges[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR11 "Saab, K. et al. Capabilities of gemini models in medicine. Preprint at 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18416
(2024)."),[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR17 "Singhal, K. et al. Large language models encode clinical knowledge. Nature 620, 172–180 (2023)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR18 "Eriksen, A. V., Möller, S. & Ryg, J. Use of GPT-4 to diagnose complex clinical cases. NEJM AI 1, AIp2300031 (2023)."),[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR19 "Nori, H. et al. Can generalist foundation models outcompete special-purpose tuning? Case study in medicine. Preprint at 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16452
(2023)."),[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR20 "Singhal, K. et al. Toward expert-level medical question answering with large language models. Nat. Med. 31, 943–950 (2025)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR21 "Yang, D. et al. PediatricsGPT: large language models as Chinese medical assistants for pediatric applications. Adv. Neural Inf. Process. Syst. 37, 138632–138662 (2024)."),[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR22 "Jin, Q. et al. Hidden flaws behind expert-level accuracy of multimodal GPT-4 vision in medicine. npj Digit. Med. 7, 190 (2024)."),[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR23 "Luk, D. W. A., Chin Tung Ip, W. & Shea, Y.-F. Performance of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 in generating accurate and comprehensive diagnoses across medical subspecialties. J. Chin. Med. Assoc. 87, 259–260 (2024)."),[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR24 "Katz, U. et al. GPT versus resident physicians–a benchmark based on official board scores. NEJM AI 1, AIdbp2300192 (2024)."). There is a paucity of prior RCTs in medicine and cardiology. Despite more than 500 observational LLM papers published in 2024, systematic reviews of LLMs in medicine have consistently shown a lack of RCTs[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR25 "Omar, M., Nadkarni, G. N., Klang, E. & Glicksberg, B. S. Large language models in medicine: a review of current clinical trials across healthcare applications. PLoS Digital Health 3, e0000662 (2024)."),[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR26 "Santos, J. F., Ladeiras-Lopes, R., Leite, F. & Dores, H. Applications of large language models in cardiovascular disease: a systematic review. Eur. Heart. J. Digit. Health 6, 540–553 (2025)."),[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR27 "Shool, S. et al. A systematic review of large language model (llm) evaluations in clinical medicine. BMC Med. Inform. Decis. Mak. 25, 117 (2025)."). In fact, a 2025 systematic review found no RCTs assessing LLMs in cardiology[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR26 "Santos, J. F., Ladeiras-Lopes, R., Leite, F. & Dores, H. Applications of large language models in cardiovascular disease: a systematic review. Eur. Heart. J. Digit. Health 6, 540–553 (2025)."), while another concluded that “randomized trials or prospective real-world evaluations are needed to establish the clinical utility and safety of model use” and that “real-world trials addressing this possibility remain sparse”[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR28 "Ahmed, M., Lam, J., Chow, A. & Chow, C.-M. A primer on large language models (LLMs) and ChatGPT for cardiovascular healthcare professionals. CJC Open 7, 660–666 (2025)."). Beyond cardiology, there are some RCTs exploring LLMs. A 2024 JAMA Network Open study[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR29 "Goh, E. et al. Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Netw. Open 7, e2440969 (2024).") randomized physicians to use GPT-4 versus conventional resources alone for diagnostic reasoning on just six non-real-world clinical vignettes and found no significant improvement in diagnostic performance (76% versus 74%, _P_ = 0.60), and no significant difference in time spent per case (519 versus 565 seconds, _P_ = 0.20), but that GPT-4 alone outperformed both physician groups by 16 percentage points (_P_ = 0.03). Similarly, a 2025 Nature Medicine RCT[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR30 "Goh, E. et al. GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks: a randomized controlled trial. Nat. Med. 31, 1233–1238 (2025); erratum 31, 1370 (2025).") randomized physicians to use GPT-4 versus conventional resources for management reasoning tasks on five expert-developed clinical vignettes and found significant improvements in overall performance (6.5% improvement, _P_ < 0.001), with management decisions improving by 6.1% and diagnostic decisions by 12.1%, demonstrating that LLMs may be more effective for treatment planning than initial diagnostic reasoning, in line with our results.

Observational studies have investigated the utility and potential of LLMs in real-world clinical tasks such as clinical letter generation[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR31 "Stephen, R. A., Dobbs, T. D., Hutchings, H. A. & Whitaker, I. S. Using ChatGPT to write patient clinic letters. Lancet Digit. Health 5, e179–e181 (2023)."), medical information communication[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR32 "Cox, A., Seth, I., Xie, Y., Hunter-Smith, D. J. & Rozen, W. M. Utilizing ChatGPT-4 for providing medical information on blepharoplasties to patients. Aesthet. Surg. J. 43, NP658–NP662 (2023)."), medical summarization[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR8 "Van Veen, D. et al. Adapted large language models can outperform medical experts in clinical text summarization. Nat. Med. 30, 1134–1142 (2024)."),[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR33 "Patel, S. B. & Lam, K. ChatGPT: the future of discharge summaries? Lancet Digit. Health 5, e107–e108 (2023).") and triaging mammograms and chest X-rays for tuberculosis[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR34 "Dvijotham, K. et al. Enhancing the reliability and accuracy of ai-enabled diagnosis via complementarity-driven deferral to clinicians. Nat. Med. 29, 1814–1820 (2023)."). Existing research on the performance of LLMs in medical subspecialties, such as cardiology[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR35 "Giannos, P. Evaluating the limits of AI in medical specialisation: ChatGPT’s performance on the UK Neurology Speciality Certificate Examination. BMJ Neurol. Open 5, e000451 (2023)."), ophthalmology[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR36 "Ka-Lok Tao, B., Hua, N., Milkovich, J. & Micieli, J. A. ChatGPT-3.5 and Bing Chat in ophthalmology: an updated evaluation of performance, readability, and informative sources. Eye (Lond.) 38, 1897–1902 (2024)."), gastroenterology[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR37 "Suchman, K., Garg, S. & Trindade, A. J. Chat generative pretrained transformer fails the multiple-choice American College of Gastroenterology self-assessment test. Am. J. Gastroenterol. 118, 2280–2282 (2023)."), neurology[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR35 "Giannos, P. Evaluating the limits of AI in medical specialisation: ChatGPT’s performance on the UK Neurology Speciality Certificate Examination. BMJ Neurol. Open 5, e000451 (2023).") and surgery[38](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR38 "Beaulieu-Jones, B. R. et al. Evaluating capabilities of large language models: performance of GPT-4 on surgical knowledge assessments. Surgery 175, 936–942 (2024)."), are also mostly limited to medical question-answering or examination benchmarking. A recent study[39](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04190-9#ref-CR39 "Chen, S. et al. Use of artificial intelligence chatbots for cancer treatment information. JAMA Oncol. 9, 1459–1462 (2023).") evaluated ChatGPT in providing accurate cancer treatment recommendations concordant with authoritative guidelines with fixed question prompts.
